This study addresses the challenge of determining eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for high-dimensional Schrödinger equations, a task that is often intractable analytically. To address this, we introduce the concept of "generalization error" within the context of neural network training. By employing a neural network to approximate eigenfunctions, we derive a corresponding "generalization mistake" that approximates the error in eigenvalue estimation. Utilizing a neural network framework, we demonstrate that the proposed generalization mistake for the eigenvalue estimation problem is equivalent to the prior generalization mistake of a two-layer neural network. This finding enables the application of existing theoretical results regarding two-layer neural networks to analyze the generalization mistake of our eigenvalue estimation approach. Furthermore, we illustrate the efficacy of this method through numerical experiments. Our results indicate that the proposed generalization mistake effectively quantifies the error in eigenvalue estimation, and that two-layer neural networks can accurately resolve eigenvalue problems in high-dimensional spaces. Additionally, we show that the two-layer neural network successfully recovers the ground state of the hydrogen atom. These contributions provide a novel perspective for analyzing the performance of neural networks in solving eigenvalue problems. Additionally, we show that RNNs can encode the required dynamics to generate sequences resembling those of the *C. elegans* strain. This study examines the equilibrium behavior of a two-dimensional Ising model featuring ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interactions and an antiferromagnetic two-body constraint that permits at most one up-spin within any triangle. We demonstrate that the constraint breaks translational symmetry, resulting in a mixed-spin woodland pattern where up and down spins coexist in a checkerboard-like arrangement. We establish the existence of a unique translation vector that defines the woodland's periodicity and calculate the constraint entropy per unit area for this periodic structure. Furthermore, we prove that the constraint entropy remains positive at all temperatures, indicating that the system avoids frustration. Finally, we derive an explicit formula for the constraint entropy and confirm its consistency with our numerical findings. These results are derived using the transfer-matrix method. Additionally, we show that the free energy per unit area is analytic at every temperature, implying the absence of phase transitions in this model. These findings align with the conjecture proposed by Guttmann and Enting regarding the absence of phase transitions in the Potts model with a constraint. The methodology employed here is also applicable to the Ising model with a star constraint, which allows at most one up-spin in any square. In that specific case, translational symmetry is not broken, and the model exhibits a phase transition at a critical temperature. This work also contributes to the ongoing debate concerning the existence of a phase transition in the Ising model with a triangle constraint. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the transfer-matrix method and the graph-theoretical approach introduced by Guttmann and Enting. The methodology used here is also relevant to the Ising model with a four-spin antiferromagnetic constraint, which allows at most one up-spin in any rectangle. In that scenario, translational symmetry is broken, and a phase transition occurs at a critical temperature. However, the transfer-matrix method becomes impractical for calculating the entropy of the ground state in that case due to the complexity of the constraint. We therefore propose a graph-theoretical approach to address this challenge. This paper is the first installment of a series; the subsequent work will present a graph-theoretical derivation of the Guttman-Enting conjecture. This paper demonstrates that any Zinbiel algebra $Z$ possesses a nilpotent derived series $(Z^{[n]})_{n\geq 1}$, thereby confirming that Zinbiel algebras are solvable. Additionally, we establish that every Zinbiel algebra is also nilpotent. Furthermore, we prove that any Zinbiel algebra whose Zinbiel constant $\alpha$ satisfies $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ contains no elements other than 0 is infinite-dimensional. Finally, we show that the Zinbiel constant of any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra must be a rational number. These findings extend analogous results previously established for dendriform algebras. However, we also identify key distinctions between Zinbiel and dendriform algebras, notably that Zinbiel algebras lack a bialgebra structure and are not necessarily pre-Lie algebras. The paper concludes by presenting several open questions. This study investigates the scattering theory for a three-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a cubic nonlinear term and an inverse-square potential. The nonlinear part of the equation is shown to be globally well-posed within the critical Sobolev space, which corresponds to the threshold for scattering. By employing a novel approach to scattering theory, we demonstrate that solutions asymptotically behave like free solutions. This method relies on a new potential scattering theory applicable to heterogeneous media, which is established in an appendix. Additionally, we establish the global well-posedness of this potential scattering theory across all relevant Sobolev spaces. A key component of our approach is the development of a novel Strichartz estimate tailored to this specific equation. This estimate is derived using a refined version of the radial Strichartz estimate, a technique that may hold independent interest. Finally, we provide an appendix detailing the proof of the radial Strichartz estimate. This appendix utilizes a representation of the Schrödinger propagator expressed through Bessel functions, originally developed by S. Jensen and A. Kiselev. We also present a new proof of this representation, offering a more direct argument compared to the original derivation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this representation remains valid in higher dimensions. Our findings are applicable to a broad class of potentials, including those that are not necessarily radial. Specifically, we prove the well-posedness of the potential nonlinear Schrödinger equation in the critical Sobolev space and establish the existence and uniqueness of scattering states. These results extend previous work by A. Golse-Foumer and F. Nier, who addressed the case of radial potentials. Our methodology is also expected to be applicable to other nonlinear equations involving inverse-square potentials. Finally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the relevant literature. This study examines a migration-transmission system where a source population feeds into a destination population through migration, while experiencing losses via extinction and mutation. The destination population subsequently undergoes transmission events, during which multiple copies of the genotype may be sent back to the source. We analyze the system's stationary behavior, deriving exact formulas for the extinction probability and the distribution of stationary source populations containing a specific number of distinct mutant types. Furthermore, we present and discuss approximate results for large population sizes and high mutation rates. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations. This framework is applicable to various domains, including evolutionary biology, information theory, and computer science. Specifically, it models the loss of information in evolutionary algorithms caused by genetic operators, as well as the potential recovery of genetic information through migration in genetic programming. Additionally, the model can represent the loss of information in social networks resulting from node deletions and edge failures, as well as the possibility of regaining such information via migration. Finally, we demonstrate that the model's applicability extends to scenarios involving the propagation of errors in data structures, such as the loss of information in a corrupted database, alongside the possibility of recovering that information through migration. These diverse applications underscore the model's broad utility. The results are detailed in the paper "Migration-Transmission Processes," which is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.03001. The interaction between the solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere generates low-frequency electromagnetic waves, known as ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves, which are detectable by ground-based magnetometers. This study employs a ULF wave model to determine the optimal frequency band for human auditory perception. By analyzing the spectrum of waves that reach the ionosphere, we identify the most prevalent frequencies. Subsequently, we evaluate various rendering techniques to ensure these ULF waves are audible. Our findings indicate that the most common ULF waves fall within the 0.5 to 2 Hz range. We conclude that the most effective method for rendering these waves is a combination of amplitude modulation and pitch variation. Furthermore, we propose that the most compelling audible representation of ULF waves occurs during geomagnetic storms, as these events produce waves with the highest amplitudes and the greatest frequency diversity. This approach offers a novel method for communicating space weather data to the general public. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ulw/ulf-audio. The minor-matrix groupoid (GP 2) is a string-diagrammatic language that is minor-equivalent to both the compact closed category and the symmetric monoidal category. This paper presents a string-diagrammatic operational semantics for GP 2, demonstrating that the category of string diagrams in which all parallel compositions are medially decomposable and all commutative squares are commutative is equivalent to the syntax of GP 2. This result establishes that the free object of this category is precisely the syntax of GP 2. Additionally, we prove that every morphism in GP 2 can be decomposed into a sequence of elementary morphisms, where each elementary morphism involves at most one pair of parallel composition. Consequently, the category of diagrams with a single pair of parallel composition is cofree over the syntax of GP 2. Furthermore, we show that the category of string diagrams where all parallel compositions are exactly medially decomposable and all commutative squares are commutative is monoidal closed, with GP 2 serving as the unit. Finally, we establish that GP 2 is minor-equivalent to both the symmetric monoidal category and the compact closed category. As a result, GP 2 acts as a cofree object for the category of string diagrams where all parallel compositions are medially decomposable and the commutative square axiom holds. This implies that any string diagram satisfying the medial axiom can be uniquely decomposed into a morphism from GP 2 and a string diagram representing the commutative square axiom. This paper extends the findings of [10] and [11]. The primary distinction lies in the fact that [10] and [11] relied on a free algebraic approach, whereas this work employs a string-diagrammatic approach. Furthermore, [10] and [11] did not address the equivalence between the syntax of GP 2 and the category of string diagrams with medially decomposable parallel compositions, nor did they establish the cofreeness of GP 2. This paper fills those gaps. The advantages of the string-diagrammatic approach over the algebraic approach are twofold: it provides a more direct proof of the equivalence between GP 2 and the symmetric monoidal category, and it enables the proof of cofreeness. The string-diagrammatic approach is also more natural, as it leverages the inherent structure of string diagrams. The photoevaporation model posits that stellar ultraviolet radiation carves out a cavity within a protoplanetary disk, creating a pressure gradient that drives gas escape. Conversely, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) models suggest that magnetic reconnection in the disk's upper layers can release gas. Both mechanisms predict that the escape flow should be most pronounced at the disk's outer edges. This study investigates the escape flow structure of the TW Hydrae disk using archival ALMA data, comparing findings against both theoretical models. We developed a novel method to derive the disk's escape flow structure from the spectral line data. Our results indicate that the flow is most significant at the outer disk edges, aligning with predictions from both the photoevaporation and MHD breeze frameworks. Furthermore, we determined that the flow velocity at the outer edges is approximately 1.5 km/s, while the flow structure at the inner edges remains ambiguous. Finally, we estimated the mass loss rate to be roughly $10^{-11}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr, a value consistent with prior studies. These findings suggest that the escape flow in TW Hydrae is likely driven by either photoevaporation or MHD processes, or a combination of both. Additionally, the measured mass loss rate is insufficient to account for the observed gas mass in the disk. These results offer valuable insights for interpreting the gas content of protoplanetary disks and for understanding the impact of disk escape on planet formation. Future observations of TW Hydrae with higher angular resolution and sensitivity are anticipated to provide further constraints on the escape flow structure. This approach offers a novel perspective on Chebyshev polynomials and establishes a foundation for further research into their properties and applications. This study examines the transient response of two-core symmetric phase-angle modulating transformers (PAMTs) subjected to direct-on-line (DOL) voltage transients. The analysis reveals that transients occurring in one core generate responses in the other core that are both qualitatively and quantitatively distinct. Specifically, the transients in the second core are significantly attenuated, typically by a factor of 100 or more. This inherent cross-core transient suppression is attributed to the magnetic coupling between the cores and the resulting cancellation of magnetomotive forces (MMFs). Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the transients in the second core are primarily driven by the MMFs produced by the secondary winding of the first core. These findings are validated through detailed finite element method (FEM) simulations. Additionally, the study proposes a novel approach to safeguard PAMTs against DOL transients by utilizing the second core as a dedicated transient suppressor. Finally, a new categorization scheme for PAMTs is introduced, distinguishing between single-use and dual-use modulating transformers based on their ability to suppress transients in a secondary core. This classification is supported by both FEM simulations and experimental data. The proposed method for mitigating transients and the new classification framework are expected to offer valuable guidance for the design of PAMTs. To facilitate these applications, the paper also provides a new analytical model for calculating PAMT transients. This model is derived from the MMF balance equation and is validated against FEM simulation results. The work concludes with a discussion on the model's limitations and potential areas for future research. Overall, this paper presents a comprehensive analysis of transients in two-core symmetric PAMTs, offering new insights and design methodologies for the field. It is anticipated to be a valuable resource for researchers and engineers working on PAMT transients. The findings are expected to advance the understanding of PAMT transient behavior and contribute to the development of more robust and efficient transformers for power electronic applications. The paper is particularly relevant to researchers and engineers engaged in the design and analysis of PAMTs, as well as those involved in the development of power electronic systems. The proposed methods for mitigating transients and the new PAMT categorization are likely to be of significant interest to this audience. The study also underscores the importance of considering cross-core transient suppression in PAMT design, a factor that has been largely overlooked in previous research. The paper is written in a clear and concise style, making it accessible to a broad audience of researchers and engineers

This paper introduces a hybrid encoding scheme designed for multi-group broadcasting within millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks. The primary objective is to enhance the robustness of mmWave signals against blockages and mitigate the high error rates caused by the narrow beams characteristic of mmWave technology. The proposed method leverages the complementary strengths of sub-THz and mmWave frequencies, alongside analog and digital beamforming, to achieve this. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the hybrid encoding approach significantly boosts robustness, thereby reducing the probability of groupcast errors. Furthermore, the method maintains low latency and high data rates, ensuring that performance remains comparable to conventional digital beamforming when line-of-sight (LoS) links are available. These findings confirm the scheme's effectiveness for multi-group broadcasting in mmWave environments. A group with an exponentially expanding Cayley graph is known to have a sub-exponential expansion for its $n$-th power. Conversely, we demonstrate that for any function $f(n)$ growing faster than linearly, there exist two groups, $G$ and $H$, whose Cayley graphs exhibit expansion rates closely approximating the bounds established by the $n$-th power expansion theorem. Specifically, the expansion of the Cayley graph for $G$ never surpasses $2^n$, whereas the expansion for $H$ is guaranteed to be at least $f(n)$. Furthermore, we establish that within the class of finitely presented groups, such groups $H$ can be constructed such that their Cayley graphs maintain expansion rates arbitrarily close to the lower bound dictated by the $n$-th power expansion theorem. Finally, we investigate the existence of groups with polynomially expanding Cayley graphs that possess only a finite number of normal subgroups. This inquiry leads to the definition of a class of groups termed "almost nilpotent," which we prove contains such groups. Additionally, we provide a negative resolution to a question posed by Gromov regarding whether groups with polynomial expansion necessarily exhibit sub-exponential expansion. As a corollary, we identify an infinite family of groups where the expansion of the Cayley graph for a group $G$ is bounded below by $n^{\log n}$. This result is achieved by constructing a group $G$ as a semidirect product of two finitely generated nilpotent groups, where the expansion of the Cayley graph for the second factor is at least $n^{\log n}$. We also examine the relationship between expansion rates and the word problem, proving that groups with polynomial expansion necessarily possess a solvable word problem. Finally, we construct a group with an expansion rate of $n^2$ that features a word problem requiring double exponential time to solve. These constructions rely on a novel class of groups termed "quasi-amenable groups," which we define and explore in this work. We establish that quasi-amenable groups are amenable and exhibit polynomial expansion, with expansion rates arbitrarily close to $n^2$. We also address the existence of quasi-amenable groups with non-trivial finite abelianization and provide a characterization of this class. Additionally, we present a characterization of quasi-amenable groups in terms of their Cayley graph expansion. This study examines the stability of a damped extended Euler-Bernoulli beam governed by the equation $u_{tt} + u_{xxxx} + a u_{ttxx} + b u_{tt} = 0$ at the nodes of a star-shaped graph. The analysis covers initial data within the domain $D(A)$, where $A$ represents the generator of the semigroup associated with the problem. The findings confirm and extend the stability results established by Messaoudi and Saidi (2012) for the case of a simple interval. Furthermore, the proof demonstrates that the methodology employed in this work is applicable to the standard Euler-Bernoulli beam equation, $u_{tt} + u_{xxxx} = 0$, on an interval, thereby recovering the results of Messaoudi and Saidi (2012). Additionally, the approach extends to the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam equation on an interval, yielding new stability results. Finally, the paper presents several examples to illustrate these theoretical findings. Notably, the examples involving the standard Euler-Bernoulli beam recover the results of Messaoudi and Saidi (2012), while the examples concerning the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam provide novel contributions. The examples are categorized into two groups: those with constant coefficients and those with non-constant coefficients. The primary challenge in this research lies in the fact that the operator $A$ is unbounded, and its domain is defined by boundary conditions that are nonlocal in both space and time. Consequently, the semigroup generated by $A$ exhibits nonstationary behavior, complicating the application of standard semigroup theory. To address this, the authors utilize the theory of evolution equations in Banach spaces, specifically the concept of evolution families, to derive the stability results. The paper concludes with an outline of the necessary theoretical background. Bayesian model averaging (BMA) is a recognized technique for forecasting model weights within model selection frameworks. However, when dealing with extensive model spaces, the Bayesian approach becomes computationally prohibitive. To address this, we introduce a machine learning model designed to predict weights for large model collections. This proposed method is evaluated using two regression datasets: one where model weights are known, and another where they are unknown. Our results demonstrate that the method achieves sufficient precision to support the investigation of $r$-process abundances in the Milky Way. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be extended to handle hierarchical model collections. By applying the method to individual $r$-process abundance patterns, we successfully identify the most probable nucleosynthetic events responsible for their production. This capability enables the differentiation between $r$-process events occurring in individual stars and those in stellar populations. Ultimately, this methodology offers a pathway to uncover the nature of $r$-process events and the characteristics of their progenitor systems. The microwave dissipation of sapphire is a critical factor in the development of superconducting quantum computers. To evaluate its impact, we measured the dielectric dissipation of high-purity sapphire at 5 GHz with a sensitivity reaching 10 parts per billion (ppb). By comparing our findings with the $10^{-4}$ Q-factor limit observed in quantum domain superconducting qubits, we determined that sapphire dielectric loss is not the primary source of dissipation in these quantum devices. Furthermore, we established a lower bound for the microwave dielectric loss tangent of sapphire at 5 GHz, which is at least 10 orders of magnitude lower than the $10^{-6}$ value previously reported in the literature. This result indicates that the intrinsic dielectric loss of sapphire is negligible in the microwave range. Additionally, we identified that surface loss is the dominant mechanism for dielectric dissipation in sapphire at microwave frequencies. These insights are essential for the advancement of superconducting quantum computing technology. Our results were achieved using a high-precision dielectric resonator method combined with a low-noise cryogenic vector network analyzer. This approach enables the measurement of the dielectric dissipation factor with sensitivity down to 10 ppb, a capability that is particularly valuable for characterizing high-quality dielectric materials in the microwave and radio frequency bands. The paper also includes a detailed discussion of the experimental techniques and their underlying principles. This study addresses a two-stage stochastic optimization framework where the first-stage model incorporates binary variables designed to handle disruptions in the second stage. The objective is to determine the optimal number of these binary variables to minimize the total cost, defined as the sum of installation expenses and the expected value of a second-stage linear program. To solve this, we introduce a novel algorithm that leverages the Lagrangian dual of the expected second-stage problem. This approach enables the efficient evaluation of the objective function, which is essential for applying a specialized branch-and-cut method. We validate the proposed method's effectiveness through a numerical study focused on a disruption management application within a public transport network. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the application analysis reveals that the optimal count of binary variables is highly sensitive to the specific disruption scenarios included in the analysis. Finally, we show that our method can identify an optimal solution for a network comprising 100 stations within a few minutes. These findings underscore the method's potential for real-world implementation in large-scale networks. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the algorithm, which is available as open-source software. Finally, we explore the method's applicability to other resilient optimization problems. This paper is the first to introduce a new approach for solving two-stage resilient optimization problems and to apply it to a real-world disruption management case study. The proposed method is versatile and can be adapted to various contexts, such as facility location, network design, and energy systems. The authors are currently extending this work to other areas, including supply chain management and energy system planning. This paper introduces H4M, a large-scale, diverse, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional dataset designed for socioeconomic analysis within urban environments. Comprising over 100 million data points, H4M offers rich, fine-grained information regarding human activities in Beijing, China. It encompasses various data types, including point data (such as GPS trajectories), time series (like crime statistics), images (such as street views), and text (including news articles). These multi-modal sources capture diverse perspectives on human behavior, ranging from individual actions to collective phenomena. The dataset is structured across multiple distributions, featuring both raw and pre-processed data. We have developed a comprehensive suite of tools to facilitate its use, which are available at https://github.com/BeijingAI4G/H4M. This paper details the dataset's characteristics and provides a thorough overview of its potential applications. We demonstrate that H4M can significantly enhance the performance of several state-of-the-art methods in multi-modal and multi-view learning, as well as in multi-task and multi-source learning for multi-distributional scenarios. Furthermore, we illustrate how H4M can improve the accuracy of various real-world tasks, such as activity recognition and activity density estimation. We anticipate that H4M will serve as a valuable resource for researchers engaged in multi-modal and multi-view machine learning, as well as those focused on multi-task and multi-source learning across multiple distributions. Our goal is to foster the development of more robust and generalizable models for socioeconomic analysis in urban settings. The dataset can be accessed at https://beijingai4g.github.io/H4M/. Graph Neural Architectures (GNAs) have recently been introduced to address challenges in graph representation learning, such as over-smoothing and over-squashing. While transfer learning is a well-established method for enhancing performance in deep learning, its application to GNMs remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the knowledge transfer capabilities of GNMs, specifically examining the impact of node and edge information on transferability. Our findings indicate that pre-training GNNs on graphs with abundant edge data and fine-tuning them on graphs rich in node information yields superior transfer performance. Additionally, we demonstrate that utilizing a pre-trained GNN as a feature extractor for downstream node classification tasks further improves results. This paper introduces a feature-driven suggestion system designed for online social networks. The core of this system is the Dual Feature Distribution Model (DFDM), which integrates two distinct feature spaces: feature extraction and feature similarity. The model leverages feature extraction to identify and represent user interests, while simultaneously utilizing feature similarity to generate personalized suggestions. By integrating these two components, the DFDM ensures that recommended items align with both user interests and existing social connections. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior recommendation accuracy compared to several state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the study confirms that the dual-feature model exhibits robust performance across various datasets and parameter configurations. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/DFDM. We introduce a multi-diffraction architecture utilizing a single micro-fabricated silicon photonic crystal waveguide to integrate the diffraction, trapping, and detection of individual cold atoms. By applying a tailored multi-diffraction design, we demonstrate that a single 100 $\mu$m-long waveguide can simultaneously generate three diffraction orders, trap a cold atom at the far-field position, and efficiently collect its fluorescence. This compact structure is designed to minimize optical losses and maximize coupling efficiency. We provide a comprehensive design framework and simulation results for such devices, which are applicable to various integrated single-atom systems, including quantum memory, single-photon sources, and single-atom networks. Furthermore, we outline potential applications for these devices in quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Our work establishes a pathway for the miniaturization of single-atom systems, thereby advancing the development of quantum technologies. This study investigates the nonlinear Hall conductivity of a two-dimensional interacting two-component Fermi gas subjected to a random flux field, which induces chaos. We demonstrate that interaction effects can be precisely calculated using a diagrammatic approach. Our findings indicate that the nonlinear Hall conductivity remains robust against interactions, a result that is clearly illustrated through the computation of the three-point function of the Hall current. Furthermore, we show that interaction effects can be exactly derived via a mapping to a non-interacting system featuring an additional field. Finally, we examine the implications of our results for the existence of a nonlinear Chern-Simons term within the Hall effective action. These conclusions are supported by numerical calculations of the nonlinear Hall conductivity. Additionally, we explore the connection between our work and the recently proposed "interaction-induced Hall effect." Finally, we discuss the experimental realization of this phenomenon in cold atoms. This research was conducted in collaboration with A. Avdoshkin, A. Burin, and A. Mishchenko. A. This paper outlines our methodology for developing a system that assists healthcare professionals in making critical decisions. Our approach integrates a review of relevant literature, an analysis of existing challenges, and a discussion of potential future directions. We begin by examining the significance of natural language processing (NLP) within the healthcare sector, followed by an overview of current NLP systems and their primary limitations. Subsequently, we introduce our proposed solution, which comprises three main components: a multi-source dataset collection, a hybrid deep learning architecture, and a data-driven pipeline designed for immediate transcription of dynamic enhancements in medical contexts. Finally, we validate our approach through a case study addressing the complex issue of dual-patient breathing during the COVID-19 outbreak. We demonstrate how our method can be applied to this scenario and conclude by discussing the broader implications of our work for the intersection of NLP and healthcare. The code and dataset associated with this project will be made publicly available. This work was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, and we hope it contributes to the ongoing global effort to combat the virus. This paper investigates the platform groups of $n$-th iteration maps for bicritical rational functions, extending the findings of J. Oversteegen and T. S. Shih regarding platform components in quadratic polynomials. Our results demonstrate that, unlike the iteration maps for quadratic polynomials, the platform groups associated with higher-order bicritical rational functions do not necessarily possess a uniform structure. Specifically, we construct explicit examples of bicritical rational functions where the platform groups for their $n$-th iteration maps are neither abelian nor nilpotent. Furthermore, we establish that for any $n \geq 2$, there exist bicritical rational functions $f$ such that the platform group of $f^n$ is virtually abelian, with the required degree of $f$ growing exponentially with $n$. Additionally, we identify a class of bicritical rational functions where the platform groups of their $n$-th iterations are virtually nilpotent, and we provide an upper bound for these groups. Finally, we offer a characterization of the platform groups for a specific family of bicritical rational functions. These findings are complemented by computer experiments conducted using the software platform Dynamica.

Molybdenum (Mo) and Tungsten (W) dichalcogenides are emerging as promising materials for nanoelectronics. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) and GW calculations to analyze the work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity of these compounds as functions of layer count. The findings indicate that GW results align more closely with DFT data than with experimental values. Specifically, the work function of MoS₂ and WS₂ decreases from 4.7 eV to 4.4 eV as the layer thickness increases from monolayer to five layers. Conversely, the ionization potential of MoS₂ and WS₂ rises from 5.0 eV to 5.3 eV when transitioning from a five-layer to a monolayer structure. Additionally, the electron affinity of MoS₂ and WS₂ increases from 2.8 eV to 3.1 eV as the thickness thins from five layers down to a single layer. These results suggest that GW calculations offer a more accurate description of the electronic properties of layered transition metal dichalcogenides compared to DFT. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that GW-calculated work functions for bulk MoS₂ and WS₂ are lower than those of graphene, indicating that GW-based electronic structure calculations are essential for designing nanoelectronic devices utilizing these materials. Finally, the observed thickness dependence of work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity in MoS₂ and WS₂ is attributed to the interaction between the top and bottom layers. These insights are valuable for the development of nanoelectronic devices based on transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to investigate the electronic properties of other two-dimensional materials. This study investigates the potential for identifying steady-state solutions in multiscale rarefied gas flows within just dozens of iterations. We demonstrate that the Navier-Stokes equations, augmented with Saffman's higher-order slip boundary condition, accurately model a three-dimensional rotating cylinder situated in a rarefied environment. The flow parameters encompass a wide range of Knudsen numbers, angular velocities, and Reynolds numbers. Our findings indicate that the slip-flow framework achieves a maximum relative error of 1% compared to direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) results. Furthermore, we observe that the slip-flow solution converges to its steady state in approximately 50 time steps, whereas both DSMC and the Euler equations require roughly 100 time steps to reach the same convergence level. These results suggest that the proposed slip-flow model offers a highly efficient approach for modeling rotating bodies in rarefied gas flows. Additionally, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of the slip-flow solution's accuracy and its dependence on various physical parameters. Finally, we examine the solution's structure and discuss its implications for the development of future slip-flow models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abdulrahman-ahmed/rotating-cylinder. The non-observation of multi-messenger events from multi-modal sources, such as gravitational waves and gamma rays, is a critical benchmark for numerous theoretical models. This study examines multi-messenger coincidences within a broad dataset from the Horizon-10T experiment, utilizing a novel coincidence search method. We identify 11 multi-messenger events, with 8 of them being multi-modal. Our analysis indicates that 7 of these 8 multi-modal events are likely due to instrumental background noise. Furthermore, we establish a stringent upper limit on the production cross-section of axion quark particles, which could be detected by both gravitational wave and radio wave observatories. This limit is applicable to axion quark particles with masses ranging from $10^{-15}$ eV to $10^{-11}$ eV and is independent of the specific production mechanism. Additionally, we set an upper limit on the axion quark particle decay rate, which is independent of the axion quark model. These findings demonstrate that Horizon-10T is a promising candidate for multi-messenger astronomy. The dataset employed in this work is publicly accessible. We investigate the interplay between magnetic and crystalline fields within the lowest Landau level (LLL) on a honeycomb lattice using a tight-binding model. By employing a generalized Peierls substitution, we derive an exact expression for the magnetic Bloch phase. This phase exhibits a periodicity of $2\pi$ with respect to the magnetic flux per unit cell, a phenomenon we term the magnetic Bloch theorem. We demonstrate that this $2\pi$ periodicity in the magnetic Bloch phase governs the reemergence of a flat band at $2\pi$ flux, which can be interpreted as a restoration of Landau quantization. Furthermore, we analyze the phase diagram of the LLL as a function of the magnetic field and reveal that the phase transition from the $4\pi$ to the $2\pi$ periodicity regime is first-order. Finally, we explore the implications of the magnetic Bloch theorem for the fractional quantum Hall effect in this system. These findings are validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, we discuss the extension of the magnetic Bloch theorem to arbitrary lattices. Our results offer a novel perspective on the fractional quantum Hall effect in moiré materials, such as twisted bilayer graphene, where the magnetic unit cell is significantly larger than that of the crystallographic unit cell. This work also establishes a framework for investigating the interplay between magnetic and crystalline fields in other lattice systems. Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations that involves determining the optimal generation schedule for power plants over a specified horizon while minimizing costs. Double beta decay in $^{204}$Pt is a process of significant interest, yet it has not yet been observed. Our calculations indicate that the half-life for the 2nd-forbidden non-unique beta decay ($t_{1/2}^{2FNU}$) is approximately $10^{25}$ years, whereas the 4th-forbidden non-unique beta decay half-life ($t_{1/2}^{4FNU}$) could reach $10^{28}$ years. These findings suggest that the 4th-forbidden transition might be detectable with a sufficiently large sample. Additionally, we explore the potential of double dark matter capture and subsequent decay within $^{204}$Pt, demonstrating that this mechanism could yield a signal comparable to that of $^{76}$Ge in the XENON1T experiment. Furthermore, we establish a lower limit for the dark matter-nucleus cross section of $10^{-45}$ cm$^2$, which is comparable to the constraints derived from the COUPP experiment. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of conducting this investigation using $^{204}$Pt as a target. Our results underscore the necessity of developing new experimental techniques to observe double beta decay in $^{204}$Pt and to investigate dark matter interactions with platinum. We establish a version of the second Noether theorem applicable to non-reversible continuous symmetries of non-equilibrium steady states within local lattice systems. This approach relies on a discrete gauge transformation that extends the original field configuration to an auxiliary field. Under specific conditions, these conditions imply the existence of a non-reversible continuous symmetry in non-equilibrium steady states, thereby generating a non-equilibrium Goldstone theorem. We demonstrate this phenomenon in the driven XY model and the driven Ising model. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the relationship between the first and second Noether theorems. A digraph is semi-transitive if the subdigraphs induced by its strong components exhibit semi-transitivity. This study demonstrates that the semi-transitive direction of a split graph is uniquely determined up to isomorphism by its underlying undirected graph, provided the split components are fixed. Furthermore, we establish that every semi-transitive digraph can be constructed from its strong components using strong semi-transitive digraphs as building blocks. Finally, we present an algorithm with quadratic complexity relative to the number of vertices that generates all non-isomorphic semi-transitive directions for split graphs. Additionally, we characterize those semi-transitive directions where the vertex sets of the positive and negative digraphs correspond to specific induced subgraphs within the underlying split graph. The paper concludes with an extensive catalog of semi-transitive directions for notable split graphs, including path, cycle, and wheel graphs. The abundance of data from the vast cosmos, as exemplified by the Rubin Observatory, offers significant opportunities for advancing artificial intelligence. This study explores the application of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) to three key classification tasks within the Rubin era: galaxy morphological categorization, supernova classification, and supernova host galaxy identification. We demonstrate that BNNs achieve performance comparable to standard feed-forward neural networks while offering a distinct advantage: quantifying classification uncertainty. This capability is essential for determining the optimal balance between maximizing the number of classified objects and minimizing errors. Our findings indicate that a classifier operating at 90% accuracy can process the entire Legacy Survey Observatory (LSO) dataset in approximately 100 days, with an expected error rate of only 0.001%. Furthermore, we show that the performance of a standard neural network can be matched using just 10% of the training data. These results suggest that BNNs are highly effective for classification tasks in the Rubin data era and that they can significantly accelerate the training process. Additionally, we have made our code and pre-trained models publicly available. This work was conducted as part of the AstroML Summer School 2022. Intermodal coupling in photonic crystal threads (PCTs) facilitates the transfer of energy between two counter-propagating modes, which can be utilized to construct a Brillouin sensor. This study presents a method for characterizing the intermodal coupling coefficient within PCTs and demonstrates its application in measuring the diffusion of intermodal energy in a 200-µm-long device featuring a 12-helix structure. The observed coupling coefficient was determined to be 0.0015, consistent with finite element method simulations. These findings indicate that PCTs are viable candidates for implementing integrated Brillouin sensors. Furthermore, the results suggest that optimizing the PCT geometry could enhance the coupling coefficient, thereby improving sensor performance. Finally, this work represents the first experimental demonstration of intermodal energy transfer in a PCT. The reported coupling coefficient is approximately two orders of magnitude lower than that of a photonic chip designed for intermodal coupling, highlighting the potential for further optimization to achieve higher performance. Additionally, the proposed PCT device offers a significant advantage over chip-based solutions by enabling the use of standard optical equipment. The combination of our efficient local search algorithm, its successful application to diverse problems, and the availability of implementation details and source code offers a valuable resource for the research community. Cyclists are vulnerable road users, and their safety is a significant concern for both the cycling community and the general public. This paper introduces a novel, intelligent system designed to detect risky situations involving cyclists. The proposed framework utilizes a deep learning-based risk identifier that operates in a video-driven manner, processing incoming video streams to determine risk levels. This identifier is developed through a new end-to-end deep learning architecture that integrates a multi-stream Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The multi-stream CNN component processes three distinct video streams: the current frame, the previous frame, and an optical flow stream derived from the two preceding frames. The LSTM component then analyzes the temporal evolution of these risk indicators. To train this system, a new dataset called CYCLIST-RISK was created, featuring 30-second video clips annotated with a binary risk label. The efficacy of the proposed approach was validated through extensive experiments, which demonstrated that the system achieves a high degree of accuracy in classifying risk situations. This paper introduces a motion planning framework designed for dynamic robots operating in uncertain environments with safety-critical constraints. The proposed approach utilizes Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to formulate motion planning as a sequence of convex optimization problems. To address environmental uncertainties, the method incorporates uncertainty-aware CBFs, ensuring that CBF-superlevel sets encompass probable robot trajectories. Furthermore, to mitigate the impact of measurement noise on the planning process, a novel resilience mechanism is developed. This mechanism ensures the motion planner remains robust against noisy data by maintaining a minimum clearance from obstacles. The resulting planner is computationally efficient, capable of generating smooth and safe trajectories for both static and dynamic systems. Simulation results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in navigating uncertain settings, while experiments on a mobile robot validate its real-world applicability. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical properties of the proposed approach. This study investigates the problem of adversarial robustness within deep learning, where a model is assumed to be a fixed component and the focus shifts to designing a learning algorithm capable of achieving robustness against adversarial examples. We propose the concept of \emph{organic robustness}, which posits that a model can be robust against adversarial inputs if those inputs are excluded from the training data. We demonstrate that an organic robust learner can be constructed by integrating a standard learner with a robustness filter. Furthermore, we establish that this algorithm attains a near-optimal trade-off between training error and generalization error. Finally, we extend this approach to scenarios involving multiple adversaries, showing that the organic learner maintains robustness against all of them. Our theoretical findings are supported by experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. We introduce a novel link invariant defined for dilation surfaces by utilizing the dilation surface associated with a specific link complement. This invariant emerges from the surface's interior dynamics, which are defined as equivalence classes of dilation surface orbits under conjugation by surface automorphisms. We demonstrate that this invariant remains unchanged under link cobordism. Furthermore, we establish that the interior dynamics of any dilation surface arise from the dilation of a torus link's dilation surface combined with the action of a Dehn twist on a cylinder's boundary. Consequently, the interior dynamics of torus links are characterized by a single fixed point, whereas for other links, the interior dynamics consist of a continuous family of fixed points alongside a hyperbolic fixed point. Finally, we construct an infinite family of links whose interior dynamics include a fixed point with a non-zero eigenvalue. These findings suggest that our invariant holds significant potential for distinguishing links. Specifically, we identify a pair of links that are not cobordant yet share the same interior dynamics, indicating that the invariant is not a complete invariant for links. Additionally, we calculate the interior dynamics for several knots and links, including the trefoil, figure-eight, and square knot. The resulting dynamics for the trefoil and figure-eight knots are identical, while the square knot exhibits distinct dynamics. This implies that the interior dynamics can differentiate between the trefoil and figure-eight knots, as well as between the trefoil and square knots. However, the interior dynamics of the figure-eight and square knots are equivalent, suggesting that this invariant may not distinguish between them. Our findings provide a solid theoretical foundation for advancing the modeling of the human mind and hold potential for applications in medical diagnostics and treatment planning. This paper introduces a new ground-based sensor network architecture designed to monitor large-scale events like earthquakes and tsunamis. The system integrates ground sensors with over-the-horizon (OTH) radar, which is considered a form of sky-based sensing. By connecting these OTH radars with ground sensor networks wirelessly, the proposed system offers expanded coverage, enhanced resolution, and improved robustness. Specifically, the study proposes a wireless linkage mechanism that allows ground sensor networks to adaptively adjust their sampling rates based on OTH radar data. This approach aims to minimize energy usage and communication overhead while ensuring that the fused observations from both ground and sky sensors remain consistent. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the system's design and implementation, supported by simulation results. These results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively reduces energy consumption and communication overhead, while maintaining the integrity of fused observations. Furthermore, the study confirms that the system can scale to accommodate a large number of OTH radars and ground sensor networks. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of potential future research directions. Keywords: Sensor Network, Over-the-Horizon Radar, Wireless Linkage, Adaptive Sampling, Energy Efficiency.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a comprehensive neutrino research initiative designed to investigate fundamental questions regarding the neutrino sector, which remains the least understood area of particle physics. By utilizing a 1.3-kiloton liquid argon time-projection chamber and a 60-kiloton wide-band neutrino source derived from neutron spallation, DUNE will leverage its unique sensitivity to multiple oscillation parameters to conduct a multifaceted analysis of the neutrino three-mixing framework. This experiment aims to deliver definitive results on CP violation in the neutrino sector, resolve the long-standing matter-antimatter asymmetry puzzle, and determine the correct ordering of neutrino mass eigenstates. Additionally, DUNE will advance our understanding of hadron production mechanisms, a critical component for neutrino sources, and will significantly contribute to the study of supernova dynamics and the investigation of historical supernova 1987A. This paper outlines the anticipated scientific achievements of the DUNE project. In reinforcement learning, experience replay is a common technique used to improve sample efficiency and stabilize training. This paper introduces a novel experience replay method that leverages the reduced variance of the empirical mean. We demonstrate that the variance of the target value estimator in reinforcement learning decomposes into two distinct components: one attributable to the policy and another to the critic. To address this, we propose a new strategy called Variance-Debiased Prioritized Replay (VDPR), which prioritizes data based on the policy-related critic term. We provide a theoretical analysis of VDPR and validate its effectiveness through experiments on both simulated and real-world robotic tasks. The results indicate that VDPR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/VDPR. Our findings suggest that VDPR holds significant potential for enhancing policy performance. Furthermore, we hope that the insights gained from this work will inspire future research aimed at improving reinforcement learning algorithms. Finally, we anticipate that VDPR will prove valuable in advancing the field of reinforcement learning.

This approach is particularly effective for applications like weather forecasting, where understanding motion is crucial. Our method employs a hybrid model that integrates a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with a motion model. The RNN captures spatiotemporal dependencies, while the motion model utilizes a learnable affine transformation to represent movement. We demonstrate that our framework surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on the Weather48 dataset. Finally, we show that the learned motion model can be applied to generate motion-informed data augmentations, thereby further boosting predictive accuracy. We investigate a system comprising $N$ interacting charged particles within a bounded region, where each pair interacts via a logarithmic potential. The random trajectory of these particles is modeled as a collection of random curves, and the random measure derived from their charges is defined as a discrete approximation of the Gaussian free field (GFF) associated with this collection. Specifically, we examine the scenario where the particle trajectories constitute a discrete approximation of a union of $n$ disjoint simple random walks, which are interpreted as discrete approximations of $n$ disjoint multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs). We demonstrate that as the discrete approximation converges to the continuous limit, the associated discrete GFF converges to the continuous GFF linked with the union of $n$ disjoint SLEs. Furthermore, we establish that the partition function of the random log-gas can be expressed as the expectation of a product of conformal covariances of the continuous GFF. Finally, we analyze the limiting behavior of the discrete GFF and the random log-gas in the context of a simply connected domain containing a closed curve. In this setting, the limiting GFF is shown to be associated with an annulus, and the limiting partition function is expressed using the modular lambda function. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the random log-gas and the conformal blocks of the Virasoro minimal conformal field theory. The findings in this work are supported by numerical simulations. This paper presents a priori estimates using the supremum norm for solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with periodic initial conditions. These estimates are derived without relying on estimates based on the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Additionally, we establish a criterion ensuring global-in-time solvability of the initial-boundary value problem for the Navier-Stokes equations within the periodic class. The proof relies on the continuity method, a priori estimates in the supremum norm, and the construction of a suitable barrier function. Furthermore, we derive estimates for the supremum norm of the initial data in terms of the Hilbert-Schmidt norm and the initial pressure. These findings offer an alternative approach to the solvability criterion for the periodic initial-boundary value problem of the Navier-Stokes equations, as formulated by Kato and Fujita. We also provide an estimate for the pressure, which serves as a criterion for the global-in-time solvability of the Navier-Stokes equations in the periodic class. The derived estimates for the velocity field and pressure are expressed through the supremum norm of the initial velocity, the supremum norm of the initial pressure, and the supremum norm of the external force. These results complement the author's prior work, which utilized Hilbert-Schmidt norm estimates for the answer. The paper concludes with a criterion for the global-in-time solvability of the Navier-Stokes equations in the periodic class, formulated using the supremum norm for the answer. This criterion is derived from the author's earlier findings regarding Hilbert-Schmidt norm estimates for the answer.

**Keywords:** incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, a priori estimates, solvability criterion, barrier function, global-in-time solvability, pressure.

We introduce a classical method for verifying quantum computations that operates within linear time. This approach builds upon the concept of clutters, which serve as a classical representation of quantum circuits. By employing the signature matrix—a classically simulable matrix that encapsulates the behavior of quantum gates—we can validate the equivalence of two clutters in linear time. This technique enables the verification of any quantum computation defined by a circuit of linear duration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method extends to clutters constructed in superlinear time by integrating it with the technique for classically simulating quantum circuits of constant depth. Our findings offer a novel perspective on the relationship between classical and quantum computation, with potential applications in the verification of quantum hardware. Additionally, we explore applications relevant to the study of complexity classes. Specifically, we establish that the class NC1 is closed under clutters of linear size and provide an NC1 algorithm for determining the equivalence of such clutters. These results rely on a new characterization of NC1 involving signature matrices. Finally, we present an application concerning the complexity of the equivalence problem for clutters, which yields an improved upper bound on the complexity of the equivalence problem for linear circuits. This improvement is achieved through a new characterization of the class TC0 utilizing signature matrices. Our work also presents a novel characterization of TC0 based on threshold circuits of constant depth and linear size. Blockchain technology has garnered significant attention within the Internet of Things (IoT) domain, offering a promising solution for establishing trust in decentralized environments. This paper introduces a new framework designed to enhance trust in IoT systems by leveraging the blockchain. Specifically, we present a use case involving a food supply chain, where a consortium of stakeholders collaborates to manage the blockchain. To address the specific challenges of this domain, we propose a novel consensus mechanism that integrates practical Byzantine fault tolerance with a hybrid approach combining proof-of-work and proof-of-stake. Additionally, we develop a specialized language for smart contracts tailored to the food supply chain context. Our evaluation results demonstrate that this proposed solution outperforms existing alternatives in terms of throughput, latency, and storage requirements. Furthermore, our proposed solution for ensuring trust in IoT systems surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions. Finally, we have released the source code for this solution on GitHub. This study introduces a method for generating the outlines of biological cells using implicit neural representations. We model the cell periphery as a closed curve represented by a neural network, which is trained via a combination of supervised learning on existing data and unsupervised learning through a novel geometry loss function. This loss function evaluates the quality of generated cells by calculating the Hausdorff distance between them and real cells. Our approach successfully produces realistic cells that closely resemble the shapes found in the training dataset. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the generated cells exhibit diversity and can capture complex, non-trivial shapes that go beyond simple convex or smooth forms. Additionally, the unsupervised geometry loss proves effective at identifying outliers in the training data, such as cells with artifacts, thereby enhancing the robustness of the method. Finally, we show that the trained model can be utilized to synthesize cell shapes for data augmentation in supervised classification tasks. Exoplanet atmospheres are frequently obscured by stellar activity, which can mimic or mimic planetary signals. While high-resolution spectroscopy is recognized for its ability to distinguish between planetary and stellar features, the specific characteristics of stellar activity at low resolutions remain less understood. This study aims to characterize these low-resolution signatures and assess the capacity of high-resolution data to filter them out. We conducted a Bayesian analysis of low-resolution (R ~ 100) H$\alpha$ observations of the active star AD Leo, utilizing a model that accounts for both stellar activity and rotation. Our results indicate that H$\alpha$ emission originates from two primary sources: the star's photosphere and magnetically active regions. By analyzing the temporal and rotational behavior of these components, we established a method to differentiate between them. We subsequently applied this approach to a suite of synthetic exoplanet transit spectra containing both planetary and stellar activity features. Our findings demonstrate that high-resolution spectroscopy effectively suppresses most stellar activity signals, though some residual emission persists. Ultimately, we conclude that low-resolution high-dispersion spectrographs are essential for characterizing stellar activity, while high-resolution instruments serve as a complementary tool to mitigate its impact. This strategy is particularly critical for future large-scale exoplanet surveys, such as the Habitable Exoplanet Observatory (HabEx) and the Large UV/Optical/Infrared Surveyor (LUVOIR). We investigate the feasibility of achieving constant curvature metrics on a surface $M$ featuring singularities at points $p_1, \dots, p_n$. Our approach involves modifying the complex structure constant $\lambda$ of the cohomology class $[\lambda \omega_0, \omega_0] \in H^2(M, \mathbb{R})$ to derive $c$-invariant 2-forms, which subsequently yield $c$-invariant metrics. We demonstrate that for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$, a solution exists provided that $\int_M \omega_0 = 0$ when $M$ is compact, and $\int_M \omega_0 = \infty$ when $M$ is non-compact. Furthermore, we establish that the resulting metric possesses singularities with specific cone angles $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ at the points $p_1, \dots, p_n$. Finally, we outline applications of this theorem to surfaces possessing conical singularities. In the compact case, we apply our findings to derive a Gauss-Bonnet formula for constant curvature metrics with cone angles $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ on a compact Riemann surface $M$. Additionally, we present an application concerning the existence of constant curvature metrics on open subsets of $\mathbb{C}P^2$ that exclude the points $p_1, \dots, p_n$. In the non-compact case, we show that if $M$ is a non-compact Riemann surface with a countable set of singularities $\{p_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, then a constant curvature metric with cone angles $\alpha_n$ at each $p_n$ exists if and only if $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n < 4\pi$. This result extends the classical Gauss-Bonnet theorem to surfaces with conical singularities. We also provide an application to the existence of constant curvature metrics on the complement of a real algebraic curve in $\mathbb{C}P^2$. Finally, we offer an alternative proof of a theorem by B. O'Neill regarding the existence of a complete metric of constant curvature on a non-compact Riemann surface with a countable set of singularities. This study investigates the swimming mechanics of the centipede *Strigamia marica* at the water surface. High-speed video analysis reveals that these animals propel themselves by generating traveling waves along their bodies, utilizing their legs to drive body segments against the water interface. The swimming motion is characterized by a low Froude number, indicating that the swimming speed is primarily dictated by the wave celerity. The swimming stroke frequency ($f$) and body wave amplitude ($A$) both increase with speed ($U$), following the relationships $f \propto U$ and $A \propto U^{1.2}$. Furthermore, the dimensionless wave amplitude ($\epsilon$) remains constant across different speeds, suggesting that the centipedes maintain a consistent swimming mode. Finally, the swimming dynamics are governed by the centipede's body length ($L$) and the water's surface tension ($\sigma$), as described by the scaling law $U \propto \sqrt{\sigma/L}$. These findings suggest that the swimming behavior of *S. marica* is optimized for the specific environments they inhabit. The data are compared with theoretical predictions and the swimming dynamics of other species. These results offer a foundation for developing bio-inspired robots capable of navigating water interfaces. This study introduces a novel, high-performance algorithm designed to simulate the diffusive propagation of tsunamis generated by asteroid impacts. The method employs a variable time-step strategy, utilizing a small initial step to accurately resolve the initial wave and progressively increasing the step size as the wave spreads outward. By applying the explicit finite difference method to the linear diffusion equation, the algorithm enables rapid simulations of the full tsunami lifecycle—from generation to inundation—achieving a speedup of 100 to 1,000 times compared to previous models. This enhancement is achieved without sacrificing accuracy, as the method maintains high precision during the early stages when the wave front is narrow and the water column is deep. The algorithm is implemented in C++ and leverages the OpenMP parallelization standard to utilize all available CPU cores. Furthermore, it is fully integrated into the high-performance numerical simulation framework known as the Parallel Virtual Machine (PVMD). We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy through several test cases, including the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor event and the 2013 hypothetical asteroid impact on Earth. These cases illustrate the algorithm's efficiency and its capacity to model the complete tsunami propagation cycle. Additionally, we present a new approach for modeling inundation, which is currently being developed. This method utilizes a two-way coupling between a hydrodynamic model and a topographic model to simulate the inundation process. Finally, we outline a research agenda aimed at simulating the entire tsunami propagation cycle for asteroid impacts on Earth and other planetary bodies. This agenda includes modeling the impact event itself, the initial wave generation, propagation, inundation, and the subsequent evolution of the affected area. Such a comprehensive approach will significantly enhance our ability to predict the consequences of asteroid impacts. We present early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of 11 optically faint yet luminous galaxies at $z\sim 1-3$, selected from the Hubble Ultra Deep Field (HUDF) and HUDF09. These objects exhibit extreme properties, characterized by stellar masses of $10^{10}-10^{11} M_{\odot}$ and star formation rates of $10-100 M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, despite being undetectable in deep optical imaging. Our analysis reveals that these galaxies are predominantly dusty, with dust masses ranging from $10^{7}$ to $10^{8} M_{\odot}$ and dust-to-gas ratios of $0.01-0.1$. Their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are best modeled by star-forming galaxies with a small fraction of AGN activity. The majority of these sources are identified as starbursts, displaying a strong correlation between dust mass and star formation rate. Furthermore, we find that these galaxies are more compact than typical star-forming systems at the same stellar mass, with half-light radii of $0.2-0.5$ kpc. Their specific star formation rates and specific dust masses are significantly higher than those of galaxies at the same stellar mass in the local universe. These findings suggest that these optically hidden galaxies represent a distinct population of starbursts that are heavily obscured by dust, offering a potential explanation for the observed discrepancy between the cosmic star formation rate density and the luminosity density derived from UV light. Additionally, they may account for a significant portion of the cosmic infrared background. Our results underscore the necessity of deep infrared surveys to uncover the full population of luminous, optically dim galaxies. Finally, we demonstrate that the observed star formation rate density at $z\sim 1-3$ can be fully explained by a population of galaxies that are 10 times fainter than the current detection limits of deep optical surveys. This study examines the curvature tensor for seven-dimensional space, introducing its geometric interpretation through a tensor defined on geometric membranes. The analysis focuses on the tensor $\mathcal{K}$, which is derived from the curvature tensor by contracting two indices. The paper establishes the algebraic and differential properties of $\mathcal{K}$, defines its geometrical membrane representation, and explores the differential properties of this new entity. Furthermore, it investigates the differential properties of the scalar $K$, obtained by contracting two additional indices of $\mathcal{K}$, and analyzes the differential properties of the symmetric traceless part of $K$. Finally, the work explores the differential properties of the Weyl tensor in seven dimensions, denoted as $W$, and its associated scalar $K_W$, formed by contracting two indices of $W$. These findings are applied to seven-dimensional Einstein spaces, revealing that the differential properties of the trace-free part of $K$ are closely linked to those of $K_W$. Additionally, the paper examines the case of seven-dimensional Euclidean space, deriving specific properties of the $\mathcal{K}$ representation that hold exclusively in this context. The conclusion emphasizes the significance of the geometrical membrane representation of the curvature tensor, noting its potential utility in various physical theories. The authors intend to expand upon these results in future publications. Finally, the paper addresses a related issue concerning the differential properties of the scalar $K$ in seven-dimensional Einstein spaces, specifically the validity of the relation $\nabla_a K = 0$, which is demonstrated to be incorrect. We examine two distinct blocking mechanisms for two-dimensional discs situated in a mass channel: (i) the formation of a "blocked disc" where the system fails to equilibrate, and (ii) the creation of a "blocked sequence" characterized by a series of transient equilibria. We analyze the specific conditions under which each mechanism occurs and the resulting structures. The primary focus is on systems where the mass distribution within the channel is non-Gaussian, as this non-Gaussianity is the fundamental driver for the blocking phenomenon. Specifically, we investigate two cases: a mass distribution with a sharp cutoff and another with a broad peak. Our findings indicate that blocking is more readily achieved in systems with a broad peak, whereas systems with a sharp cutoff tend to form blocked sequences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the presence of a broad peak in the mass channel can be effectively modeled by incorporating a Gaussian component into the phase-space density of the system. Finally, we outline the implications of these results for star formation within molecular clouds. This study serves as a sequel to Paper I, which established the foundational concepts of blocking. The El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a primary driver of climate variability, yet its global impacts are not uniform. While the Pacific region experiences the most direct effects, other areas are influenced by the complex interaction between the two components of ENSO: the atmospheric pressure fluctuations known as the Southern Oscillation (SO) and the oceanic temperature anomalies termed the El Ni\~no phenomenon (ENSO). This study investigates the distinct global precipitation patterns associated with these two elements. By analyzing monthly precipitation data from 1950 to 2018, we identified unique precipitation signatures for both the SO and ENSO components. Furthermore, we examined the temporal evolution of their respective contributions to global precipitation patterns. Our findings indicate that the SO component exerts a stronger influence on global precipitation patterns than the ENSO component. Additionally, we observed that the relative influence of the SO component is more pronounced during extreme precipitation events, such as severe droughts and floods. These results underscore the necessity of distinguishing between the SO and ENSO components when studying the global impacts of ENSO. Finally, we developed a method to quantify the differential impact of these two components on global precipitation patterns. This approach involves calculating the differential trace of the global patterns linked to the SO and ENSO components, which can be applied to other climate variables. The proposed method is validated through its application to global temperature patterns. The source code for this method is available at \url{https://github.com/EnriqueGonzalez/impact-analysis}. We examine the evolution of non-affine growth in a two-dimensional model where particles are added to the surface of a square lattice, resulting in a flat geometry with four-fold symmetry. This growth is driven by the non-affine field, which stems from the anisotropy of the local growth rate. By employing X-ray scattering, we analyze the anisotropy of the non-affine displacement field and its correlation length. Our findings indicate that the decay of the Fourier transform of the non-affine displacement field follows a power law, with the exponent dependent on the scattering angle. Additionally, the decay of the non-affine displacement correlation function is also governed by a power law, where the exponent is a function of the anisotropy parameter. These results demonstrate that the anisotropy of the non-affine growth field can be effectively investigated using light scattering. Furthermore, we show that the anisotropy of the decay of the non-affine displacement correlation function can be described by a modified anisotropic diffusion equation. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the anisotropy of the non-affine growth field and the anisotropy of the local growth rate. These insights are applicable to understanding the formation of non-affine patterns in various systems, including thin films, epitaxial layers, and biological tissues. Our findings also offer a potential explanation for the anisotropic growth patterns observed in the early stages of tumor development. This study examines a single-species demographic model incorporating age structure and behavioral responses within a polluted environment. The analysis focuses on the existence, uniqueness, and stability of the positive equilibrium, as well as the stability switch and oscillatory behavior of the system. Furthermore, numerical simulations are utilized to validate the theoretical findings. Additionally, the biological significance of the proposed model is explored. The results indicate that the environmental carrying capacity exerts a significant influence on the system's dynamics.
