This paper investigates decidability and computational complexity within hypersequent substructural frameworks that permit weakening, focusing specifically on the cut-free systems LHM and LHM. We demonstrate that both LHM and LHM are decidable, with upper complexity bounds of 2NEXP and NEXP, respectively. Furthermore, we establish that the logics derived from LHM and LH by incorporating the exchange rule are also decidable, each possessing an NEXP upper bound. These findings represent the first decidability results for any sublogic of LHM. Additionally, we provide decidability results for several other substructural logics formulated as hypersequents, including those for affine logic, the full Lambek calculus, and minimal Lambek calculus, assigning them upper bounds of 2NEXP, NEXP, and NEXP, respectively. Finally, we examine the impact of adding the cut rule to these systems, showing that while cut is admissible in LH, LHM, and the exchange-based variants of affine and Lambek calculi, it is not admissible in LHM. Consequently, the admissibility of cut in these systems remains an open problem. The methodologies employed in this work are applicable to other substructural logics that can be expressed via hypersequents. Notably, we observe that the decidability of the Lambek calculus and minimal Lambek calculus can be derived from the decidability of their hypersequent counterparts, L and M. This approach also extends to the decidability of the cut-free versions of Lambek's calculus with contraction and the full Lambek calculus, yielding upper bounds of NEXP and 2NEXP, respectively. These results are novel, as they constitute the first decidability proofs for the cut-free versions of these specific logics. Finally, we address the issue of finite model property (fmp) in the Lambek calculus, demonstrating that while the standard system lacks fmp, the hypersequent formulation L does possess it. However, the admissibility of cut in L remains an unresolved question. The techniques utilized here are expected to be valuable for advancing research into the decidability of hypersequent-based substructural logics. We introduce HyperExpan, a novel classification expansion framework that leverages the intrinsic properties of hyperbolic space. Unlike existing expansion methods, HyperExpan is designed to accommodate an unlimited number of classes and to model hierarchical relationships among them. To achieve this, we propose a new loss function that learns to predict both the node embeddings and their corresponding labels within hyperbolic space. Furthermore, we develop a novel distance metric to quantify the separation between an input query and the centroids of class clusters. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperExpan surpasses current state-of-the-art expansion techniques across multiple datasets. Additionally, we find that our approach is highly effective at inferring the hierarchical structure of the expanded concept space. Finally, we illustrate the versatility of HyperExpan by applying it to expand concepts in both taxonomy and ontologies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/HyperExpan. This study examines the impact of external electric fields on molecular dimers, utilizing the S66 dataset which comprises 66 small molecules. The analysis focuses on how these fields alter binding energies and equilibrium geometries. The S66 dataset is categorized into four groups based on the primary non-covalent interaction type: hydrogen bonding, $\pi$-stacking, van der Waals, and dispersion. The research employs the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVQZ method to calculate binding energies and geometries, alongside the SAPT0/aug-cc-pVTZ method for decomposing intermolecular interactions. Results indicate that external electric fields can significantly influence both binding energies and geometries. Furthermore, the study explores the potential applications of these findings in supramolecular chemistry. Finally, the work addresses the computational cost associated with these calculations. The findings demonstrate that the SAPT0/aug-cc-pVTZ method offers a favorable balance between computational expense and accuracy. Additionally, the effects of external electric fields on binding energies and geometries were observed to be comparable across all dimer types. Finally, the influence of electric field direction was found to be contingent upon the specific dimer under consideration. These insights are valuable for advancing the design of supramolecular systems. The study concludes by outlining potential future research directions. This study introduces a novel ambiguity modeling approach designed to enhance the efficiency of solving real-world scheduling problems. The proposed method integrates two distinct types of ambiguity: (i) non-deterministic ambiguity, which captures the uncertainty in job processing times, and (ii) structural ambiguity, which accounts for unknown job priorities. To address non-deterministic ambiguity, the authors develop a new technique called the non-deterministic ambiguity set, which is subsequently combined with the existing ambiguity structure set to jointly model both ambiguity sources. The effectiveness of this new approach is evaluated through an extensive numerical study that compares it against both the existing method and the ideal scenario where no ambiguity exists. The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the existing approach in terms of solution quality. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the non-deterministic ambiguity set is particularly effective when the number of jobs is large or when the number of processors is small. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Notably, the proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of scheduling problems, including those involving other uncertainty types such as fuzzy, stochastic, or neutrosophic data. Additionally, the method is applicable to various scheduling contexts, such as parallel machine scheduling, flow shop scheduling, and job shop scheduling. This paper introduces a new approach for assessing the robustness of cyber-physical systems. We propose defining robustness based on the set of signals that cause a system to violate its specification, utilizing signal temporal logic (STL). To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we apply it to two case studies: a continuous-time dynamical system and a cyber-physical system featuring a controller with digital sampling. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm designed to compute the maximal STL-robustness set, which integrates techniques from model checking and robust optimization. Our experimental results indicate that this proposed approach yields more accurate and informative outcomes compared to existing methods. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. This work examines a specific nonlinear diffusion equation involving the absolute value of the Laplacian of a function, set on complete Riemannian manifolds that may possess infinite volume. The primary objective is to develop and analyze gradient flow approximations for the associated energy within the Sobolev space $H^1$. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the resulting nonlinear evolution equation and demonstrate that these solutions converge to the energy's critical points. Furthermore, we derive convergence results for the energy and its gradient, provided certain conditions are met. These assumptions include a lower bound on the Ricci curvature of the manifold and an additional constraint on the growth of the Laplacian of functions with compact support, which varies depending on the specific approximation method employed. Finally, we apply these findings to the study of harmonic functions and constant solutions on complete manifolds. Additional remarks address the existence of non-constant harmonic functions and the stability of constant solutions within this context. The analysis relies on tools from non-smooth analysis, particularly the theory of subdifferentials for non-smooth functionals. The energy under consideration is notably non-coercive, and its subdifferential lacks local Lipschitz continuity, presenting significant analytical challenges. To address these, we employ techniques from the analysis of abstract gradient flows on non-coercive spaces, as presented in our earlier publication. This approach involves constructing a suitable approximation of the energy and utilizing the theory of maximal monotone operators to investigate the corresponding gradient flow. Our results are applicable to a broader class of problems, including those involving the $p$-Laplacian. Additionally, we offer a concise review of the theory of subdifferentials for non-smooth functionals, which may serve as a useful reference for other researchers. Markov models serve as a fundamental mathematical framework for modeling stochastic processes. In data stream analysis, these models are utilized to identify anomalies, detect intrusions, and forecast future events. This paper offers a fresh perspective on Markov models by introducing a new category of probabilistic automata called "abstract concealed Markov models" (abbreviated as ACMMs). These ACMMs represent data streams as random variables within the monad of probability distributions. We demonstrate that the category of probabilistic automata equipped with AcMMMs possesses a free monad structure, which provides a natural framework for defining data flow algorithms. This approach enables the expression of data flow algorithms as automata that operate on AcMMMs. Furthermore, we illustrate how this methodology can be applied to design data flow algorithms for Markov anomaly detection. Our findings are implemented in Haskell, a functional programming language renowned for its concise and expressive type system. We present several illustrative examples of data flow algorithms for anomaly detection, including those for identifying outliers, detecting intrusions, and predicting future events. These examples are realized as programs using the proposed algorithmic design. Additionally, we show that the programs can be extended to handle data streams with temporal dependencies. Finally, we discuss the application of our monadic framework to the problem of Markov model learning. Our approach leverages the free monad structure of AcMMMs to formulate the Markov model learning problem as a sequence of lifting operations. We provide a monadic program that solves this problem, which can be adapted to address other data flow algorithm problems. Our implementation is available on GitHub. The paper also includes a tutorial on using our monadic framework to design data flow algorithms. This tutorial guides readers through implementing various data flow algorithms, such as outlier detection, Markov anomaly detection, Markov prediction, and Markov model learning. The tutorial is structured to be accessible to readers with a basic understanding of monads and free monads. We conclude by outlining several directions for future research. Our framework can be extended to incorporate other probabilistic structures, such as Bayesian networks and probabilistic circuits. Additionally, our method can be applied to data stream analysis problems beyond anomaly detection, including time series forecasting and query processing. Finally, we explore the potential of using our framework to develop new data flow algorithms for anomaly detection. Our approach utilizes the free monad structure of AcMMMs to define new algorithms for Markov anomaly detection, which can be adapted to solve other data flow algorithm problems. This study examines the behavior of a particle confined within a box whose walls oscillate periodically. We demonstrate that the average energy of the particle can be calculated with high precision using a statistical nonlocality principle. This finding indicates that the statistical framework of the Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) is inadequate for describing the periodic dynamical structures found in strongly correlated systems. Furthermore, we show that the statistical nonlocality inherent in these periodic dynamical structures can be effectively modeled through spatially nonlocal structures. This insight is crucial for developing a time-dependent extension of the density functional theory known as time-dependent density functional theory. Additionally, we have implemented a time-dependent local density approximation (TDLA) and applied it to investigate the periodic dynamical structures of a particle in a box. Our results indicate that the TDLA accurately captures the qualitative features of these periodic dynamical structures. Finally, we examine the periodic dynamical structures of a two-dimensional electron gas subjected to a strong magnetic field. We find that the statistical nonlocality of periodic dynamical structures in this scenario is more pronounced than in the case of a particle in a box. This enhanced nonlocality is attributed to the interplay between the periodic dynamical structure and the quantum Hall effect. Consequently, the spatially nonlocal structure, which successfully describes the one-dimensional case, fails to adequately describe the two-dimensional case. This discrepancy underscores the necessity of incorporating both temporal and spatial nonlocality into the density functional. We conclude that the spatially nonlocal structure derived from the GGA is insufficient for describing periodic dynamical structures in two-dimensional systems with strong electron-electron interactions. To address this, we propose a novel method for constructing the exchange-correlation potential that incorporates both temporal and spatial nonlocality. This approach is based on the observation that the periodic dynamical structure in a two-dimensional electron gas under a strong magnetic field can be approximately represented as a product of temporal and spatial nonlocal structures. We show that this new construction yields a more accurate exchange-correlation potential than the GGA. Finally, we apply this newly constructed exchange-correlation potential to a two-dimensional electron gas with moderate electron-electron interactions. Our findings reveal that the periodic dynamical structure in this case exhibits greater complexity than in the strong interaction regime. We introduce a phenomenological framework designed to investigate flexible scattering amplitudes across all kinematic regimes. This approach is grounded in the analytic properties of these amplitudes and their expansion within the soft limit. By applying this formalism to various processes involving quarks, gluons, and electroweak bosons, we derive constraints on the subleading soft functions governing these expanded terms. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this method can be extended to final-state observables, such as jet cross sections, and explore potential generalizations to massive particles and beyond-the-soft-limit regions. Finally, we outline future extensions of the approach, including its application to final observables beyond jets and its relevance to final-state jet substructure. Our findings will be implemented in the open-source Python package feffnet. This work represents a collaboration between phenomenologists and theorists. Additionally, we provide a pedagogical overview of modern techniques in scattering amplitude theory, covering eikonal expansions, soft limits, and analytic properties. These resources are available in the accompanying lecture notes. We anticipate that this framework will serve as a valuable tool for analyzing final observables in the near future. Additionally, we have developed a series of exercises to reinforce the material presented in these notes, which can be accessed through an online platform. We examine the impact of the Casimir effect on blackbody thermodynamics, specifically focusing on zero-point energy shifts caused by boundary conditions. Our analysis reveals that these boundary effects result in negative pressure and a reduced internal energy compared to standard blackbody radiation. Furthermore, we explore how these boundary conditions influence the system's entropy. Finally, we apply these findings to a photon gas confined within a box, demonstrating that the box's dimensions produce measurable corrections to the photon gas thermodynamics. These results offer potential experimental verification through the study of boundary effects in blackbody radiation. Additionally, we briefly discuss the implications of these findings for the cosmological constant problem. We examine a beeping network where each node operates in one of two modes: beeping or listening. Nodes in beeping mode broadcast silence, whereas those in listening mode detect beeps from at least one neighboring node in beeping mode. The objective is to minimize total beeping duration by identifying a small subset of nodes to activate for broadcasting silence, ensuring that all other listening nodes can perceive at least one beep from a neighbor. This problem is analyzed within the framework of graph theory. We establish both upper and lower bounds for this optimization. Specifically, for any graph $G$, we demonstrate that a set $S$ satisfying the requirement exists with a size bounded by $|S| \leq \frac{1}{2} \log_2 \chi(G)$, where $\chi(G)$ denotes the chromatic number of $G$. Furthermore, we prove that for every integer $k \geq 2$, there exists a graph $G$ such that the minimum size of such a set is at least $\frac{1}{2} \log_2 \frac{\chi(G)}{k} - 1$. Additionally, we explore the problem's complexity and propose a randomized algorithm that solves it efficiently. This algorithm operates in expected $O(n+m)$ time with high probability, where $n$ represents the number of nodes and $m$ the number of edges. The approach involves identifying a maximal independent set and selecting a random subset of these nodes to beep. We also present a straightforward algorithm with a worst-case running time of $O(n+m)$ that identifies a set $S$ of size at most $\frac{1}{2} \log_2 \chi(G)$. This method relies on iteratively removing nodes with a degree of at most 1 and subsequently identifying a maximal independent set from the remaining subgraph. Finally, we extend our findings to the weighted variant of the problem. In this scenario, each node is assigned a weight, and the goal is to select a set $S$ that minimizes the sum of these weights. We illustrate that this weighted problem is NP-hard. However, we also provide a polynomial-time algorithm that solves it efficiently. The algorithm identifies a maximal independent set and then selects the node with the minimum weight from this set to beep. We also demonstrate that this approach yields a set $S$ whose total weight is at most $\frac{1}{2} \log_2 \chi(G)$ times the optimal weight. Finally, we establish that the problem remains NP-hard

This study investigates the pressure-dependent critical temperature of H$_{3}$S hydride hydrosulfide, a high-temperature superconductor, by employing the density functional theory-based finite temperature molecular dynamics method. The analysis examines the pressure-induced evolution of the H$_{3}$S crystal structure, phonon dispersion relations, and electronic band structures. Results indicate that the pressure-driven phase transition from the CImma to the P6_3/mmc structure occurs at 200 GPa. Furthermore, the study explores the phase transition's impact on the isotope effect on critical temperature (TC) and the pressure-dependent TC. Notably, the isotope effect on TC diminishes as pressure increases, vanishing entirely at 200 GPa. Additionally, the pressure-dependent TC exhibits a non-monotonic trend, peaking at 210 GPa. These findings offer valuable insights into the superconducting mechanism of H$_{3}$S hydride. The associated computational code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1990/PhononDispersion. Finally, the paper discusses the potential for experimental verification of these results. Motion planning for robots operating in dynamic environments is a critical research area. This paper introduces a new method that leverages the temporal and spatial evolution of dynamic objects to generate spatially restricted motion plans. The proposed approach integrates these restrictions into the motion planning process, thereby reducing the search space and enhancing computational efficiency. Furthermore, the method introduces a novel dynamic spatial restriction, which is derived from the temporal evolution of objects and embedded into the planning process. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness using a case study focused on motion planning within a busy airport baggage claim area. Results indicate that the proposed approach significantly decreases computation time compared to standard methods, such as those based on the A* algorithm. Additionally, the method successfully generates motion plans for complex scenarios involving numerous obstacles with varying speeds and trajectories. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Spatial-Restriction-Creation-for-Motion-Planning. The accompanying video can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222. Finally, we outline several potential future research directions. First, the current method assumes perfect knowledge of object evolution, which is often unavailable in real-world applications; therefore, future work should address scenarios where object evolution is uncertain. Second, the method currently generates plans for a single robot; extending it to handle multiple robots simultaneously is another promising avenue. Third, the method produces a single plan, whereas real-world applications often require generating multiple plans to ensure robustness against uncertainties. Fourth, the method is not inherently real-time, as it does not account for the time required to compute a plan; thus, future research should aim to develop real-time solutions. Finally, the method is currently limited to two-dimensional settings, and extending it to three-dimensional spaces is a valuable future direction. We believe these extensions will further improve the method's effectiveness and applicability. We hope this paper inspires future research in this domain. Thank you.

Keywords: motion planning, dynamic environments, spatial restrictions, motion planning uncertainty, real-time motion planning, 3D motion planning.

This study addresses the challenge of selecting a collaborative user group within a multiuser MIMO downlink framework, where the base station jointly optimizes precoding and power allocation to maximize the sum rate of the selected users. To achieve this, the authors propose a novel encoding technique that transforms the original combinatorial optimization problem into a convex one by applying an $l_{0}$ norm penalty to the power allocation vector. This encoding ensures that non-selected users receive zero power, effectively treating them as if they do not exist within the optimized system. The resulting convex problem is solved using the group LASSO algorithm, which simultaneously performs variable selection and coefficient estimation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed group LASSO method achieves performance comparable to exhaustive search solutions while maintaining a low computational complexity. Furthermore, the paper illustrates the application of this approach in a massive MIMO context. The results indicate that the group LASSO algorithm significantly outperforms the standard LASSO method, which selects users based on the magnitude of their channel coefficients. Additionally, the group LASSO approach proves to be more robust against channel estimation errors than the conventional LASSO method. Finally, the study shows that the proposed group LASSO method can identify the optimal user set in massive MIMO systems, a capability that standard LASSO lacks. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions of this work. Keywords: Collaborative user selection, multiuser MIMO, precoding, power allocation, group LASSO, massive MIMO. We demonstrate that the affine variety semirings (PVS) and monoid varieties (PMS) derived from data concerning rational functions on a tropical curve $C$ are finitely produced over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$. This result holds under the condition that the tropical semiring is valued in $\mathbb{R}$, with the valuation of a rational function $f$ defined as $v(f)=-\deg_{\infty}(f)$. Furthermore, we establish that the logical function semifield (LFS) associated with $C$ is also finitely produced over $\mathbb{T}$. This finding extends a theorem by K. Ziegler, which asserts that the tropical semiring of a tropical curve is finitely produced over $\mathbb{T}$. Additionally, we provide a characterization of when a PVS or PMS is finitely produced over $\mathbb{T}$ based on the properties of its $\mathbb{R}$-points. As an application, we characterize the LFS of a tropical curve $C$ as a finitely generated semifield extension of the LFS of its skeleton. The proofs rely on the observation that the coordinate rings of tropical varieties are generated by monomials of rational functions on $C$ whose valuations lie within a specific subset of the PVS or PMS. This insight also enables the construction of a finite set of rational functions on $C$ capable of generating the LFS of $C$ over $\mathbb{T}$. The primary tool employed is the Riemann-Roch theorem for $C$. Finally, we present an example of a tropical curve $C$ for which the PVS and PMS are not finitely produced over $\mathbb{T}$, and we characterize the LFS of $C$ in this specific case. This example is inspired by the work of M. Sanyal. The paper concludes with several open questions. The $Q$-procedure is a straightforward yet effective technique for deriving the Boltzmann equation's collision term, yet it lacks a rigorous justification. This paper presents a formal argument grounded in hyperviscosity, demonstrating that the $Q$-procedure consistently converges to the Boltzmann collision operator. Furthermore, we illustrate that this approach can be applied to both hard and soft potentials. Finally, we outline an avenue for future research to address the challenge of justifying the Boltzmann equation's linearized collision operator.

GLOSSARIES consist of concept-name (CN)-definition (D) pairs, where definitions are rich in domain-specific terminology. By training on these definition gaps, Dict-BERT acquires an enhanced understanding of concepts within a particular domain. We evaluated Dict-BERT on the English Wikipedia domain, which contains the largest collection of CN-D pairs available. Our findings indicate that Dict-BERT surpasses standard BERT in understanding domain concepts and in completing sentences within that domain. Additionally, we demonstrate that Dict-BERT can identify the concept being defined in a passage, a capability that conventional pre-trained models lack. Finally, we show that fine-tuning Dict-BERT on natural language inference tasks yields improvements over models trained solely on general corpora. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple parties, each holding distinct data dimensions, collaborate to train machine learning models. This paper investigates a specific VFL application in education, where schools possess student data with varying feature dimensions and jointly aim to enhance student outcomes. We introduce a novel framework for VFL privacy attacks, enabling one or more participating schools to compromise the privacy of others. This approach leverages a specific VFL architecture that allows attackers to bypass the limitations of traditional membership inference attacks. Our pragmatic attack framework demonstrates that, with minimal additional computational cost, an attacker can successfully infer private information from a model trained on disjoint data dimensions. We validate this through experiments on a real-world education dataset, showing that our attack achieves a 10% improvement in accuracy compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we explore the application of this attack framework in other domains, such as healthcare. Finally, we discuss potential defenses against our proposed attack framework. We investigate the exclusive two-body decay of $B$ mesons into a baryon and a dark antibaryon, where the dark antibaryon originates from a hidden sector interacting with the Standard Model solely through a massive mediator. Utilizing QCD light-cone sum principles, we derive the hadronic transition form factors for $B \to B_q B_l$ processes, involving transitions from the $B$ meson to both the light and heavy antibaryons. We compute the branching ratios for these exclusive decays and analyze their sensitivity to the mediator's mass. Furthermore, we establish constraints on the mediator mass by comparing our predicted branching ratios with experimental limits. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting dark antibaryons at the LHC. Our findings indicate that the baryon-to-baryon conversion signal could be observed if the mediator mass falls below approximately 10 GeV. Additionally, we note that the baryon-to-antibaryon signal may be obscured by the substantial background arising from baryon-to-baryon transitions. However, we demonstrate that this background can be effectively mitigated by reconstructing the missing mass of the antibaryon in the final state. We conclude that the proposed baryon number violating process is detectable at the LHC, with the primary challenge being the accurate reconstruction of the antibaryon in the final state. This study underscores the necessity of developing advanced antibaryon reconstruction techniques for the LHC. Our results suggest that the baryon number violating process $B \to B_q B_l$ is accessible to the LHC, and we recommend that future LHC analyses incorporate this channel in their search strategies. We also emphasize the need for further research to explore the antibaryon sector at the LHC. Our findings may have significant implications for the future, potentially leading to the discovery of the antibaryon sector and a deeper understanding of the dark sector. This paper introduces a new intelligent urban defense system designed to manage the allocation of defensive resources amid socio-cyber-physical attacks. This game evaluates multiple attack scenarios and utilizes a learning algorithm to identify the optimal strategy for resource distribution. The study demonstrates that the equilibrium of this defense game can be effectively approximated through a sequence of learning processes. The results indicate that the developed algorithm successfully identifies the most appropriate tactical strategy for each scenario. Additionally, the algorithm's performance is analyzed in terms of computational complexity and execution time. Finally, the paper discusses potential extensions of this work, such as implementing distributed algorithms and enhancing the model's robustness. The study concludes that the proposed algorithm offers a practical and effective solution for safeguarding critical assets from diverse attack types. This study examines the thermodynamics of a black star confined within a cavity, focusing on the impact of a background cosmological constant $\Lambda$. We demonstrate that the system's temperature exhibits a minimum, and at constant entropy, the black star undergoes a first-order phase transition at $\Lambda = \Lambda_{\rm crit}$, shifting from a high-temperature state just below the critical value to a low-temperature state just above it. Furthermore, we establish that the Hawking--Page phase transition also occurs for the black star at a specific critical $\Lambda$. These findings indicate that the black star's thermodynamic behavior closely mirrors that of a conventional black hole. Additionally, we identify a novel phenomenon where the black star can exist in two distinct states at the same temperature and entropy within a narrow range of $\Lambda$ values. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the cosmological constant problem. This work extends our earlier research [Phys. Rev. D 101, 064010 (2020)] to include scenarios with negative $\Lambda$. Our findings may hold significance for understanding the relationship between black hole thermodynamics and the cosmological constant problem. The AWAKE experiment at CERN investigates beam-beam interactions by utilizing a proton beam to drive proton-driven linear wakefields within the LHCb ring. This study examines beam emission generated by the betatron resonance, a phenomenon anticipated to occur during the Run 2 phase. The analysis employs a 3D particle-in-cell code to model the proton beam propagation and electron beam dynamics. Results indicate that electron emission is triggered by the proton beam's breathing mode, initiating at the beam pipe boundary and subsequently amplifying through the breathing mode itself. The simulation predicts an initial electron emission of approximately 10^4 particles, which is expected to be detectable. Furthermore, the study explores the potential for controlling this emission by adjusting the proton beam's initial profile. These findings could inform strategies for managing beam emittance in future proton-driven wakefield accelerators. Additionally, the observed emission is identified as a form of self-Compton scattering, a process that could be investigated in future experiments. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these results for the AWAKE experiment and their broader relevance to the field of plasma accelerators.

This study introduces a new algorithm for learning differentially private (DP) decision trees in a distributed environment. The approach employs a noisy binary search technique to privately identify the optimal split point for a given feature, ensuring that the resulting private split is provably more accurate than a noisy alternative. We demonstrate that this method achieves $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP and present a novel, provably precise variant that surpasses current state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we propose a new, provably precise algorithm for private hyperparameter tuning, which we integrate with the decision tree learning process. Our experimental results indicate that these algorithms can be executed within a few minutes on a single machine, producing decision trees that are nearly as accurate as those generated by non-private methods. Finally, we release the first open-source library for DP distributed decision tree learning. This paper introduces a novel inertial dynamical system featuring a vanishing Tikhonov regularization term, designed to robustly guide the approximate trajectory of an accelerated gradient method toward the minimum norm solution for convex feasibility problems and convex minimization tasks involving Tikhonov regularization. This study examines how extended impurities influence microwaves traveling through the superconducting state of cuprates. We demonstrate that microwaves detect kinetic energy-driven superconductivity, and their propagation is governed by the ratio of impurity scattering to superfluid velocity fluctuations. Consequently, the microwave conductivity of these materials can be tuned by adjusting the impurity concentration and the energy driving the superconductivity. These findings offer a potential explanation for the anomalous microwave conductivity observed in cuprates. Furthermore, our results indicate that the superconducting mechanism in cuprates is distinct from that in iron-based superconductors. Finally, this work suggests that microwaves serve as a valuable tool for investigating kinetic energy-driven superconductivity. The research was conducted using the open-source Python package `scipower`. Plants are vital to human existence, yet their form is dictated by environmental factors like sunlight, water, and wind, often resulting in shapes that are less than ideal for specific applications. This paper introduces GrowSpace, a framework designed to sculpt plants into arbitrary 3D structures. By integrating a 3D shape prior with a growth model, GrowSpace directs plant growth toward a target geometry. The system was validated on two datasets: one featuring 3D structures created from point clouds of leaves and flowers, and another comprising 3D models from the COSEG dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that GrowSpace can successfully generate plants that closely replicate these target shapes. Furthermore, the framework enables the creation of novel plant structures that are both aesthetically pleasing and functional. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertk2/growspace. This work was presented at the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) conference in 2021.

We establish a new cycle property for Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs) with arbitrary cliques, demonstrating that for any subcollection of these cliques, there exists a unique conformal map sending them to the upper half-plane that almost surely preserves the image of the remaining subcollection. This result relies on the quantum gluing formula for quantum disks, which we derive using the absolute continuity of the corresponding Liouville Conformal Field Theory (LCFT) measures. We further provide an alternative proof of the absolute continuity of the quantum disk measure relative to the LiCFT measure, leveraging the stochastic Loewner equation. Additionally, we offer a novel construction of the SLE cycle, which yields the absolute continuity of the quantum disk measure as a consequence. These findings have significant implications for the absolute continuity of LCFT measures on general Liouville surfaces. Finally, we present an application to the absolute continuity of Brownian motion conditioned to avoid a set of points. These results are derived in collaboration with Jianfeng Yang. We evaluated various OpenCV algorithms for image preprocessing within the context of face detection and recognition using the MORPH-II database. Our analysis covered face detection, skin color segmentation, face alignment, face cropping, and face reconstruction. The study compared the performance of CV2's Haar cascade classifier against OpenCV's DNN module, specifically utilizing the Caffe framework with the VGG-16 model. This paper introduces a novel deep learning approach to the diversification challenge, which involves distributing a fixed budget across multiple assets to minimize risk. We utilize a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) to model the distribution of optimal portfolio weights, conditioned on the returns and volatilities of individual assets. Furthermore, we show that the trained GAN can effectively recover the optimal weight distribution from a given set of asset characteristics. India is poised to launch its inaugural space telescope within the next few years, with a planned launch mass of approximately 1,000 kg. This document outlines the scientific and technical rationale behind the proposed Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST). The primary scientific goals of INSIST are to characterize the atmospheres of exoplanets, investigate the origins of the solar system, and study the formation and evolution of galaxies. To achieve these objectives, the telescope is designed to operate in the 0.4 to 2.5 $\mu$m wavelength range, utilizing a 1.2-meter primary mirror. The payload architecture comprises a high-resolution spectrograph (HRIS) covering 0.4 to 2.0 $\mu$m and a medium-resolution spectrograph (MRIS) spanning 0.6 to 2.5 $\mu$m. Additionally, a wide-field imager (WFI) with a 0.5-degree field of view and a 0.1-degree instantaneous field of view is included to facilitate target acquisition and enable multi-object spectroscopy. The HRIS is engineered to deliver a resolving power of 100,000, while the MRIS offers a resolving power of 10,000. The paper also addresses the necessary technologies and their development timelines, alongside a proposed mission profile. Ultimately, INSIST is envisioned as a flagship-class mission capable of delivering transformative results in exoplanet science. This task force should be responsible for defining the mission profile, developing a technology readiness plan, and preparing a comprehensive mission proposal. Furthermore, it is suggested that the task force be established as an independent entity, free from the constraints of existing institutes or departments. Finally, the paper outlines a strategy for securing funding and outlines the steps required to initiate the mission. This study investigates the utility of natural cubic splines in analyzing longitudinal data from Alzheimer's disease clinical trials. We introduce a novel spline-based approach designed to estimate the mean longitudinal trajectory of biomarkers over time for both treatment and placebo groups. This method facilitates the evaluation of treatment effects and their interactions with other variables. By employing a unified framework, we can assess treatment impacts across various time scales, such as short-term versus long-term effects. Additionally, the proposed technique offers a flexible model for estimating mean trajectories, enabling the detection of subtle changes that might be missed by simpler methods. Furthermore, we develop a test for nonlinearity to determine whether a nonlinear model is necessary for a specific dataset. A simulation study is conducted to compare the performance of our method against a linear model, revealing that the spline-based approach yields superior results. Finally, we apply this methodology to data from an Alzheimer's clinical trial. The findings indicate that the nonlinear model provides a more accurate estimation of mean trajectories for both treatment and placebo groups, while also demonstrating that the treatment effect varies over time. These results underscore the value of using nonlinear models to enhance the precision of Alzheimer's disease treatment effect estimates. The global enhancement of action (GEA) method is introduced to identify action sequences that are most likely to drive transitions between states. GEA functions as a black-box optimizer that enhances the probability of a transition by uniformly increasing the likelihood of every time step within the transition period. This approach is applicable to any environment where a policy is represented as a product of temporal distributions. The method's efficacy is validated through experiments on a 2D pendulum system and a 3D double-gimbal system. Furthermore, GEA successfully uncovers complex transition routes in the 3D double-gimbal system that were previously unidentified. These findings demonstrate that GEA can reveal intricate transition routes in dynamical systems, offering a pathway to a deeper understanding of their underlying mechanisms. The GEA technique is implemented in PyTorch and is publicly accessible at https://github.com/kevinzhang99/GEA. Additionally, the code required to reproduce the results presented in this study is available on the authors' GitHub repository. This paper introduces the concepts of the standard semigroup spectrum and standard group spectrum for both semigroups and groups. For groups, the standard structure space consists of all maximal subsemigroups that are also subgroups, equipped with the topology generated by the zero sets of semigroup characters. We demonstrate that the standard structure spaces of abelian groups are homeomorphic to compact Hausdorff spaces. Furthermore, the paper establishes the standard representation of groups using semigroups and group ideals through sheaves of semigroups over group spectra. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the standard spectrum of a group and the classical spectrum of its semigroup algebra. Finally, we outline several open problems regarding standard structure spaces.

This paper addresses the challenge of mapping natural language to SQL queries. While previous research has primarily focused on either semantic parsing or supporting techniques, we introduce a novel end-to-end cross-domain approach that integrates both aspects. Specifically, we employ a task-to-SQL module to generate task-specific queries, which serve as a bridge to enhance the main text-to-SQL parser. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the Spider and WikiSQL benchmarks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/End-to-End-Cross-Domain-SQL.

This study addresses the secure navigation of multi-robot systems by introducing a data-informed, risk-averse Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework. This approach utilizes data-driven risk metrics to quantify the probability of collisions and other adverse events, integrating them into a new MPC formulation. The resulting optimization problem minimizes a cost function that balances collision risk against mission objectives, such as energy efficiency and path smoothness. To ensure computational efficiency, the paper develops a method for calculating these data-driven risk metrics, leveraging a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model to learn the joint distribution of robot states from historical data. Furthermore, a computationally efficient algorithm is proposed to solve the MPC optimization problem. The proposed framework is validated through simulations of multi-robot navigation scenarios, demonstrating its ability to significantly reduce collision risks while maintaining robust performance. The results indicate that the method effectively balances risk aversion with mission goals, even under conditions of uncertainty and limited computational resources. Overall, this work presents a promising framework for secure multi-robot navigation, offering a practical solution for real-world applications. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Risk-Averse-MPC.

We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a dwarf galaxy situated approximately 780 kiloparsecs from the Milky Way. This object exhibits a high metallicity of $Z=0.017$ and a low central dark matter density of $\rho_{DM}(0) = 1.1 \pm 0.3 M_{\odot} \text{pc}^{-3}$. The study presents a new kinematic analysis of And XXV, utilizing a sample of 12 stars with radial velocities ranging from $-100$ to $-180$ km/s. By applying a Bayesian dynamical model, we determined the galaxy's mass within 1.5 kpc to be $M(1.5 \text{kpc}) = 1.0 \pm 0.2 \times 10^7 M_{\odot}$, with a mass-to-light ratio of $\Upsilon_V = 1.0 \pm 0.2$. These findings indicate that And XXV is likely a member of the Andromeda galaxy's dwarf galaxy group. Furthermore, the low central dark matter density suggests that And XXV may have experienced a recent interaction with the Andromeda galaxy. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. This study examines various approximations for simulating the thermodynamic properties of humid air, evaluating their accuracy against exact models and their thermodynamic consistency. Our findings indicate that while several commonly used methods fail to qualify as equation-of-state formulations, specific modifications to these approaches can be recast in this manner. These adjustments offer a thermodynamically consistent framework for modeling humid air. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these modified equations can be efficiently solved for the required state variables. The proposed modifications involve either employing a more precise value for the specific heat capacity of dry air or utilizing a more accurate approximation for the latent heat of vaporization. Additionally, we present a new equation-of-state formulation that is both thermodynamically consistent and highly accurate. This model is derived from the Peng-Robinson equation of state, originally designed for pure substances, by incorporating terms to account for the presence of water vapor. We demonstrate that this model achieves an accuracy of approximately 0.01% for enthalpy and 0.001% for entropy across a broad range of temperatures and pressures. Finally, we outline how to derive the necessary partial derivatives of this model for use in computational fluid dynamics simulations. The source code for all equations presented in this work is accessible via a public repository. This code was utilized to benchmark the computational efficiency of the various equations against the exact model. The results confirm that the most efficient approximation is the ideal gas law, followed by the van der Waals equation. In abstract algebra, the concept of an outer algebra refers to a structure built from a base set where elements are combined with those of the algebra. This paper extends the study of outer algebras into matroid theory. We define and examine outer matroids, demonstrating that they possess numerous properties analogous to standard matroids. Additionally, we explore outer polymatroids, which serve as a relaxation of the outer matroid concept. The work also investigates outer homomorphisms and mappings between outer matroids, proving that many familiar matroid properties are retained in this generalized context. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of an $n$-fold outer matroid, representing another generalization of the outer matroid concept. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of the applications of outer matroids. Overall, this study aims to broaden the framework of outer algebra to encompass matroid theory.

We introduce a new method for training dialogue state tracking (DST) models that incorporates ASR uncertainty. To model this uncertainty, we utilize word confusion networks (WCN) as a compact representation of the full probability distribution over the ASR output. By integrating this WCN distribution into the input of a DST encoder, we enable the DST model to process a condensed representation of the ASR posterior distribution. We evaluated our approach using the DSGE dataset, which features both English and German utterances. The results demonstrate that modeling ASR uncertainty enhances performance, particularly in handling incorrect transcriptions. Additionally, our method yields substantial improvements in handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, which are common in natural language. Finally, we show that DST models trained with this approach are more robust to variations in the training data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexanderkoster/asr-uncertainty-for-dst. The trained models can be downloaded from https://github.com/alexanderkoster/asr-uncertainty-for-dst/releases/tag/v1.0.0. Our implementation is open-source and compatible with any ASR system that provides a WCN representation of its output. Furthermore, we plan to release a Python package that encapsulates the entire DST training pipeline, including the handling of ASR uncertainty. This package will support any WCN-based ASR system and is designed to be easily extensible for incorporating additional features. We anticipate that this package will facilitate future research in modeling and handling ASR uncertainty within dialogue systems. We introduce a method to calculate intricacy for universal entry frameworks. First, we establish the concept of intricacy for these frameworks and demonstrate that it aligns with the intricacy of the underlying languages. Second, we prove that the intricacy of a universal entry framework remains invariant regardless of the specific set of target languages selected. Third, we derive an explicit formula for this invariant value. Finally, we apply these findings to the situations where the framework comprises all deterministic context-free languages and all context-free languages. As an application, we establish that the intricate encoding length is equivalent to the Sipp length for deterministic context-free languages and is bounded by the yield length for context-free languages. Additionally, we show that the intricate encoding length exceeds the yield length for certain context-free languages. Furthermore, we prove that the intricate encoding length surpasses both the Sipp length and the yield length for specific deterministic context-free languages. Finally, we provide an upper bound for the intricate encoding length of deterministic context-free languages using yield length. These findings represent the first instance of utilizing intricacy to investigate the relationships among various length measures associated with context-free languages. The techniques developed in this study are also applicable to other universal entry frameworks. Quantum entanglement is a fundamental resource for numerous applications, including teleportation, superdense coding, and quantum key distribution. However, the standard method for quantifying entanglement in optical systems, known as entanglement of formation, is often difficult to calculate and lacks a direct experimental measurement protocol. This study introduces a protocol to determine the optimal fidelity achievable through local operations and classical communication (LOCC) for a given biphoton state. This approach enables the optimal assessment of entanglement within quantum optical systems. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to various biphoton states, such as those generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing and parametric down-conversion. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's utility in the context of biphoton teleportation. Our findings indicate that the optimal entanglement between biphoton states is typically lower than that of the standard two-qubit entanglement of formation, thereby revealing previously unrecognized entanglement resources in quantum optical systems. These results hold significant potential for advancing quantum information processing tasks. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package, OptimalLOCC, to facilitate the implementation of this protocol. The package is accessible at https://github.com/QuantumOpticsResearchGroup/OptimalLOCC. Our code is also available within the Python package PyQEM, which can be found at https://github.com/QuantumOpticsResearchGroup/pyQEM. PyQEM is a versatile tool for simulating quantum experiments involving quantum optics, quantum information, and quantum computing. It supports a wide range of sources, including quantum emitters, lasers, and lasers driven by quantum emitters, as well as various optical elements and circuits. Users can construct their own quantum circuits and perform measurements, enabling the simulation of diverse quantum experiments. PyQEM is also accessible at https://github.com/QuantumOpticsResearchGroup/pyQEM. This study examines the characteristics of low-frequency (approximately 100 Hz) coherent toroidal modes observed in the JET tokamak, specifically those resembling palm trees. The analysis utilizes data from the JET Electron Cyclotron Emission Radiation (ECER) diagnostic, which tracks the radial distribution of optically thin cyclotron radiation from a specific electron population. By applying a Fourier transform to the temporal evolution of this radial distribution, the research identifies the presence of coherent toroidal modes. These modes are linked to the periodic fluctuations of the magnetic axis, a phenomenon also detected using JET motional Stark effect (MSE) polarization measurements. The study further demonstrates that the toroidal mode numbers of these palm tree modes correspond to the Fourier components of the magnetic axis oscillation. Additionally, the radial structure of the palm tree mode is shown to be governed by the radial profile of cyclotron emission, which is determined by the radial distribution of the fluctuating electron population. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for understanding the origin and nature of palm tree modes. The proposed model suggests that these modes arise from a combination of magnetic axis oscillations and a specific population of electrons, such as those generated by neutral beam injection. This work offers a comprehensive framework for interpreting the origin and nature of palm tree modes, which is essential for analyzing their impact on tokamak performance. The findings are expected to be applicable to other tokamaks. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of the proposed model. Although pretraining has emerged as a highly effective strategy for numerous NLP tasks, it remains unclear whether models derived from pretraining can effectively handle basic arithmetic operations. This study introduces a straightforward benchmark designed to evaluate the capabilities of both domain-specific and general-purpose pretraining models in the context of incremental learning. Our findings indicate that the primary obstacle for these models lies in the lack of arithmetic data during both pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed benchmark can be readily expanded to include more complex tasks. Ultimately, we offer several practical recommendations to enhance the ability of pretraining models to perform arithmetic. This study examines how the spatial arrangement of synapses influences the dynamics of recurrent networks of integrate-and-fire neurons. We introduce a generalized model featuring two distinct spatial dimensions, where synapses are distributed randomly within a specific area. By deriving an analytical expression for the average post-synaptic potential, we demonstrate that the mean coupling strength scales with the inverse of this area. Furthermore, we show that the network's firing rate depends on this mean coupling, thereby linking firing rate to the area of random synapse distribution. Finally, we validate our analytical findings through numerical simulations. Additionally, our findings may help explain how the development of synapses in specific regions contributes to the emergence of complex behaviors. Program fixes are a critical component of program repair, yet identifying effective fixes remains difficult due to the vast search space. While many existing approaches rely on fault localization to generate fault fragments, this process often fails to pinpoint the exact faulty code, resulting in an inadequate search space. To address this, we introduce antagonistic patch creation, a technique that automatically generates patches by synthesizing antagonistic code. This method utilizes a neural network to generate patches based on the syntactic and semantic characteristics of antagonistic code. We evaluated our approach using the Defects4J dataset, comparing it against the state-of-the-art tool, Magpie. Our results demonstrate that antagonistic patch creation successfully repairs 10 out of the 10 new cases that Magpie failed to resolve. Furthermore, analysis of the generated patches reveals that they incorporate syntactic and semantic features similar to those found in actual program patches. To our knowledge, this is the first study to employ antagonistic code for program repair. This study investigates the capability region of grouped independent and identically distributed full-duplex two-way channels. In this setup, two users exchange information over a shared wireless link, with each user capable of simultaneously transmitting and receiving full-duplex signals. The users employ grouped data spectrum processing to achieve a finite number of groups, where each group contains an infinite number of data dimensions. We demonstrate that the capability region of this channel is the convex hull formed by the union of the capability regions of all possible data spectrum processing schemes. Furthermore, we derive the capability region for a specific scenario involving time-varying channels. Finally, we compare the achievable rates using data spectrum processing against traditional time-division and frequency-division strategies. The findings indicate that the proposed data spectrum approach yields a significant performance gain compared to both time- and frequency-division methods. Additionally, the derived achievable rates are shown to be tight. The results also reveal that the achievable rate for each user is bounded from above by the minimum of the user's channel capacity and the sum-rate capability of the channel. These upper bounds are achieved when the number of data spectrum groups is sufficiently large. Finally, we examine the capability region for a specific instance of the channel and provide a numerical illustration of the performance gains. The paper concludes with a discussion on the potential application of data spectrum processing in other communication scenarios. This work represents the first effort to introduce the concept of data spectrum processing to the field of wireless communications. The capability region analysis is expected to be valuable for future research on data spectrum processing in various communication systems. We introduce a new method for analyzing 3-dimensional flow, designed to determine the collision structure and equation of state (EOS) of nuclear matter. This technique is demonstrated using data from Au+Au collisions at 19.6 GeV conducted at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). The collision geometry is categorized into three distinct types: head-on, mid-central, and peripheral. By measuring the average transverse momentum ($p_T$) of charged particles as a function of their polar angle, we observe that $p_T$ increases with the centrality of the collision. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the slope of the $p_T$ distribution and the collision type. This relationship is modeled using a first-order Taylor expansion of the $p_T$ spectrum, where the slope is defined as $a_1$. We demonstrate that $a_1$ exhibits a linear correlation with the collision type. Additionally, we examine the connection between the intercept $a_0$ and the collision type, finding that $a_0$ is nearly independent of centrality. Finally, we explore the link between the ratio $a_1/a_0$ and the collision type, revealing that this ratio decreases as the collision type shifts from head-on to peripheral. These findings are interpreted within the framework of the relativistic mean-field model. By incorporating the EOS into the model, we successfully reproduce the experimental data, thereby validating the efficacy of this new analysis approach. This methodology offers a novel tool for investigating nuclear EOS and determining the specific impact of the collision type on the resulting data. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to both isospin-symmetric and asymmetric systems. We anticipate that this technique will prove valuable for analyzing data from the Beam Energy Scan program at RHIC and for experiments at the Future Circular Collider. This paper introduces a new, decentralized wireless transmission framework utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). By leveraging the inherent properties of GNNs, the system enables the transmitter to dynamically adapt to channel conditions and the receiver to adjust its decoding strategy without any direct interaction between the two parties. Additionally, we propose a novel training methodology for GNN-based transmitters that eliminates the need for a digital-to-analog conversion module. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed scheme achieves a substantial reduction in Bit Error Rate (BER) compared to existing GNN-based transmitters and significantly outperforms traditional training approaches used in wireless GNN research. Furthermore, we confirm that the proposed GNN architecture is feasible to implement on FPGA hardware. Finally, we establish a new baseline for decentralized communication by showing that our method outperforms other established schemes in this domain. This study investigates the temporal evolution of homicide rates in the Brazilian state of Goiás between 2002 and 2014, analyzing data from 200 municipalities. The analysis reveals that, excluding the years 2002 and 2003, the homicide time series exhibits stationarity. Furthermore, the series displays long-range dependence characterized by a Hurst exponent of approximately 0.7, indicating that the state experienced a persistent trend toward increasing homicide rates. Additionally, the data demonstrates anti-persistence in first differences, suggesting a tendency for the homicide rate to revert to its mean. Cluster analysis indicates that, starting in 2003, the municipalities can be divided into two distinct groups: one with consistently higher rates than the state average and another with consistently lower rates. This division remained stable until 2011, after which the group with higher rates split into two subgroups. Finally, the study examines the impact of specific events, such as the inauguration of the state prison system in 2008 and the 2014 World Cup, on homicide trends. These events were found to have no significant effect on the homicide rate in Goiás. The research concludes that, despite the 2014 World Cup, the state failed to achieve a reduction in homicides, thereby missing the opportunity to reverse the upward trend observed since 2003. This outcome is attributed to the absence of a comprehensive, state-wide strategy to combat violence. Instead, Goiás has relied on isolated, sporadic initiatives, such as the "Pacote de Medidas para a Segurança Pública" introduced in 2012, which have proven ineffective in reducing homicide rates. The paper underscores the necessity for a coordinated, statewide approach to security to successfully curb violence. Finally, the study recommends that future research incorporate additional variables, including socio-economic factors and the political landscape, to better understand the causes of homicide in Goiás. This would involve employing more sophisticated statistical models capable of analyzing the complex interactions between social, economic, and political variables. Such an approach would provide a more holistic understanding of the issue and facilitate the design of more effective public policies. Ultimately, the paper emphasizes the need for a comprehensive, integrated strategy to address violence in the state. By adopting a more sophisticated analytical framework, researchers can gain deeper insights into the multifaceted nature of homicide in Goiás and contribute to the development of more effective public policies. This approach would enable a more nuanced understanding of the problem and support the creation of targeted interventions

Axion-based solar models are examined using the upcoming French IAXO experiment, with a specific focus on the BabyIAXO subscale version. The study analyzes the axion flux generated by the axiglon mechanism within the Sun's core, a process driven by the non-uniformity of the temperature gradient. This mechanism is investigated across a range of parameters, including the coupling constant $g_{\phi qq}$, the axiglon mass $m_{\phi}$, and the axiglon lifetime $\tau_{\phi}$. The analysis evaluates the axion flux and energy production rate, determining the parameter space where these signals remain undetectable by BabyIAXO. Furthermore, the study explores the potential for futureIAXO to detect these signals and outlines the necessary experimental upgrades to achieve this. Finally, the impact of axiglon decay on the axion signal is considered, specifically regarding the resulting time-dependent flux. Overall, BabyIAXO is shown to be sensitive to a broad parameter space, with the axiglon's lifetime playing a critical role in determining detectability. Additionally, the axiglon mechanism is identified as a promising source of continuous gravitational waves, with a detailed discussion of the associated parameter space. This work establishes a foundation for future research into axion-like particles and their cosmological implications. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D (3D plus respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) sequence designed for whole-body imaging. The protocol incorporates a variable echo train length (ETL) that dynamically adapts to the respiratory cycle, alongside a variable echo spacing (VES) that shortens during the inhalation phase to capture motion. This approach enables the acquisition of 3D volumes at specific respiratory instants, facilitating retrospective respiratory gating. By utilizing a free-breathing strategy, the method ensures high temporal resolution and rapid data collection. The proposed technique was evaluated on a 3T scanner using a phantom and a healthy volunteer. Results demonstrated that the motion-adjusted 4D T2-TSE sequence successfully captured both phantom and in vivo respiratory motion. Furthermore, the 3D volumes exhibited high isotropic spatial resolution, and the images displayed excellent contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The study concludes that this free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D T2-TSE approach offers a robust solution for whole-body imaging. Additionally, the method is versatile and can be readily adapted for imaging other moving organs, such as the heart and brain. Finally, the technique is compatible with various pulse sequences, including T1-weighted and contrast-enhanced 3D T2-weighted turbo field echo sequences. This work holds significant potential for advancing motion-adjusted 4D MRI applications. This paper demonstrates that for submersion functions on the plane of the form $f(x,y)=y+g(x,y)$, where $g$ is a continuous function vanishing at the origin, the topological similarity class of $f$ at $(0,0)$ is determined by the topological equivalence class of the foliations defined by $y+g(x,y)=c$ near the origin. Specifically, these foliations are classified based on the local topological properties of their separatrices. Furthermore, we establish that the collection of topological similarity classes for such functions constitutes a complete lattice under the relation of topological equivalence. The results presented herein were previously announced in [10]. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the measures of topological equivalence between planar germs and their associated limitations. Finally, we extend these findings to a broader context by proving the validity of our main theorems for submersion functions where the perturbation term is continuous in both variables. In this generalized setting, the foliation classes are defined by the local topological properties of separatrices within a sectorial neighborhood of the origin. We also offer a detailed discussion regarding the existence and uniqueness of topological representatives for these classes. The methodology employed relies on the theory of topological normal forms for continuous vector fields and the topological classification of their orbits. This approach was originally developed by the first author in his doctoral thesis [11] and has since been the foundation of his research. To our knowledge, this specific application to the topological equivalence of submersion functions represents a novel contribution. We anticipate that these findings will facilitate the development of a comprehensive theory for the topological classification of submersion functions and related geometric objects. Finally, we outline several open problems in this area.

Arid and semi-arid environments feature sparse vegetation characterized by strong inter-plant competition for limited water, a factor that has driven the development of numerous vegetation pattern models. These models typically rely on the assumption that plants respond to the local average water availability within their immediate surroundings. However, this local approximation may fail to accurately represent water availability in these settings. To address this limitation, we introduce a non-local water availability metric that accounts for competition across a broader spatial scale. We subsequently develop a reaction-diffusion-advection framework incorporating this non-local measure. Our analysis demonstrates that this model can generate both spotted and banded patterns, contingent upon specific parameter values. Furthermore, we find that the model's predictions align with experimental data. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique designed to compress high-dimensional vectors into lower dimensions while approximately maintaining their $L_2$ norm. This paper investigates the resilience of such compressed representations against adaptive inputs. We demonstrate that for a fixed number of rows, if the count of adaptive inputs grows sufficiently large, the resulting estimates fail to approximate the original vectors within the $L_2$ norm. Furthermore, we establish that this limitation is tight, as a number of rows that is linearly proportional to the total number of adaptive inputs is both necessary and sufficient to ensure that the estimates do approximate the inputs in the $L_2$ norm. Our findings are complemented by extensions applicable to sparse inputs and to norm definitions beyond the $L_2$ norm. Finally, we present experimental results indicating that the theoretical upper bound on estimates is tight. To our knowledge, this represents the first formal analysis of CountSketch's robustness against adaptive inputs. Additionally, we explore the algorithm's resilience to adversarial inputs, a topic that has received limited attention in prior research. Our results indicate that while the original CountSketch algorithm is not resilient to adaptive inputs, a modified version is. We provide a theoretical analysis of this variant and support our findings with experiments. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ashwinbhat/CountSketch}. This paper investigates the differentiability of functions defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$ based on the differentiability properties of functions on $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. Specifically, we examine the scenario where a function $F: \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ is known to be differentiable, and we analyze the differentiability of a function $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ under the condition that its component functions are partial derivatives of $F$. We establish key differentiability properties for $f$ and provide a counterexample demonstrating that, in general, $f$ cannot be expected to possess higher-order differentiability. Furthermore, we present a sufficient condition that ensures $f$ is differentiable. As an application, we derive a sufficient condition for the existence of a primitive for a given vector field. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the differentiability of $f$ and that of a related function $g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$, whose components are integrals of the partial derivatives of $F$. We demonstrate that if $g$ is differentiable, then $f$ is also differentiable, and we provide a counterexample showing that the converse does not hold in general. Finally, we offer an application of these findings to the theory of partial differential equations. In this context, we consider a vector field $F$ and a function $f$ such that the partial derivatives of $f$ correspond to the components of $F$. We further establish that if $F$ is continuously differentiable, then $f$ is differentiable, and we note that the converse is not generally true. Finally, we demonstrate that if $F$ is infinitely differentiable, then $f$ is also infinitely differentiable. These results provide a foundation for the study of conservative vector fields and their associated potentials. This study introduces a novel, context-sensitive approach to evaluating vocal entrainment within dyadic conversations. By modeling inter-speaker acoustic interactions through a cross-correlation framework, the method quantifies entrainment by analyzing the phase-locking of one participant's fundamental frequency to the other's. The findings demonstrate that this new approach surpasses traditional methods in both sensitivity and specificity. Furthermore, the research reveals that entrainment is not uniform across all dialogue segments; instead, it fluctuates in response to the specific conversational context. These results offer a deeper understanding of entrainment mechanisms and establish a robust foundation for developing more effective computational models to assess dyadic vocal entrainment. We introduce DUVET, a survey designed to investigate how galactic outflows regulate star formation in the disk galaxy NGC 253. By combining high-resolution observations of the [CII] 158um and [FeII] 1.64um lines with a CO(2-1) map, we identified a large-scale outflow extending over 1.5 kpc from the galactic center. This outflow exhibits a complex morphology characterized by a primary axis oriented roughly perpendicular to the galactic disk, alongside several smaller, distinct outflows. Our analysis reveals that the [CII] outflow aligns with the CO(2-1) disk, whereas the [FeII] outflow displays a morphology that is largely independent of the CO(2-1) distribution. Furthermore, the [FeII] emission shows a strong correlation with the [CII] line, suggesting that [FeII] serves as a robust tracer of the outflow. We propose that the [FeII] emission originates from the photoionization of iron in the outflow by the [CII] line radiation generated within the star-forming disk. These findings indicate that galactic outflows are driven by stellar feedback from the star-forming disk, with the [FeII] line providing a direct probe of the feedback's impact on the interstellar medium. Consequently, the [FeII] line offers a valuable tool for studying galactic outflows and the feedback mechanisms that regulate star formation. This study represents the first application of the [FeII] line to a galactic outflow, and we anticipate that future [FeII] observations of galactic outflows will yield significant insights into the feedback processes governing galactic evolution. The rise of automotive networks has created a demand for privacy-preserving edge cognition, a concept that involves collaborative processing across multiple vehicles to achieve shared goals while safeguarding individual privacy. This paper introduces a framework that enables vehicles to jointly accomplish tasks without compromising privacy, specifically by allowing them to share data for training machine learning models without exposing the underlying information. The proposed solution employs a novel communication protocol that leverages the inherent structure of these collaborative tasks to minimize communication overhead. We evaluate this approach using a real-world dataset for pedestrian detection, demonstrating that the framework can detect pedestrians with high accuracy while significantly reducing the data shared between vehicles. Our results indicate that the framework can detect pedestrians with an accuracy of 95% while reducing the shared data by up to 90%. Furthermore, we show that the framework can be extended to other tasks, such as traffic light recognition, achieving similar levels of privacy protection. We believe this framework will be valuable for developing privacy-preserving edge cognition in automotive networks and hopes to inspire further research in this area.
