We have previously identified a hidden companion to the accelerating star HD 123847, which is hypothesized to be a brown dwarf. In this study, we apply a Bayesian framework to constrain the properties of brown dwarf companions for HD 123847, as well as to derive the masses and orbital parameters of companions for four other accelerating stars: HD 101065, HD 102265, HD 106906, and HD 169830. For HD 123847, we determined that a brown dwarf companion is highly probable, with a mass between 10 and 30 Jupiter masses and a semi-major axis of 100 to 300 astronomical units. For the remaining four stars, we found that brown dwarf companions are unlikely, as the observed accelerations are more readily explained by stellar mass loss. Consequently, we conclude that the acceleration of HD 123847 is best explained by a brown dwarf companion, whereas the accelerations of the other four stars are more likely caused by stellar mass loss. This finding underscores the necessity of accounting for mass loss when investigating the nature of companions to accelerating stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Bayesian methods are effective for simultaneously constraining the weights and distances of hidden companions to multiple stars. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation of brown dwarfs. The Internet of Things (IoT) has become a cornerstone of modern smart environments, enabling the interconnection of devices and systems. Within this framework, home appliances are typically managed through centralized cloud platforms, which introduce significant security vulnerabilities and privacy risks. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a novel intelligent system for tracking home appliances using a hybrid approach that integrates positioning data from the Time of Arrival (TOA) method with the decentralized Ledger technology of a private Blockchain. This solution offers a robust mechanism for monitoring appliance status while ensuring data integrity and privacy. The study demonstrates the system's effectiveness through a simulation of an indoor residential setting. Results indicate that the proposed Blockchain-based tracking system achieves an average error rate of 0.0001% in monitoring appliance states, thereby enhancing the security and privacy of the IoT ecosystem. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. Keywords: Internet of Things (IoT), Home Appliances, Positioning, Time of Arrival (TOA), Blockchain.

This paper introduces a method for quantizing Lloyd-Gaussian (L-) values within Lloyd-Gabor (L-G-) based encoders using deep learning. By applying a learned quantization function to the infinite L-G- domain, we can precompute these quantized L-values offline. This approach enables the use of a finite L-G- encoder while maintaining performance comparable to an infinite L-G- system. Furthermore, we extend this quantization strategy to support Gray-coded encoding. The proposed method is validated through simulations on a 5G New Radio (NR) downlink scenario. Results demonstrate that our deep learning-driven quantization technique achieves a 2 dB gain over uncoded L-G- encoding and matches the bit error rate (BER) of fully coded L-G- encoding across all tested L-values. Additionally, the method reduces the bit error rate of the Lloyd-Gabor encoder by 10% compared to Lloyd-encoding. Finally, we confirm that the quantization function can be efficiently implemented on a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). The source code for the deep learning model is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/Deep-Learning-Driven-Quantization-of-L-Values-for-Gray-Coded-Encoding.

This study examines the Upper Addition problem, which involves determining if an input graph can be transformed into an upward planar graph through the addition of vertices and edges, subject to the constraint that new vertices are placed at the top. We demonstrate that this problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the count of added vertices. Furthermore, we establish that if the number of vertices to be added is limited to a constant $k$, the problem admits an algorithm with running time $O(n^{k+1})$. Additionally, we investigate the Upward Planar Augmentation problem, where edges may be added to achieve an upward planar graph, and we prove that this problem is also W[1]-hard under parameterization by the number of added edges. Finally, we show that Upward Planar Augmentation can be solved in $O(n^k)$ time when parameterized by $k$. These findings are complemented by a detailed analysis of the running times for the proposed algorithms. Our results indicate that, for any fixed $k$, the running time is nearly optimal, as it cannot be improved to $o(n^k)$ unless the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false. We also explore the relationship between the parameters representing the number of added vertices and the number of added edges. Specifically, we prove that if an algorithm solves Upward Planar Augmentation in $f(k, \ell, n)$ time, where $k$ is the number of added edges, $\ell$ is the number of added vertices, and $f$ is a computable function, then there exists an algorithm solving the Upper Addition problem in $O(n^{\ell + k})$ time. A strength-$t$ covering array (CA) is defined as an $N\times t$ matrix with entries from a set of $s$ symbols, where every possible ordered $t$-tuple of symbols appears in at least one row. The CA is termed minimal when $N$ reaches its lowest possible value. The concept of a tiny strength-$2$ CA was recently introduced by the authors in [1], where it was demonstrated that every tiny strength-$2$ CA functions as a covering array. This paper extends that work by establishing the theoretical framework for tiny strength-$2$ CAs, deriving the specific formula for the number of distinct symbols, and proving that all constructed arrays are minimal. Furthermore, we present a novel construction method for tiny strength-$2$ CAs that yields arrays with a reduced count of distinct symbols compared to those produced by the algorithm in [1]. Finally, we provide a computational framework to generate and analyze these arrays.

The primary goal of failure reproduction is to identify the root cause of a failure so it can be addressed and prevented from recurring. A recent approach, known as Directed Genetic Algorithm (DGA), utilizes code call graphs and historical fault data to locate faults by minimizing the distance between historical and current code call graphs. This study aims to evaluate DGA through a partial replication of its original publication. We executed 100 runs of the algorithm on the failure datasets provided in the source material, which include two versions of the Apache web server and the Linux kernel. Our results indicate that DGA successfully reproduces faults in 60% of the cases presented in the original paper. Furthermore, we identified several issues and limitations within the tool that could hinder its effectiveness. Finally, we propose several avenues for future research to address these challenges. This work is part of the partial replication initiative for automated fault localization techniques, which can be accessed at https://github.com/fgarcia2002/applied-replication-dga. Additional details are available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222.

The vortex lattice in type-II superconductors is thought to undergo a transition from a triangular to a square arrangement as the applied magnetic field increases. This structural shift is significant because the vortex-skeleton symmetry aligns with that of the underlying charge-4m order, which is believed to drive the high-$T_\textrm{c}$ pseudogap phase. We present direct, real-space visualization of this grid transition in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_{6+\delta}$ using scanning tunneling microscopy. Our findings reveal a distinct symmetry change occurring at $B_\textrm{sq}$ = 10.5 $\pm$ 0.2 T, where vortex ordering shifts from predominantly square to predominantly triangular. This critical field aligns with the onset of a field-induced phase transition previously observed in STM studies of the pseudogap state. Furthermore, the ratio $B_\textrm{sq}$/ $B_\textrm{c2}$ is consistent with theoretical predictions derived from a model incorporating strong vortex-vortex interactions mediated by charge-4m order. These results offer compelling evidence that the vortex lattice and charge-4m order are intrinsically linked. Additionally, we observe that the vortex skeleton is highly disordered at low fields, a phenomenon we attribute to the presence of point defects. Finally, we demonstrate that the vortex-skeleton symmetry can be manipulated by adjusting the tunneling bias voltage. These capabilities hold promise for advancing the study of the vortex state in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ superconductors. This study investigates the entrainment phenomenon within conversational interactions, specifically examining how speakers adjust their speech rate to match their conversation partners. We introduce a new, unsupervised metric called "Entrainment Distance" to quantify the extent of this process. Our findings indicate that the distance between a speaker's adjusted speech rate and their partner's original rate serves as a reliable proxy for entrainment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a deep neural network can effectively predict a conversation partner's adjusted speech rate based on the initial rates of both participants and the distance between them. Finally, we apply this predictive model to estimate the distance between adjusted and baseline speech rates, revealing that our predictions align closely with the actual values observed in the data. These results suggest that neural networks can accurately model the distance between adjusted and baseline speech rates, thereby providing a robust method for detecting entrainment. The proposed model is also validated across multiple dialogue datasets. The source code for this work is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Entrainment-Models.

Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical task in video analysis that involves identifying action boundaries and classifying them. While supervised methods have yielded promising results, the field is increasingly shifting toward unsupervised techniques to eliminate the need for extensive manual annotations. Existing unsupervised approaches typically rely on pre-defined heuristics, such as specific video properties or pre-trained models, which restricts their adaptability to diverse scenarios. This paper introduces Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP), a novel framework for unsupervised temporal action segmentation. SSCAP is built upon a new framework for temporal action division that leverages the inherent temporal structure of videos. It employs a self-supervised learning strategy to derive a task-specific representation from raw videos, enabling the discovery of a latent action space. To ensure robustness against variations in video length and content, the proposed framework utilizes a self-supervised loss function designed to capture the co-occurrence of actions within temporal segments. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SSCAP achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, evaluations on two real-world datasets highlight its superior generalization capabilities. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYiYi/SSCAP. This paper examines two distinct approaches to providing feedback in software testing education: the traditional detailed method and the non-traditional inquiry-based method. The study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of these two systems when teaching core concepts of software testing. To achieve this, an empirical study was conducted involving 40 undergraduate students divided into two groups, with each group receiving feedback via one of the two methods. The findings indicate that the inquiry-based approach yields superior results compared to the conventional detailed feedback system. Consequently, the authors recommend that educators adopt the inquiry-based method to enhance the teaching of software testing concepts. The paper concludes with a discussion of the study's implications and suggestions for future research. Keywords: Software Testing Education, Feedback, Inquiry-Based Learning, Empirical Study. Atmospheric retrievals for exoplanets and brown dwarfs are becoming increasingly sophisticated, yet they face significant hurdles due to the vast number of molecular species and their complex interactions. To address this, we introduce EXOPLINES, a repository of line-by-line absorption cross-sections for molecules prevalent in exoplanetary atmospheres. These data are accessible via the open-source Python package exoplanetlines, which also offers pre-computed cross-sections optimized for retrieval applications. Currently, EXOPLINES includes databases for H2O, CO, CH4, NH3, and H2S, with a focus on accuracy and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the utility of these pre-computed cross-sections by performing retrievals on the TRAPPIST-1 system. Our results indicate that using EXOPLINES reduces retrieval computation time by a factor of 100 compared to calculating cross-sections on the fly, while introducing negligible biases in retrieved parameters. We anticipate that EXOPLINES will facilitate the rapid analysis of large exoplanet datasets, thereby accelerating the search for biosignatures. The repository is hosted at https://github.com/astro-berkeley/exoplanetlines, and the package is available on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/exoplanetlines/. The current release (v1.0.0) contains databases for H2O, CO, CH4, NH3, and H2S, with additional species planned for future updates. We encourage the community to contribute further molecular databases to enhance the repository's scope. This work investigates the relationship between the axioms of classical logic programming and the nonmonotonic logic programming framework introduced by Ans\^o and Ferri (2000). We demonstrate that the latter framework can be derived from the former by applying two straightforward transformations to the rules of a classical program. The first transformation involves converting the body of each rule into a disjunction, thereby creating a disjunctive program. The second involves treating the antecedents of all rules as non-strict integrity constraints applied to the entire program. We establish that the answer sets generated by the nonmonotonic program through Ans\^o and Ferri's original semantics are equivalent to those produced by the classical program when the two transformations are applied. Furthermore, we show that this equivalence extends to the enhanced version of Ans\^o and Ferri's framework that incorporates weak disjunction. These findings offer a novel perspective on the connection between classical and nonmonotonic logic programming, as well as between disjunctive and nonmonotonic logic programming. Additionally, we examine the equivalence between Ans\^o and Ferri's framework and the answer sets of classical programs under the classical stable model semantics. Finally, we explore the equivalence between Ans\^o and Ferri's framework and the answer sets of disjunctive programs under the disjunctive stable model semantics. Our results indicate that the latter equivalence holds only under specific conditions, which we define and analyze. These insights provide a fresh perspective on the interrelations among classical, disjunctive, and nonmonotonic logic programming. Quantum resources, such as entanglement and coherence, are fundamental to the quantum information era. This letter establishes the foundational framework for general quantum resource theories, which are defined by a chosen set of free states. We demonstrate that for any such theory, there exists a unique family of monotones that fully characterize the free operations permitted within the theory. Furthermore, we prove that these monotones can be derived from a single, canonically defined function. This finding offers a comprehensive and unified approach to analyzing quantum resource theories. As a practical application, we examine the relationship between two widely studied resources: quantum coherence and quantum asymmetry. Our results indicate that these resources are equivalent, meaning the sets of states that can be generated from each other via incoherent operations are identical. Additionally, we provide a complete set of monotones for the theory of quantum asymmetry. Our findings are supported by an open-source Python package, Qure, available at https://github.com/Quantum-Information-Theory/Qure. The source code for this letter can be found at https://github.com/Quantum-Information-Theory/Qure/tree/master/letters/wang2021initial. We introduce a new framework for evaluating the data-analytic properties of sufficient statistics in exponential family models. Our approach relies on the concept of "sufficiency relative to a class of transformations," which encompasses a broad category of data reductions. We demonstrate that conditioning on such reduced data preserves key frequentist properties, including unbiasedness, mean squared error, and admissibility. Furthermore, we extend these findings to data conditioning, a technique that leverages the invariance of data summaries under specific transformations. This methodology allows us to derive data-dependent estimators that dominate standard frequentist benchmarks, such as the maximum likelihood estimator. We illustrate the framework's utility by re-examining several well-known examples from the literature and applying it to a novel case study. The proposed methodology is implemented in the R package expfam. Data availability: expfam. Software availability: expfam. R. This work addresses inference challenges in robust-tailed and potentially non-stationary multidimensional time series. We introduce a vector autoregressive model featuring robust tails and a time-varying mean, which accommodates non-stationarity through a flexible specification of the time-varying second moment. A key contribution is a new class of quasi-likelihood estimators that achieve consistency and asymptotic normality even when the time-varying mean is estimated with errors. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for estimating the mean that yields consistent estimators with asymptotic normality. These methodologies are demonstrated using daily stock return data from the S&P500 index. Additionally, we develop a testing framework to assess the constancy of the mean and the time-varying second moment, offering a significant advancement over prior testing approaches. Finally, we apply these methods to analyze the time-varying mean and second moment of daily stock returns within the S&P500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average indices. The analysis reveals that the second moments of both indices exhibit a sharp increase during the 2008 financial crisis, accompanied by a notable rise in the cross-correlation between the two markets. Furthermore, the mean of the second market demonstrates a clear upward trend, a pattern that is less evident in the first market. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for non-stationarity and robust tails when analyzing these specific stock markets. The paper concludes with a comprehensive simulation study. This study addresses the offline distance-$r$ dominating ensemble problem, which involves identifying a distribution of distance-$r$ dominating sets with minimal expected size for a given set of graphs. While previous research has primarily focused on graphs where all distance-$r$ dominating sets share the same size, we advance the field by extending these findings to include sparse graphs of high girth that possess varying sizes. Our approach introduces a novel randomized algorithm that operates in expected polynomial time and achieves a distribution within this new framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method yields superior results compared to existing algorithms in specific cases. Finally, we establish that the problem is NP-hard even when restricted to graphs with a girth of 7. Additionally, we present a randomized algorithm for the offline distance-$r$ dominating ensemble that runs in polynomial time and provides an approximation ratio of $O(\log \log n / \log \log \log n)$, improving upon the previously best-known ratio of $O(\log n / \log \log n)$. This improved ratio is achieved by leveraging a recent constant-factor approximation algorithm for the offline dominating ensemble problem. The primary contribution of this work is the extension of prior results to sparse high-girth graphs, thereby broadening the applicability of existing algorithms. We also provide a detailed analysis of the performance of previous algorithms in this specific context. Finally, we propose an open problem regarding the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm that produces a distribution of distance-$r$ dominating sets with an expected size within a constant factor of optimal for this problem. Our proposed solution to this open problem would represent a significant advancement in the field. We believe this paper will be of interest to researchers working on graph domination problems, particularly those interested in the offline distance-$r$ dominating ensemble problem. This work investigates the connection between bulk and boundary states in disordered elevated-order topological insulators (EOTIs). While the bulk state is characterized by an extended wavefunction, the boundary states are localized. We demonstrate that the topological invariant of the boundary state remains robust against the boundary condition applied to the extended state. These findings are illustrated through a model of a two-dimensional square lattice with a square-root potential. Additionally, we examine the impact of disorder correlation on this correspondence and identify the specific conditions under which the correspondence breaks down. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the design of topological quantum systems. These conclusions are derived from numerical simulations and analytical reasoning. We introduce a neural rendering approach that utilizes a brightness field to depict scenes. By representing brightness as a continuous function of 3D space, we can efficiently sample it from a compact latent code to generate novel views. We evaluate this method against state-of-the-art techniques, including neural radiance fields, on both synthetic and real datasets. Our results demonstrate that the brightness field can be learned from a small set of RGB images and stored within a minimal 128KB latent, achieving visual quality comparable to other methods while offering superior rendering speed. Furthermore, we show that a single latent can be initialized from a single image to significantly boost rendering performance. In 2020, speckle interferometry observations at the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope (SOAR) were conducted using the upgraded instrument, which features a new optical design, enhanced wavefront control, and improved data processing capabilities. This update expands the field of view for planet detection to 1.5 arcseconds and enables the detection of planets with contrasts as low as 10^-5 at 0.2 arcseconds. The instrument successfully identified a companion star with a contrast of 10^-5 at 0.2 arcseconds from the ground. Additionally, speckle interferometry measurements yielded precise angular separations for the binary systems 61 Cyg A, 61 Cyg B, and 61 Cyg C, achieving a precision of 1 micro-arcsecond. These results align with predictions from orbital ephemerides. Furthermore, the paper reports new measurements of the angular separation between the components of the binary system HD 106906. The observed separation of 25.4 +/- 0.2 micro-arcseconds is consistent with previous speckle and adaptive optics measurements. Finally, the study confirms that the planet HD 106906 b, with a mass of 11 Jupiter masses, orbits at a distance of 650 AU from its host star. This large separation and the planet's mass are difficult to explain under standard planet formation models. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings. We introduce a novel framework for chiral algebras, termed cosmic chiral algebras, which are constructed from a Lie algebra equipped with a symmetric invariant bilinear form, known as the cosmic algebra. This structure is derived from the kinematic algebra, a specific subalgebra defined by null relations within the symmetric bilinear form. We demonstrate that any cosmic chiral algebra possesses a corresponding dual cosmic algebra, where the roles of the symmetric bilinear form and the null relations are interchanged. This duality establishes a new relationship between Lie algebraic constructions and the concept of "hue-kinematics duality" found in scattering amplitude theory. Furthermore, we identify a specific class of cosmic chiral algebras that correspond to the holomorphic sectors of integrable sigma models. This correspondence enables the derivation of the classical equations of motion for the sigma model from the cosmic chiral algebra and facilitates the construction of its conserved charges. Piston-driven shock waves are a common feature in solar jets, yet their formation and evolution remain poorly understood. This study presents LOFAR observations of a jet-driven piston surge, revealing a complex structure with a leading edge and a trailing region. The surge's leading edge moves at approximately 100 km/s, while the trailing region exhibits a more intricate pattern. We propose that the surge originates from a jet in the low corona, driven by magnetic reconnection. The surge's leading edge aligns with the jet's leading edge, whereas the trailing region likely results from the jet's expansion and interaction with surrounding magnetic fields. These findings offer valuable insights into the formation and evolution of piston-driven shock waves in the low corona. Additionally, the detection of the surge by LOFAR at 150 MHz indicates that such jets are associated with non-thermal radio emission, a phenomenon previously observed in jets at higher altitudes. This suggests that jets are a significant source of low-frequency radio emission in the low corona. This study introduces a novel approach to modeling dynamics within random swirl flows by utilizing functional random differential equations. The authors first establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for a specific class of these equations, which are defined by conditional stochastic differential equations with functional generators. Subsequently, this framework is applied to a random swirl flow model, demonstrating that the associated Fokker-Planck equation admits a unique solution under a specified growth condition. Finally, the paper examines the long-term behavior of solutions to the functional random differential equation and the Fokker-Planck equation, revealing that the system exhibits ergodic properties. These results are achieved through the application of forward equations, functional differential equations, and functional analysis techniques. The methodology presented offers a new perspective for analyzing random swirl flow models and holds potential for broader applications in related fields. Additionally, the authors provide a numerical simulation of the random swirl flow model to validate their theoretical findings. This work extends the research presented in \cite{KKS20}. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be efficiently executed on quantum hardware but difficult to simulate classically. This study examines the entanglement within the final state of boson sampling by analyzing the scaling of entanglement entropy for single and multiple modes. We observe that entropy for a single mode remains low, whereas entropy for multiple modes increases. These findings are supported by numerical simulations and theoretical derivations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that entanglement can be quantified by examining the purity of the reduced density matrix, which is determined by calculating the distribution of squared amplitudes across all possible output configurations. This approach offers a method to estimate entanglement without requiring the full state vector. Our results indicate that the distribution of squared amplitudes converges to a Gaussian distribution as the number of modes grows, with the variance of this distribution serving as a measure of entanglement. Additionally, we show that the variance of the output distribution for a specific subset of modes can be utilized to quantify entanglement between that subset and the remaining modes. Finally, we explore the relationship between entanglement and the probability distributions of the final outputs. These insights provide a pathway to assess the feasibility of verifying the quantum advantage of boson sampling. To facilitate this, we have developed an open-source Python package that enables the calculation of entanglement measures for boson sampling. Temporal data series are fundamental to numerous scientific disciplines, yet their analysis remains challenging due to high dimensionality, noise, and the need for rapid pattern recognition. This study introduces a novel monitored learning approach utilizing a deep convolutional neural network to identify brief, high-dimensional patterns within noisy temporal series. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on two complex datasets: one comprising noisy calcium imaging recordings from neurons in the mouse visual cortex, and another involving noisy electrophysiological recordings from cardiac cells. The results indicate that the approach successfully extracts meaningful patterns, enabling the classification of distinct biological states and the detection of specific events. Furthermore, the method offers a unified framework applicable to diverse experimental techniques, including calcium imaging, electrophysiology, and optogenetics. The associated software is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leopoldlab/monitored-learning. These tools can facilitate the automated, high-throughput analysis of temporal series in life sciences, thereby enhancing the reproducibility of experimental outcomes. The findings are published in *Scientific Reports* (2018).

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are widely recognized for their ability to manage temporal dependencies, yet the specific mechanisms by which they achieve this remain poorly understood. This study investigates the internal states of RNNs tasked with solving a non-trivial memory problem within a partially observable environment. We demonstrate that these states encode information essential for addressing the task. Furthermore, we show that a straightforward autoencoder can recover this relevant information, even though the raw states contain extraneous details unrelated to the task. These findings indicate that the capacity of RNNs to handle temporal dependencies arises from the interaction between their recurrent structure and the specific demands of the environment. Additionally, we present a straightforward reinforcement learning approach that replicates the behavior of RNNs in this setting. This method utilizes a pre-trained convolutional neural network to extract an environment representation that reveals the necessary temporal information. By employing a simple state-based algorithm to retain this data, we prove that the RNN's capabilities can be reproduced without relying on recurrent connections during the decision-making process. Consequently, our results suggest that the environment's partial observability is a critical factor in the emergence of RNN behaviors. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the broader question of how neural networks can effectively solve problems in partially observable settings. Our approach offers a straightforward solution to this challenge. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/andrewjg/convex-state-representation. This paper introduces a new weakly-guided action detection framework grounded in the principle that actions are context-dependent. We term this approach "Weakly-Guided Action Detection" (WGAD). To implement WGAD, we first develop a method for learning action contexts using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). Subsequently, we design a two-stream network that integrates action contexts with visual and audio features to realize WGAD. We evaluate our method across three datasets: UCF101, HMDB51, and JHU-UCF101. The results demonstrate that WGAD surpasses state-of-the-art action detection techniques. Furthermore, our method is the first to achieve state-of-the-art performance in action detection using audio features. Finally, we show that WGAD successfully identifies actions within scenes containing multiple instances. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/weakly-guided-action-detection.

This paper details the methodology, results, and findings from the 2021 Image Resemblance Challenge (IRC), an international competition focused on identifying matching images from two distinct datasets. The task required determining whether pairs of images were true matches or random, with the ranking criterion being the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. The challenge was structured into two phases: a development phase involving two tracks—object matching and scene matching—and a subsequent validation phase with three tracks—object matching, scene matching, and image matting. This work specifically addresses the development phase outcomes and the discoveries resulting from the validation phase, which included the object matching, scene matching, and image matting tracks. A total of 102 teams from 38 countries participated, submitting 309 solutions across all tracks. The winning entries were: (i) Team 101 (Russia) for the Object Matching track, (ii) Team 102 (Russia) for the Scene Matching track, and (iii) Team 103 (Russia) for the Image Matting track. The primary findings include: (i) the significant impact of image matting on image matching, (ii) the critical role of color and texture features in image matching, and (iii) the substantial influence of image augmentation on matching performance. Additionally, the study highlights the limitations of current image matching techniques and proposes future research directions. The code and data utilized in this work are accessible at https://github.com/alexeykolesnikov/IRC2021.

This work examines diffusion processes and specific parabolic differential equations that exhibit degeneration, focusing on how perturbations influence their asymptotic behavior. We address boundary conditions within the sticky, conservative, and killing frameworks, as well as the corresponding boundary behaviors of the associated semigroups. Furthermore, we analyze metastability in a specific context, demonstrating a homogenization result for a notable instance of a parabolic equation with a moving keyhole degeneration. Finally, we explore the interplay between the scale function, the generator, and the semigroup in this degenerate setting. The study relies on a novel approach utilizing the theory of quasi-Lipschitz functions. These findings are applicable to a broad class of degenerate diffusion processes, including those with one-sided degeneration, and extend to scenarios involving a finite number of degeneration points. Additionally, the methodology is adaptable to scenarios where the diffusion coefficient diverges. The paper includes several examples, such as those with a square root diffusion coefficient, to illustrate the findings. The discussion also touches upon related literature, including the study of metastability in one-dimensional diffusion processes. This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter under intense magnetic fields using the LOCV approach. We observe that the LOCV method yields results consistent with those obtained via the Brueckner-Bethe-Gupta (BBG) approach, which does not account for magnetic field effects. Furthermore, the LOCV framework incorporates the full impact of magnetic fields on nuclear matter, including spin polarization. Our findings indicate that while magnetic fields significantly alter the symmetry energy, they have a negligible effect on the incompressibility modulus. Additionally, we observe that the magnetic field's influence on the effective mass is substantial only at low densities, with its effects diminishing rapidly as density increases. Finally, we conclude that magnetic fields do not affect the transition density for the neutron drip. These results are compared with existing literature, and we provide a comprehensive discussion of the observed effects. Finally, we note that the LOCV approach offers the advantage of being applicable to both finite nuclei and nuclear matter. This paper introduces a novel privacy-preserving framework designed to enhance the performance of federated learning (FL) models in the context of education. Our approach addresses two critical challenges: ensuring privacy within FL and the high communication costs associated with exchanging large-scale data. To tackle these issues, we propose a new framework called Differential Privacy Recurrent Education (DP-REC). This system integrates a privacy-preserving mechanism with a communication-efficient data processing algorithm. DP-REC is built upon two core components: a privacy-preserving data processing module and a federated learning module. The former employs a recurrent neural network (RNN) to compress and preprocess data, thereby reducing communication overhead, while the latter utilizes this processed data to train FL models. We evaluated DP-REC using three real-world datasets and compared its results against two baseline methods. Our findings demonstrate that DP-REC significantly outperforms the baselines in both privacy protection and communication efficiency. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to analyze the specific contributions of each component to the overall framework. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion of DP-REC's advantages and potential limitations. We hope this work inspires future research in the field of privacy-preserving FL. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus-Auriga and Perseus molecular clouds using the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) to investigate the correlation between FUV luminosity and star formation rates (SFR). Our results indicate that the FUV luminosity of young stellar clusters in Taurus-Auriga correlates with their SFRs, whereas the luminosity of the young cluster in Perseus does not. This discrepancy is attributed to the significant extinction affecting Perseus, which is estimated to be approximately 1.5 magnitudes higher than in Taurus-Auriga. Consequently, we conclude that FUV luminosity serves as a reliable indicator of SFR in young stellar clusters within the Taurus-Auriga region but is unsuitable for determining SFRs in the heavily obscured clusters of Perseus. Furthermore, we determined the extinction toward GALEX's line of sight to the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus region to be $E(B-V) = 0.11 \pm 0.01$ mag. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future FUV observations of young stellar clusters. (Abridged)

We introduce a multi-phase game framework designed to model decision-making processes involving incomplete knowledge. This approach is particularly applicable to scenarios where data is gathered in distinct phases, each characterized by specific constraints. We investigate the development of cognitive structures within this game and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a unique limit structure. Furthermore, we propose two algorithms for constructing this limit structure and provide a complexity analysis for each. Finally, we demonstrate the application of our findings and algorithms in the context of network topology discovery. The performance of these algorithms is evaluated through both simulations and real-world experiments. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithms are highly efficient, with the second algorithm outperforming the first in terms of computational efficiency. Additionally, we show that the second algorithm surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Cognitive-Structure.

Approximate membership inquiry (AMI) data structures utilize filtering to speed up collection management by maintaining a smaller, separate structure that omits certain elements. While this typically introduces false negatives, the process can still be exact if the inactivated elements are subsequently reinserted. This paper presents a novel AMI structure, called the hash-based inquiry filter (HIF), which employs a minimal collection size and a straightforward algorithm. We demonstrate that HIF offers superior performance compared to existing methods, including Bloom filters and bit arrays. Furthermore, we introduce a new filtering strategy, known as the sampling filter (SF), which is false positive free and achieves the smallest possible collection size. SF operates by randomly sampling elements from the input stream and storing them in the structure. Although HIF and SF are not directly combinable, we develop a hybrid approach, the HIF-SF filter, which integrates both techniques. This combination leverages the low space requirements of SF for a subset of elements and the efficiency of HIF for the remainder. Our analysis confirms that HIF-SF outperforms both HIF and Bloom filters in terms of time and space complexity. Additionally, we show that SF is more space-efficient than Bloom filters, which are widely used for similar purposes. Finally, we establish that SF is optimal among all sampling filters, as no other filter can use less space. This optimality is proven by deriving a lower bound on space usage for any AMI structure, demonstrating that SF meets this bound. Consequently, SF is also optimal for any AMI structure that relies solely on random sampling. To our knowledge, this is the first result to provide a lower bound for any AMI structure. Our findings are supported by extensive experimental results. We conducted a large-scale study comparing HIF, Bloom filters, bit arrays, and various other filters, including a new variant of Bloom filters called the Bloom filter with sampling (BFS). The experiments confirm that HIF and SF outperform Bloom filters and bit arrays, and that HIF-SF outperforms HIF. Additionally, we observe that BFS is more space-efficient than Bloom filters, and that HIF-SF is more space-efficient than BFS. Finally, we show that HIF-SF is optimal among all filters that combine HIF and SF. These results are consistent with our theoretical analysis. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive framework for AMI structures, with HIF-SF emerging as a highly efficient and versatile solution. We demonstrate that spinor particles within a degenerate Fermi gas can transform into composite molecules through laser-induced three-body recombination. This approach offers a pathway to create molecules with rotational temperatures in the gigahertz range directly from atomic spinor states. The proposed method is applicable to any fermionic isotope that supports p-wave molecular formation. Furthermore, this technique enables the investigation of spinor relaxation mechanisms driven by three-body recombination. By utilizing this proposal, researchers can explore spinor states in the quantum regime and advance the field of quantum simulation. Additionally, the findings may have applications in quantum information processing. Our results are validated through numerical simulations. These experiments are feasible with current technology and can be implemented using ultracold $^{40}$K atoms. The required laser power is minimal, and the process occurs rapidly, with a timescale of approximately 10 milliseconds. Additionally, the rotational temperature of the resulting molecules is exceptionally low, around 100 millikelvin. Finally, the spinor relaxation time is determined to be roughly 100 milliseconds. This paper introduces a multi-scale Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems. The approach relies on a multi-grid strategy that integrates a high-resolution fine grid with a coarse grid featuring low-resolution approximations. This low-resolution data is generated through a kernel-mixture model, which combines a Gaussian kernel to represent low-frequency components and a Gaussian-Wigner-Ville kernel to model high-frequency components. The framework is implemented using a two-grid system: the coarse grid utilizes low-resolution fields to mitigate the computational expense of solving the full Navier-Stokes equations, while the fine grid maintains high resolution to ensure accuracy in capturing complex flow dynamics. The coarse grid's low-resolution fields are dynamically updated based on the fine grid's solution. The method is validated through three numerical experiments involving fluid-structure interactions with moving boundaries. These cases demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively reduces the number of particles required to resolve the fluid, thereby lowering computational costs without compromising solution accuracy. Furthermore, the framework is capable of handling multi-phase flows, as illustrated by a numerical simulation of a rising bubble. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the framework's advantages and potential future research directions. Telepresence robots (TPRs) are increasingly popular for remote operation, yet their performance is often hindered by limited mobility, slow movement, and imprecise navigation. This study investigates the cognitive load and perceived quality of experience (QoX) associated with controlling TPRs across various network conditions. To achieve this, we developed a realistic driving interface and conducted user testing using three distinct TPRs. We assessed QoX through subjective evaluations and measured cognitive load using the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). Our findings indicate that the PVT serves as a reliable indicator of cognitive load, which correlates strongly with subjective QoX scores. Furthermore, we identified that the specific TPR model, network bandwidth, and driving interface significantly influence both cognitive load and QoX. These results offer valuable insights for designing control interfaces and selecting appropriate TPRs to optimize the user experience. The dataset, including the TPR models, driving interface, and PVT implementation, is publicly accessible to facilitate reproducibility. The mass distribution of the Solar System's giant planets is a critical factor in theories regarding the formation and evolution of the planetary system. This study investigates the impact of gas accumulation occurring simultaneously during the final stages of the growth of Jupiter and Saturn. We conducted two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of gas accretion for both individual and concurrent scenarios, utilizing a model where the accreted gas mass is proportional to the disk's surface density at the planet's edge. Our findings indicate that concurrent accretion results in a 20% reduction in the final mass of Jupiter and a 40% reduction for Saturn. Furthermore, the simulations reveal that this simultaneous accretion process significantly alters the structure of the protoplanetary disk. Specifically, it generates a secondary peak in gas surface density at the outer edge of the Jupiter accretion gap, which is approximately 10 times higher than the surrounding disk. This outcome suggests that the formation of the giant planets may have been more complex than previously thought, and that the current mass configuration of the giant planets serves as a key indicator of the specific conditions and timing of their accretion. These insights are essential for refining models of planet formation and for interpreting the characteristics of exoplanetary systems. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation of the Solar System and for the broader understanding of planet formation processes. Carbon nanotube films are widely used in electronic applications, yet the mechanisms driving their conductivity remain poorly understood. This study investigates the electronic transport properties of armchair carbon nanotubes using a suspended device architecture. We observed that the conductance of individual nanotubes fluctuates significantly with temperature, exhibiting a minimum near 100 K. These findings are best explained by a model where phonons facilitate electron tunneling between adjacent nanotubes, a process that becomes less effective at both very low and very high temperatures. This mechanism offers a pathway to enhance the performance of carbon nanotube films. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the phonon-assisted intertube tunneling rate can be modulated by applying a gate voltage, which alters the phase matching between electrons on neighboring tubes. This capability to control intertube conductance via gating holds significant potential for advancing the development of carbon nanotube-based electronics. Additionally, we show that the phase of the electron wavefunction can be tuned by varying the phonon energy, a phenomenon that may enable the creation of phonon-based quantum devices. Finally, we discuss the potential for utilizing this effect in quantum information processing. Our results provide a foundation for the design of new electronic and quantum devices that leverage phonon-assisted tunneling. We introduce a novel token-firing game played on a finite, connected, undirected graph with a fixed number of chips distributed across its vertices. This game serves as a refined counterpart to the chip-firing game; specifically, when a distribution of chips is sufficiently large, every sequence of stable firing moves eventually leads to a unique pair consisting of a stable vertex configuration and a decomposition into disjoint spanning trees. We demonstrate that for any two initial chip distributions that yield the same number of spanning trees in their respective decompositions, a sequence of moves exists that transforms one distribution into the other without passing through any intermediate unstable configuration. Furthermore, we establish that the number of disjoint spanning trees resulting from the stabilization of a chip distribution remains invariant under specific graph symmetries. These findings are derived from an analysis of the Abel-Jacobi map associated with the graph, which we show possesses a Prym structure rather than a standard Jacobian structure. Consequently, our results can be interpreted as instances of Riemann's existence theorem tailored to this particular Prym structure. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive description of the image of this map and examine its implications for the sandpile group. Finally, we explore the relationship between these results and the recently formulated inverse problem for the discrete Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation. A key component of this investigation involves a new family of graphs, which we term "Prym graphs," designed to exhibit the necessary Prym structure. We also examine the properties of these Prym graphs and their corresponding Abel-Jacobi maps. The work concludes with several open questions. We establish that observations of cosmic birefringence impose constraints on global symmetries within quantum gravity. Specifically, we demonstrate that the shift in polarization angle, $\Delta\psi$, in a background with curvature $k$ can be expressed as $\Delta\psi = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{d\psi}{dt} dt = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{d\psi}{dk} dk$. This relationship indicates that the magnitude of the angle shift is governed by the product of these two factors. Furthermore, we show that $\frac{d\psi}{dk}$ remains independent of the specific quantum gravity theory, whereas $\frac{d\theta_{CS}}{dk}$ varies depending on the theory. Consequently, we derive that the theory of axion inflation, which predicts a non-zero $\frac{d\psi}{dk}$, is compatible with the upper limit on $\Delta\psi$ observed in the Planck CMB data. In contrast, the theory of Kaluza-Klein monopole black holes, which predicts a non-zero $\frac{d\theta_{CS}}{dk}$, is restricted by the same Planck data upper bound on $\Delta\psi$. This study examines the Mumford hypothesis, which asserts that the $b$-invariant of a pair $(X,\Delta)$ is fragile: for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a log Calabi-Yau pair $(X_\epsilon,\Delta_\epsilon)$ arbitrarily close to $(X,\Delta)$ such that the $b$-invariant of the new pair is at most $1-\epsilon$. We demonstrate that this hypothesis holds true for any log Calabi-Yau pair $(X,\Delta)$ where $\Delta$ comprises only log canonical (lc) centers. Furthermore, we establish that the $b$-invariant is also fragile in the context of log canonical pairs. The proof relies on a non-trivial extension of the Keel-Brown-Reid contraction theorem, applicable to pairs $(X,\Delta)$ where $\Delta$ includes lc centers, and may be of independent interest. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the $b$-invariant for pairs with log canonical singularities and present a formula for the $b$-invariant of a pair $(X,\Delta)$ where $\Delta$ is lc. Finally, we offer a counterexample to a variant of the $b$-principle. The paper concludes with several open questions. This work is a collaboration with J. P. Demailly. The transferability of deep learning models is a critical capability that has garnered significant attention due to its potential to enhance data efficiency and bolster security. This study re-examines transferability by establishing two fundamental agreements: first, the existence of a shared subspace within deep models that is transferable across different tasks; second, the transferability of a specific model component from a source task to a target task, contingent upon the alignment of their shared subspace. Based on these principles, we propose a unified framework for transfer learning. This framework is versatile, supporting various strategies such as fine-tuning, feature extraction, and subnetwork transfer. Extensive experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively validates the prudence of these two agreements. Furthermore, the results indicate that our approach can achieve performance comparable to or superior to existing methods. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYiYi1998/Shared-Subspace. The rapid dissemination of information is a critical factor in the success of marketing campaigns, advertising strategies, and public health initiatives. While numerous studies have examined how network topology influences the speed of information spread, this work demonstrates that the velocity of dissemination is primarily driven by a network's modular structure. We introduce a topological metric that quantifies modularity and establish that it dictates the speed of diffusion. This metric is defined as the ratio of within-module to between-module edges. Our findings indicate that when the network is predominantly between-module, this ratio approximates the network's average degree. Furthermore, we illustrate that the modularity-based velocity of information flow can be accurately approximated using only the count of between-module edges. These results offer a quantitative framework for designing and optimizing information campaigns to achieve rapid and efficient distribution. Additionally, we validate these theoretical results through simulations of the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model across various network topologies. Finally, we apply these insights to real-world social networks, demonstrating that our framework enables the identification of network substructures that facilitate swift information propagation. These identified substructures are characterized by low modularity and a high average degree. Our framework provides a foundation for developing cost-effective strategies to accelerate information diffusion. Specifically, we propose a low-cost approach for designing and implementing information campaigns by targeting nodes with low modularity scores. This paper introduces the concept of "distinctiveness" for Lagrangian submanifolds, demonstrating that this property is quantifiable through the Lagrangian spectral invariants and the Fourier coefficients of the Lagrangian angle's 1-form. We apply this notion to establish the quantitative form of the Thomas-Yau conjecture within the monotone case. Additionally, we investigate the qualitative implications of this result and outline several natural directions for future research. The definitions and the proof of the quantitative Thomas-Yau conjecture are subsequently generalized to the non-monotone setting. Finally, we define "mass" for Lagrangian submanifolds and prove that the mass is bounded below by the absolute value of the zeroth Floer homology invariant, $|e_0(L)|$. This finding provides quantitative support for the conjecture that the mass of a Lagrangian submanifold is minimized precisely when it is distinct. The paper concludes with an exploration of the relationship between distinctness and the Calabi-Yau conjecture. The notion of distinctness can be extended to broader contexts, such as non-compact Lagrangian submanifolds and distinctiveness for other geometric structures. This study presents a time-domain precision analysis of the Standard Perturbation Model (SPM) for unamplified links, utilizing a discrete-time approach. The analysis incorporates the fiber's refractive index profile, the launch condition, and the group delay profile. Results indicate that the discrete-time SPM offers a precision comparable to the continuous-time formulation, with the sole distinction being a time resolution defined by the launch condition. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the SPM can be extended to multi-channel scenarios, enabling the calculation of cross-channel four-wave mixing (X-FWM) within unamplified links. Finally, the findings are validated against a precision finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation of the same link. These results provide a foundation for developing a precise model of the distributed nonlinear phase shift in links where the SPM is currently the prevailing model. Additionally, the developed model is applicable to both unamplified and amplified links. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/alejo2000/SPM. It examines the theoretical foundations of ISEAs, detailing their components and how they interact. Furthermore, it surveys various techniques employed in these attacks, analyzes specific case studies, and reviews existing tools designed to facilitate ISEAs. Orchestrating distributed systems is a difficult task that has traditionally depended on domain-specific tools, forcing developers to adapt to the specific features and limitations of each instrument. This paper introduces Ozy, a universal orchestration vessel designed to provide a consistent interface across all orchestration domains. By doing so, it enables the safe and efficient reuse of code and patterns, thereby reducing development costs and accelerating time-to-market. The paper outlines the design and implementation of Ozy, demonstrates its application in creating specific vessels like Tigris and Flute, and presents initial evaluation results. These findings indicate that patterns and code can be reused with minimal effort, resulting in a significant reduction in both effort and errors. Furthermore, Ozy's design and implementation are available as open-source software. This reentrant phase manifests as a resistivity minimum at low magnetic fields within the 5/2 quantum Hall plateau region. These results offer valuable insights into the phase diagram of the fractional quantum Hall effect and the requirements for realizing the 5/2 topological phase. Additionally, our study provides a quantitative analysis of the impact of Landau-level mixing on the topological phase transition. Finally, we demonstrate that the reentrant 5/2 topological phase can be modeled using a phenomenological model incorporating a finite density of disorder. These results are derived from high-resolution magnetotransport measurements conducted at low temperatures. Overparameterized models are common in machine learning, yet their necessity remains unclear. This paper demonstrates that computational constraints can necessitate overparameterization. Specifically, we examine a statistical learning problem where data is generated by a simple function, but the learner is restricted to a limited class of efficient algorithms. In this context, the learner must select a hypothesis from a larger class to achieve optimal generalization error. We establish that the size of this hypothesis class must scale with the complexity of the learner's computation. Furthermore, we introduce a learning problem where the learner is a constant-size neural network with a specific architecture, proving that the required hypothesis class size grows exponentially with the learner's parameter count. Finally, we present a hypothesis class that is difficult for constant-size neural networks to approximate, suggesting that efficient neural networks may be unable to approximate certain structures even when they do not require a large hypothesis class. These findings indicate that computational limits can drive the need for larger model sizes. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this phenomenon and the broader hypothesis of a "neural tangent gap," showing that our results imply the existence of such a gap. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the study of deep learning. Finally, we propose a new hypothesis class that is intractable for any constant-size algorithm, regardless of its architecture. This result suggests that the overparameterization required by computational limits can be exponential even when the learner's parameter count is unbounded. This research investigates the Bohr compactification of discrete Bohr-compact groups, with a specific focus on their topology of uniform convergence toward the trivial representation. While earlier work by the second author and A. Blass established that every countable Bohr-compact group possesses a completion under this topology which remains countable, the current study demonstrates that for any closed subgroup $G$ of a free Bohr-compact group of countable rank, the completion of the direct summand $G$ is isomorphic to the completion of the entire group. This finding generalizes the result mentioned above and represents a significant extension of the findings by the first and third authors. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of those closed subgroups of free Bohr-compact groups of countable rank that constitute Bohr-compact groups, and we examine the topology of uniform convergence on Bohr-compact groups. The paper concludes with an analysis of the compactness of uniform convergence for various classes of Bohr-compact groups. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the topology of uniform convergence and the original topology on discrete Bohr-compact groups, with a particular emphasis on $p$-adic groups. Finally, we present examples of topological groups where the Bohr topology is not compact, yet the topology of uniform convergence on their completion is Hausdorff. These examples include $p$-adic groups, the Bohr compactification of the rationals, and the Bohr compactification of the additive group of a countable field of characteristic $0$. The study also addresses the compactness of uniform convergence for the Bohr compactification of the additive group of a free abelian $p$-group of countable rank. The methods developed herein are also applicable to the study of the Bohr compactification of the additive group of a vector space over a finite field. The paper concludes with an outline of the connections between the topology of uniform convergence and the topology of pointwise convergence on the dual group of a Bohr-compact group. This paper introduces a Branch-and-Bound algorithm designed to address dial-a-ride problems in metropolitan areas. The objective is to minimize the number of passengers requiring carpooling while ensuring all others are served within a specified time limit. To achieve this, we developed a branch-and-bound method utilizing a tailored graph representation. This graph is constructed from a time-expanded network, where each node signifies a passenger's arrival at a stop, and edges represent the boarding of a specific vehicle on a defined route. We present a linear programming relaxation of this graph model, which serves as the basis for a lower bound calculation. This relaxation is solved using a specialized simplex variant that prioritizes passenger flow. Furthermore, we designed a heuristic to generate an initial feasible solution, which acts as the upper bound for the search process. Finally, we implemented a branch-and-bound strategy that prioritizes passengers with the fewest available options to carpool, aiming to reduce the count of unserved individuals. Numerical experiments were conducted on instances featuring up to 100 vehicles and 1,000 passengers. The results demonstrate that the algorithm can solve instances with 100 vehicles and 500 passengers in under 10 seconds. However, solving instances with 500 vehicles and 1,000 passengers proved computationally infeasible within a 24-hour limit. These findings indicate that the proposed algorithm is effective for dial-a-ride problems involving a moderate number of vehicles. Future research should focus on enhancing the algorithm's performance to handle instances with a larger number of vehicles. Additionally, we plan to explore the application of this approach to other dial-a-ride scenarios, such as those found in large cities or at major events. Finally, we intend to investigate the potential of using a column generation approach to improve the lower bound. This would involve solving a restricted master problem to obtain a lower bound and then generating new columns to tighten it further. The challenge lies in efficiently identifying these new columns, which could be addressed through a pricing problem solved via a specialized branch-and-cut algorithm. This algorithm would need to incorporate constraints to ensure the feasibility of the resulting solution. By integrating column generation, we can potentially achieve even tighter lower bounds and, consequently, better solutions. Overall, the proposed algorithm offers a promising approach to dial-a-ride problems, and we believe that further research and development can lead to even more effective solutions. The study introduces a new multi-modal, multi-insight pretraining model designed for product search and recommendation within the e-commerce domain. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative condition that causes irreversible damage to the brain, leading to a gradual loss of cognitive abilities. The electronic structure of the $5d$ transition metal alloy $Hf_{0.5}Ta_{0.5}$ was investigated using density functional theory. This correlated system exhibits a metallic band structure characterized by a significant spin-orbit interaction of approximately $0.5$ eV. The study demonstrates that the band gap in the half-filled $d$-shell of $Hf_{0.5}Ta_{0.5}$ is substantially greater than that of its constituent elements, $Hf$ and $Ta$. Additionally, the material displays a strong spin polarization of roughly $0.5$, which is comparable to the polarization levels found in $5d$ ferromagnets. These findings indicate that $Hf_{0.5}Ta_{0.5}$ is a promising candidate for spintronic applications. The research was conducted using the VASP code, with the Hubbard $U$ parameter determined via the constrained linear muffin-tin orbital method. The resulting band structure and density of states were analyzed using the VASP2TB code. The calculated band structure reveals that the majority spin bands are positioned lower in energy than the minority spin bands. Furthermore, the density of states shows a sharp peak near the Fermi level, indicating a high degree of electronic state localization. These results suggest that $Hf_{0.5}Ta_{0.5}$ possesses a complex electronic structure with potential for use in spintronic devices. The study concludes that $Hf_{0.5}Ta_{0.5}$ is a viable candidate for such applications. We investigate a metastable vacuum state within a six-dimensional warped geometry, situated on a small, compact interval, which offers a geometric framework for dark matter. This dark matter candidate, termed "shadow matter," resides in the lowest-lying Kaluza-Klein mode of a massless scalar field and can account for the entire density of matter in the universe. The shadow matter remains stable over cosmological timescales due to a metastable vacuum protected by an approximate conformal symmetry. We introduce a novel approach to enhance the sampling of DNA conformational space by integrating rigid body dynamics with molecular dynamics. This technique, termed "rigid foundation biasing" (RFB), utilizes a hybrid model where the scaffold DNA is represented as rigid bodies, while the remaining DNA is modeled as flexible all-atom structures. RFB serves as a minimal biasing potential that constrains the system to a specific conformational state. We demonstrate that RFB can be effectively combined with both replica exchange molecular dynamics (REMD) and Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD). REMD and GaMD are established methods for accelerating the sampling of biomolecular conformational transitions; our findings indicate that integrating RFB with these approaches yields superior sampling of DNA conformational transitions compared to using REMD or GaMD alone. Furthermore, we show that RFB can be employed to restrain the scaffold DNA in a specific conformational state, thereby facilitating the study of the dynamic behavior of DNA-bound proteins. These results suggest that RFB offers a versatile and efficient strategy for accelerating the sampling of DNA conformational transitions. Additionally, we have implemented the REMD and GaMD versions of RFB within the CHARMM-GUI web server, enabling users to easily construct these systems. This implementation facilitates the investigation of DNA conformational transitions and DNA-bound protein dynamics, which are often difficult to capture using standard MD methods. The availability of these tools will facilitate the study of DNA conformational transitions and DNA-bound protein dynamics, which are typically inaccessible through conventional molecular dynamics simulations. The arithmetic-geometric mean (ANS) entropy compression algorithm achieves near-optimal entropy reduction for data with specific statistical properties. However, its widespread adoption has been hindered by the complexity of its theoretical analysis. This study examines the algorithm's performance through empirical evaluation, focusing on two key metrics: the maximum entropy compression ratio and the algorithm's stability. Our findings indicate that while the average compression ratio closely aligns with theoretical predictions, significant deviations occur in certain scenarios. Furthermore, we observe that the algorithm's behavior varies across different data distributions. These results offer valuable insights for selecting entropy compression methods tailored to particular data characteristics. Pore water within cementitious materials is not merely a passive component; it is an intricate mixture of ions and molecular species that governs the material's dielectric response. This response is a critical factor in various applications, including non-destructive testing, the interpretation of electrical resistivity tomography data, and the assessment of concrete's durability and quality. This study investigates the dielectric properties of cementitious pore fluids by examining the complex permittivity of both pristine and aged pore fluids. Our findings indicate that the evolution of pore fluid chemistry over time significantly alters the material's dielectric behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Bland-Davis model, which incorporates the effects of ionic strength and salinity, effectively describes these observed dielectric responses. This model relies on three parameters: the permittivity of the solid phase, the radius of the cement grains, and the permittivity of the pore fluid. By fitting this model to the experimental data, we can quantify the changes in ionic strength and salinity of the pore fluid as the cement paste ages. Ultimately, this research establishes a robust framework for analyzing the dielectric response of cementitious materials, thereby enhancing our ability to monitor their performance throughout their service life. This approach is particularly valuable for developing new non-destructive testing methods to evaluate the durability of these materials. We introduce a straightforward cosmological deduction derived from three-dimensional correlations within the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. This approach relies on the fact that the correlation function of Lyman-$\alpha$ forest absorption is proportional to the matter correlation function, scaled by the mean absorption intensity. This proportionality holds true in both linear and non-linear cosmological regimes. Consequently, the slope of the logarithmic mean absorption intensity versus redshift provides a direct measurement of the cosmological density parameter $\Omega_0$. This method is applicable to any sufficiently deep survey of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. We demonstrate that the three-dimensional correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest can be accurately modeled using the Zel'dovich approximation. Furthermore, we show that the slope of the mean absorption intensity versus redshift, calculated via the Zel'dovich approximation, aligns with the slope predicted by the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Finally, we illustrate that the slope of the mean absorption intensity versus redshift can be determined from a single, deep, and wide survey of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. This technique offers a direct, model-independent means of measuring $\Omega_0$ and is expected to become feasible with upcoming data from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Additionally, we discuss the potential for extending this method to other cosmological probes. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations. This study reports the first successful transfer of both horizontal and vertical emittances from a proton beam to a hydrogen like-ion (HLI) beam within a single experimental run at the Proton Driver for Intense Neutrino Sources (PDINS). The experiment utilized a novel emittance exchange scheme combining a radiofrequency quadrupole (RFQ) with a quadrupole octupole. The HLI beamline was configured to match the proton beam into the RFQ, enabling the resonance-driven exchange of transverse and longitudinal emittances between the proton and HLI modes. Subsequent quadrupole focusing successfully decoupled the transferred emittances. Measurements of the final beamline optics confirmed the transfer of all three emittance components, with the horizontal emittance increasing by a factor of 1.5. This achievement demonstrates a new method for manipulating the phase-space distribution of co-propagating charged particles. Furthermore, the results indicate that the technique is applicable to other particle species and could be utilized to enhance the performance of high-intensity proton drivers. This study examines the information-theoretic complexity of Boltzmann networks, which are directed acyclic graphs designed to model the joint distribution of binary variables. We evaluate two specific metrics: the mutual information between inputs and outputs, and the excess mutual information, defined as the gap between total mutual information and redundancy. Our findings indicate that while both metrics rise with network size, they exhibit distinct behaviors regarding network depth. Specifically, excess mutual information grows linearly with depth, whereas mutual information plateaus after reaching a specific depth threshold. These results are derived from a rigorous analysis of randomly structured networks with uniform weights, alongside simulations of networks with varying architectures. This paper introduces a new approach to human-swarm engagement utilizing a distributed Deep Neural Network (DNN) architecture for hand gesture recognition. The system is designed to be easily adaptable for real-time gesture tracking and recognition across a distributed environment. The proposed framework comprises two primary components: a gesture recognition algorithm and a swarm control algorithm. The gesture recognition algorithm employs a distributed DNN architecture to identify gestures in real-time, while the swarm control algorithm leverages these recognized gestures to direct the movement of multiple robots. We introduce a novel ensemble approach that integrates two neural network systems to enhance classification accuracy. The first system utilizes a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from blood cell images, which are then fed into a fully connected layer for categorization. The second system employs a vision transformer to capture both local and global image features, with these features processed by a fully connected layer to determine the cell type. By combining the outputs of these two systems, we achieve a classification accuracy of 99.1% on the dataset. Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols have been suggested to accelerate the ground-state preparation of the two-dimensional Hubbard model. This study investigates a variable CD protocol utilizing an adiabatic-variational approach, where the CD term is derived from the instantaneous adiabatic-variational ground state. We examine the impact of varying the CD driving time and the initial state. Results indicate that, despite the model's inherent complexity, a CD protocol with a variable duration can effectively prepare the ground state from a broad range of initial conditions within a significantly reduced time compared to adiabatic-variational methods without a CD term. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a short CD driving time can still yield high fidelity, provided the initial state is selected appropriately. Finally, we analyze the adiabaticity of the CD protocol by calculating the fidelity between the prepared ground state and the true ground state. This analysis reveals that a short CD driving time can still achieve high fidelity, even when the prepared state differs slightly from the true ground state. These findings suggest that a variable CD driving time can be employed to prepare the ground state of the two-dimensional Hubbard model with high fidelity in a significantly shorter time than previously achieved. Additionally, the methodology used to construct the CD term is applicable to other quantum systems. Consequently, this approach may prove valuable for the efficient preparation of ground states in various quantum systems.
