We introduce a novel photon-photon science initiative grounded in laser-plata physics. This approach aims to create intense, large-volume photon fields within laser-plasma interactions, thereby enabling photon-photon science through highly nonlinear quantum electrodynamic processes. The program is designed to advance photon-photon research across three distinct energy regimes: optical-optical, X-ray-X-ray, and gamma-gamma. To achieve this, we have established a comprehensive framework that integrates laser-plasma modeling with photon-photon interaction calculations. This framework is currently being utilized to identify optimal laser-plasma configurations for the target photon fields. Our findings indicate that laser-plasma interactions can generate photon fields reaching up to 10^14 W/cm^2 in the optical range, 10^20 W/cm^2 in the hard X-ray range, and 10^24 W/cm^2 in the soft gamma-ray range. These results demonstrate that laser-plasma interactions offer a viable pathway for exploring previously inaccessible regimes in photon-photon science. Furthermore, we have developed a user-friendly, open-source tool to facilitate the investigation of photon-photon science via laser-plasma interactions. This tool is publicly accessible at https://github.com/llnl/laser-plasma-photon-photon-physics. This study examines the stability of the $Z_2$ symmetry within a two-Higgs-doublet model, utilizing the most recent LHC Run 2 data. We determine the sensitivity of various Higgs boson searches to the soft-breaking parameter $m_{12}$, which stabilizes the $Z_2$ symmetry, by analyzing the Higgs boson mass matrix. Our findings indicate that the $Z_2$-symmetric scenario is viable only for $m_{12} \lesssim 100$ GeV. Furthermore, we observe that searches for the Higgs boson in the $\tau^+\tau^-$ and $b\bar{b}$ channels are the most sensitive to $m_{12}$, whereas the $\mu^+\mu^-$ channel offers the least sensitivity. Additionally, we note that the $\tau^+\tau^-$ search exhibits a sharp cutoff at $m_{12} \approx 100$ GeV, a feature that may be attributed to the specific methodology employed in that analysis. Finally, we present the current experimental constraints on the $Z_2$-symmetric case and discuss potential future improvements. These results can be accessed via the online tool \href{https://www.hepdata.net/submission/10000} {HEPData submission 10000}. This paper introduces a novel method for transferring information from Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) to Resource Description Frameworks (RDF), utilizing both algebraic and logical approaches. The method employs a restricted form of Datalog to define views over Relational tables, where each table corresponds to an RDF class. Furthermore, the approach supports the import of existing RDF data by enabling views on these RDF classes. To ensure type consistency during the transfer, the method incorporates Shape Expressions, which outline semantic constraints for RDF classes and properties. We demonstrate that this proposed method subsumes the widely adopted EAV (Entity-Attribute-Value) technique. Additionally, we outline a strategy for validating whether a specific RDF instance adheres to the type constraints established by a given relational schema. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept implementation of this method. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. This work extends the study presented at the 14th International Conference on the Theory and Application of Cryptographic Techniques (CRYPTO 2014). We introduce pyStoNED, a Python library designed for the nonparametric enveloping frontier method. The library's architecture promotes code reusability and extensibility, while its interface is designed to be user-friendly. It supports various nonparametric and semiparametric approaches, including those by Simar and Wilson (2007, 2017), as well as parametric models like stochastic frontier models. Additionally, pyStoNED offers tools for comprehensive frontier evaluation, such as calculating efficiency scores, estimating distances to the frontier, and conducting inference. The library is freely accessible at https://github.com/PyStoNE/pyStoNE. This paper demonstrates its application using two datasets: the German energy industry and a simulated dataset. The latter is specifically crafted to illustrate pyStoNED's capabilities regarding inference, including confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. Furthermore, pyStoNED is integrated into the R package StoNE, which can be installed via `install.packages("Stone")`. Both implementations yield identical results, highlighting the complementary nature of the two environments. The primary distinction lies in their focus: pyStoNED emphasizes flexibility and extensibility, whereas R-StoNE prioritizes ease of use and accessibility. The R package is available at https://github.com/PyStoNE/R-StoNE. The paper includes a tutorial demonstrating how to install pyStoNED and apply it to the German energy industry dataset. The primary contribution of this work is the development of pyStoNED, which enables users to implement a wide range of envelopment frontiers, perform detailed frontier assessments, and conduct thorough inference. The code is released under the MIT license, allowing free usage, modification, and distribution. The repository also contains a collection of example scripts that illustrate various functionalities, including parametric frontiers, efficiency scores, distances, and inference. The authors acknowledge that pyStoNED is a work in progress and welcome contributions from the community. This includes bug reports, feature requests, and pull requests, which can be submitted via the project's issue tracker at https://github.com/PyStoNE/pyStoNE/issues. The authors also invite users to explore the package's capabilities and share their findings. Finally, the authors express gratitude to the pyStoNE team for their support and collaboration. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of pyStoNED and potential areas for future improvement. The code is released under the MIT license

This study examines the $t \bar t \phi$ production channel at the LHC for a scalar resonance $\phi$ with Standard Model-like couplings, assuming a mass $m_\phi$ of 100, 200, and 300 GeV. The analysis focuses on the Higgs-like scalar's self-coupling, its coupling to the top quark, and its total width. We evaluate the sensitivity of the $t \bar t \phi$ process to these parameters using the full Run 2 dataset, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 150 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The investigation covers all decay modes of the $\phi$ particle, including the diphoton channel, and demonstrates that the process remains sensitive to these parameters up to the kinematic limit imposed by the scalar mass. Furthermore, we show that the Higgs signal can be isolated from the dominant Standard Model $t \bar t \gamma \gamma$ background by applying a cut on the scalar mass. Finally, we present the projected sensitivity of the LHC to the Higgs signal within this channel. Our findings indicate that the process can probe the Higgs width up to its maximum possible value, while the signal-to-background ratio for the $t \bar t \phi$ process is approximately 1:10. Additionally, the projected sensitivity to the $\phi$ self-coupling is estimated to be around 10% for a scalar mass of 100 GeV. These results suggest that the $t \bar t \phi$ process will play a crucial role in future investigations of the Higgs signal. The study also explores the potential of the High-Luminosity LHC, where the sensitivity to the Higgs self-coupling could improve by a factor of 2 to 3. Finally, we discuss the prospects of the High Energy LHC (HE-LHC) for studying the Higgs signal in this channel. Our findings indicate that the HE-LHC could achieve a sensitivity to the self-coupling of 5% for a scalar mass of 100 GeV, a level of precision that will be essential for determining the nature of the Higgs boson. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for the future of particle physics research. This study investigates data enhancement as a technique for generating synthetic data to enhance performance in inverse text standardization (ITS-T). Data enhancement operates as a text-to-text transformation, functioning similarly to data augmentation in image processing but applied to text. We evaluate several data enhancement methods, including back-translation, noise injection, and text generation, to create synthetic data for training ITS-T models. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained on this synthetic data surpass those trained solely on the original data. Furthermore, we find that combining synthetic data with original data yields superior outcomes compared to using synthetic data alone. Our findings indicate that data enhancement is a highly effective approach for improving ITS-T performance. The source code and synthetic data utilized in this work are accessible at https://github.com/abhi-1999/ITS-T-Data-Enhancement. Additionally, this paper has been accepted for publication in the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).

**Keywords:** Inverse Text Standardization, Data Enhancement, Synthetic Data, Machine Translation, Abstractive Summarization.

**1. Introduction**

Multilingual Machine Translation (MT) has proven to be a potent instrument for breaking down language barriers, yet it has not fully resolved the issue of textual communication. While MT transforms text from one language to another, it often fails to address variations in text style, structure, and formatting. For instance, a sentence in English might be written in British English, whereas the target sentence requires American English. Similarly, a paragraph in one language might be structured differently from the paragraph in another language. These style, structure, and formatting discrepancies can hinder effective communication, making it essential to standardize text across different languages. This process, known as Inverse Text Standardization (ITS-T), aims to normalize text regardless of its language, style, structure, or formatting.

ITS-T is a relatively novel research area that has garnered significant attention in recent years. The primary objective of ITS-T is to standardize text across various languages, styles, structures, and formats. This task is particularly challenging because it involves handling diverse text types, such as news articles, emails, and social media posts, which often contain informal language, slang, and other non-standard elements. Additionally, ITS-T requires the preservation of text structure and formatting, which is not a common requirement in other NLP tasks.

We investigate the topological characteristics of interacting one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems. Initially, we analyze a lattice model featuring asymmetric hopping and onsite interactions, demonstrating that point-gap topology is destroyed when interactions become sufficiently strong. Furthermore, we establish that this mechanism for eliminating point-gap topology in non-Hermitian lattices cannot be replicated by non-interacting systems. Finally, we explore how this phenomenon can be observed experimentally. Our findings reveal that point-gap topology is fragile within interacting systems, and we propose that this interaction-induced topological transition can be detected through the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian. Additionally, we show that this topological transition can be monitored via the spectral properties of the density matrix. These results offer new insights into the behavior of non-Hermitian topological systems and suggest pathways for future experimental research. Specifically, we demonstrate that the model under study can be realized using Bose-Einstein condensates. Finally, we outline a method to experimentally detect the point-gap topological transition via the eigenvalues of the density matrix. This paper introduces a new framework for integrating social speaker characteristics into generated speech. We utilize a two-stage process: first, a social speaker embedding is extracted from a training corpus using speaker embeddings and social trait descriptors; second, this embedding is embedded into a latent space of a neural speech generation model trained on a large dataset. This approach enables the synthesis of speech by a virtual speaker possessing specific social attributes. Our method achieves high-quality, natural-sounding speech, as evidenced by low Mean-Square-Error (MSE) scores and strong performance on the Mozilla Speech Processing (MSP) benchmark. Additionally, we demonstrate that the generated speech effectively conveys the intended social characteristics. The code and data required to replicate these results are publicly accessible at https://github.com/cedric-bernard/Social-Traits-Synthesis. We investigate a phenomenological framework combining $A_4$ flavor symmetry with a $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge symmetry. Within this model, the dark matter candidate is identified as a linear combination of the right-handed neutrinos, which are responsible for the model's neutrino mass generation mechanism. This scenario is analyzed in detail within the context of the dark matter relic density and direct detection experiments. Furthermore, we examine the phenomenological consequences of neutrinoless double beta decay and the generation of a baryon asymmetry. Our findings indicate that the proposed dark matter candidate can account for the observed relic density and is potentially detectable in direct search experiments. Additionally, the model predicts a neutrinoless double beta decay scale of approximately $10^{10}$ and a baryon asymmetry of roughly $10^{-10}$. Finally, we demonstrate that the dark matter can be detected at the Large Hadron Collider through the production of right-handed neutrinos. These results suggest that the model is viable and can be tested in the near future. Finally, we conclude that this scenario offers a promising avenue for further investigation. In this framework, the dark matter is not a new particle but rather a linear combination of right-handed neutrinos, which are essential for explaining the smallness of neutrino masses. This approach avoids the stringent constraints typically imposed on traditional dark matter candidates. Moreover, the model provides a comprehensive explanation for flavor phenomena, including neutrino oscillation data, the CKM mixing matrix, and the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry. Additionally, it predicts a non-zero value for the effective neutrino number, $N_{\rm eff}$, which can be tested in future cosmological observations. Finally, the model predicts a relatively large neutrinoless double beta decay scale of about $10^{10}$, a value that can be probed in upcoming experiments. In summary, this model offers a unified explanation for flavor phenomena, dark matter, and the matter-antimatter asymmetry, while also predicting a relatively large neutrinoless double beta decay scale. The minimal distance concept is applied to the collective motion of triaxial nuclei. The phase space is partitioned into cells based on the distances between nucleons, and the probability distribution function is derived from the average occupancy of these cells. This distribution function is subsequently utilized to calculate the potential energy of the collective motion. The resulting potential energy landscape features valleys that direct collective motion along specific paths, with the shape of these valleys varying depending on the nucleus. The study examines collective movements within these valleys for three specific nuclei: $^{120}$Xe, $^{124}$Xe, and $^{128}$Xe. Furthermore, the influence of the parameter $\lambda$ on the potential energy landscape and collective motion is analyzed. Finally, the findings are compared with other theoretical frameworks and experimental data. This work represents the inaugural application of the minimal distance concept to investigate collective motion in triaxial nuclei. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/MDP. This paper introduces the concept of polyphase Golay complementary structures (GCSs) of order $L$, which extend polyphase Golay complementary sequences (GCSs) to Golay complementary polynomials (GCPs). We establish two constructive methods for generating infinite families of binary and quaternary GCPs that satisfy the GCP condition, thereby enabling the construction of polyphase GCSs and providing specific examples. Additionally, we present two new constructive methods for polyphase GCSs derived from existing sequences. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between polyphase GCSs and polyphase constant-amplitude sequences (CASs), demonstrating that polyphase GCSs with zero autocorrelation can be utilized to construct polyphase CASs. Finally, we propose two design approaches for polyphase GCPs based on real and imaginary sequences, which yield new results. Numerical examples are provided to validate the proposed constructions. These GCPs hold potential applications in OFDM systems, particularly for designing zero-correlation zones. The paper concludes with an outline of future research directions. Notably, the novel constructions of polyphase GCSs and GCPs presented in this work are expected to significantly advance the field of GCP research. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to address polyphase GCPs. The results herein offer a foundation for future research in this area. Furthermore, the proposed constructions of polyphase GCSs are anticipated to have a profound impact on the field of GCS research. The paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews the definitions of polyphase GCSs and GCPs; Section III introduces the definition of polyphase GCPs; Section IV details the construction of polyphase GCSs from polyphase GCPs; Section V explores the link between polyphase GCSs and polyphase CASs; Section VI addresses the design of polyphase GCPs; and Section VII concludes the paper. This paper introduces a deep autoencoder architecture designed to identify alterations in color photographs by merging two distinct feature representations derived from the image. The initial representation is generated by a deep convolutional autoencoder that processes the raw image, while the second representation stems from a model trained to predict the image's illumination. By combining these two feature sets, the proposed architecture enhances the detection of manipulated pixels within the photograph. Extensive experiments conducted on the Forensic Image Manipulation Database (FIMD) demonstrate that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods for unsupervised pixel-level alteration detection in color images. Furthermore, the method is evaluated on the widely used Forensic Photo Anti-Manipulation (FPA) dataset, yielding promising outcomes. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-ayman/Deep-Feature-Integration. The results confirm that the proposed method effectively detects various image manipulations, including copy-paste, cloning, and blending techniques. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against quality degradation caused by JPEG compression and Gaussian noise. Finally, the approach demonstrates superior performance in revealing alterations within images that were previously undetectable by existing state-of-the-art algorithms. We outline a cyclical cosmology grounded in the $\Lambda CDM$ framework, where each cycle comprises an expansion phase followed by a contraction. The universe expands following a Big Bang, decelerating under gravity until it reaches a maximum size defined by the Hubble radius. As it approaches this limit, it undergoes a Big Crunch, transitioning into a Big Bang that initiates the subsequent cycle. This process repeats indefinitely. We demonstrate that the Hubble radius remains constant throughout the expansion, while the Hubble parameter undergoes an infinite discontinuity at the onset of contraction. Furthermore, we show that the scale factor follows a power-law evolution during the radiation and matter-dominated eras, and we derive the corresponding temperature evolution. We also examine the Hubble flow, finding that the Hubble parameter exhibits a similar power-law behavior in both epochs, though with an exponent differing by a sign. Additionally, we analyze the evolution of the density parameter $\Omega$, which asymptotically approaches unity at the end of both radiation and matter-dominated phases. Finally, we address the issue of the cosmological constant, proposing that it may be negative. We conclude by discussing the implications of this cyclical model. These findings are based on a straightforward application of the Friedmann equations. The cyclical nature of this cosmology offers a potential resolution to the Big Bang singularity. Moreover, the Big Crunch could serve as the Big Bang for the next cycle, thereby eliminating the need for cosmic inflation. This model also provides an explanation for the observed acceleration of the universe's expansion. Ultimately, we suggest that the cyclical $\Lambda CDM$ cosmology offers a viable alternative to the standard Big Bang model. This work is intended to inspire further research into cyclical cosmologies. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details the cyclical $\Lambda CDM$ framework; Section 3 explores its consequences; and Section 4 presents our conclusions. Appendix A provides a derivation of the scale factor's behavior, while Appendix B examines the evolution of the temperature. Appendix C addresses the Hubble parameter's evolution, and Appendix D discusses the density parameter. Finally, Appendix E examines the evolution of the density parameter $\Omega$. This work examines the connection between the dimer model and massless Dirac fermions within a background gauge field. We demonstrate that the dimer partition function, which corresponds to the product of two Pfaffians, yields the same result as the fermion partition function, consistent with the Pfaffian-fermion correspondence. This equivalence holds true even in the presence of a background gauge field. Furthermore, we show that both formulations—the dimer model and the massless Dirac fermion model with a background gauge field—satisfy the same constraint: the winding numbers of the respective holonomies around the lattice must be even. Consequently, the fermion winding number constraint is interpreted as a manifestation of the spin-statistics theorem. Finally, we examine the duality between the dimer model and the vortex model, revealing that the duality between these two models is contingent upon the winding number constraint. As a result, the vortex model fails to capture the duality between the fermion model and the dimer model. We also explore the vortex model's relationship with the dimer model, noting that it does not satisfy the duality with the fermion model. Ultimately, we conclude that the vortex model cannot serve as a dual to the fermion model. These findings underscore the necessity of carefully selecting the appropriate dual formulation when investigating the duality between the dimer model and the vortex model. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these results for the fermion condensation dual of a $Z_2$ gauge theory. Specifically, we find that the fermion model, which is dual to the dimer model, cannot act as a dual for the $Z_2$ gauge model because the $Z_2$ gauge model is equivalent to the vortex model. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the vortex model does not satisfy the spin-statistics theorem. Finally, we address the issue of fermion condensation in the $Z_2$ gauge model. We show that the fermion condensation dual of the $Z_2$ gauge model is actually the vortex model, not the fermion model. This is because the fermion model describes a system with an odd winding number, whereas the $Z_2$ gauge model corresponds to a system with an even winding number. Thus, the fermion condensation dual of the $Z_2$ gauge model is the vortex model. We examine two mutually inhibiting neural populations, where each cell within a population exhibits distinct firing rates and interspike intervals. This system is modeled using a system of two coupled maps, where the coupling between maps is established via piecewise linear transformations. We demonstrate that chimeric states emerge when one population fires synchronously with a constant interspike interval, while the other fires asynchronously with variable intervals. Specifically, we identify the precise conditions under which even distribution of variability arises, a phenomenon that contrasts with prior research on this topic. Furthermore, we illustrate how this model can be derived from a system of two mutually inhibiting integrate-and-fire neurons with piecewise linear subthreshold dynamics. Finally, we explore the link between this system and a more general model featuring smooth interspike interval variability. In both scenarios, we observe that the distribution of variability in the asynchronous population is governed by the distribution of firing rates in the synchronous population. Additionally, we show that this variability can be either even or uneven, contingent upon the specific system parameters. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. This study investigates the resilience of control policies against stochastic disturbances in continuous-state, linear-quadratic (LQ) control environments. Resilience is defined as the ability to maintain a high mean reward while minimizing reward variance. We introduce a model-driven exploration strategy that utilizes a controller model to identify the most promising control actions for learning robust policies. Our approach, which integrates this method with deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), is evaluated across various synthetic LQ control scenarios. The results demonstrate that our method surpasses both model-free and model-based baselines in achieving superior performance. Furthermore, we highlight the method's potential for real-world applications by presenting a case study on a quadrotor. We introduce a graph-theoretic approach to calculating the slice monoid of an elevated slice algebra, utilizing multi-layer graphs. Initially, we define these algebras and their associated multi-layer graphs, demonstrating that the slice monoid of every elevated slice algebra corresponds precisely to the multi-layer graph's automorphism group. Subsequently, we construct specific multi-layer graphs where the automorphism group is trivial, thereby yielding elevated slice algebras with a trivial slice monoid. Finally, we examine the automorphism groups of these constructed graphs and the resulting slice monoids of these algebras. Additionally, we present an example of a multi-layer graph where the automorphism group is non-abelian, which implies the existence of an elevated slice algebra with a non-abelian slice monoid. This work extends our earlier research presented at the 2021 International Conference on Algebra and Number Theory. The term "elevated slice algebra" was introduced in that paper. We introduce a tensor network approach to calculate the mirrored entropy of a random pure state within a many-body system, extending the method originally developed by Penington [arXiv:1911.11957] for one-dimensional matrix product states. This technique is applicable to any stochastic tensor network, including those based on multi-scale entanglement renormalization, and can be extended to determine the entropy of a subregion in a random state, a task previously addressed by Li and Yang [arXiv:1912.07499]. Our findings indicate that the entropy of a subregion in a random state scales extensively with system size, exhibiting a subleading term that decreases with increasing bond dimension. These results offer a deeper understanding of the relationship between randomness and entanglement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entropy of a subregion in a specific tensor network model, which captures the entanglement structure of a many-body eigenstate, also scales extensively with system size. This suggests that the eigenstate eigenvalue hypothesis [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 090603 (2019)] may not hold in one-dimensional systems. Additionally, we explore the connection between our method and the concept of typicality in quantum mechanics. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the eigenstate eigenvalue hypothesis. We investigate heritable data within the context of a two-dimensional, continuous random field model featuring a finite correlation length, which is subjected to random deletions and repopulation with new, uncorrelated values. This framework represents a simplified version of the error-correcting code problem found in biological systems. Our findings indicate that the competition between the preservation of old data and the introduction of new values leads to a phase transition, resulting in either the retention of a single copy of the initial data or its complete loss. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical exponent governing this transition is universal and can be derived analytically. Finally, we validate these results using numerical simulations. These results have significant implications for the physics of living systems, as they suggest that the design of error-correcting codes in such systems is constrained by the dimensionality of the data and its correlation length. Additionally, our work provides a foundation for future research into the physics of living systems. By applying this clock to a spin-1/2 particle traversing a double-barrier potential, we demonstrate that the resulting durations align with prior findings derived from various methods. Furthermore, we show that the tunneling time remains invariant under time-reversal, regardless of whether the system is in a unitary or non-unitary state. Intestinal worm categorization serves as a critical diagnostic tool for determining treatment strategies. While deep learning has been widely applied to various domains, its use in this specific area remains limited. This study introduces a deep belief network (DBN) model for classifying intestinal worms. The proposed approach begins by training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from worm images, followed by the training of a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) using those features. These components are subsequently integrated into a unified DBN model. The research evaluates worm categorization performance across three distinct datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the significant contributions of both the CNN and MLP to the overall performance. This study examines a class of non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance games involving two insurers, where each firm may operate under one of two distinct economic regimes. The joint evolution of these regimes is modeled as a continuous-time Markov chain. The insurers' asset dynamics are described by time-inhomogeneous jump-diffusion processes, with control mechanisms implemented through investment and proportional reinsurance strategies. The objective for both firms is to maximize the expected discounted utility of their profits. By applying the stochastic maximum principle, we derive the necessary conditions for optimality and establish the existence of an open-loop Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a viscosity solution to the associated system of nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Quasi-Variational Inequality (HJBQVI) systems, which characterizes this Nash equilibrium. Finally, we illustrate the application of these findings through a numerical example. Additionally, the methodology is extended to a scenario involving a single insurer, yielding a corresponding open-loop Nash equilibrium. This work represents the first instance of analyzing non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance games with regime switching and proportional reinsurance within the context of jump-diffusion models. The findings hold significant implications for the development of non-zero-sum stochastic control models applicable to the insurance sector. Finally, the model's practical utility is underscored by its application to the China Insurance Group Corporation. We introduce a new dataset of 1,000 active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies, identified through multi-wavelength observations from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Extensive Survey (HiSC-ES) and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE). By analyzing the morphologies of these hosts, we aim to investigate the relationship between host structure and AGN characteristics. Leveraging HiSC-ES imaging data, we apply a machine learning approach to classify host galaxies as either disk or spheroid types. Our results indicate that, on average, disk-type hosts are more massive and luminous than spheroid-type hosts. Furthermore, we find that disk-type hosts are more prevalent in the lower redshift range ($0.0 < z < 0.5$) and at higher luminosities, whereas spheroid-type hosts are more common at higher redshifts ($0.5 < z < 1.0$) and lower luminosities. Additionally, AGN identified as disk-type hosts exhibit a higher likelihood of being radio-loud and possessing higher bolometric luminosities compared to those in spheroid-type hosts. These findings suggest that the physical properties of host galaxies are intrinsically linked to the properties of their central AGN. Finally, we demonstrate that the HiSC-ES survey is capable of accurately classifying AGN host galaxies into disk or spheroid categories. This study represents the first effort to characterize the morphologies of AGN host galaxies at $z < 1$ using machine learning. This study examines short-distance correlations within nuclear matter using a phenomenological approach. The analysis demonstrates that the majority of these correlations involve three nucleons, with a smaller fraction attributed to two-nucleon correlations. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the probability of finding four or more nucleons at very short ranges is negligible. These results are derived by fitting the phenomenological model to the one- and two-nucleon reduced density distributions, which are calculated from the probabilities of finding one or two nucleons in specific phase-space regions. These probabilities are subsequently determined by fitting the model to the single- and two-nucleon inclusive cross sections observed in $^{12}$C(p,p) and $^{12}$C(e,e') experiments. The calculated reduced density distributions align well with prior theoretical predictions. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these results for nuclear structure and reactions. Notably, the data suggest that the short-range correlations previously inferred from inclusive cross sections are predominantly three-nucleon in nature. This conclusion contradicts the conventional view that such correlations are mainly two-nucleon, a perspective that has been the basis for many theoretical models and the interpretation of various nuclear phenomena. Consequently, the current analysis may necessitate a reevaluation of existing theoretical models and the interpretation of phenomena previously attributed to two-nucleon short-distance correlations. Specifically, three-nucleon correlations may play a more significant role than previously assumed in phenomena such as the EMC effect, the Pauli enhancement of the neutron-deuteron cross section, and the suppression of the $\Delta$ resonance in the nucleon-deuteron system. Additionally, the analysis indicates that the three-nucleon short-distance correlation length is approximately 1.5 fm, which is notably larger than the lengths associated with two-nucleon correlations. This finding may have important consequences for the understanding of nuclear forces and the structure of nuclear wave functions. Ultimately, the current analysis may require a fundamental rethinking of the nature of short-distance correlations in nuclei and their impact on a wide range of nuclear phenomena. This is a significant and potentially revolutionary conclusion that could have far-reaching implications for nuclear physics. However, it is important to note that the current analysis is based on a phenomenological model and may require further refinement and validation through more rigorous theoretical and experimental studies. Nevertheless, the potential impact of these findings on our understanding of nuclear physics is substantial, and the need for further investigation is clear. We introduce a novel approach to investigate magnetorotronic states within fractional quantum Hall systems. This method involves decomposing the Laughlin wave function into magnetron and Rydberg components, thereby expressing the reduced Hamiltonian in a rydronic basis. We demonstrate that the magnetron part encompasses numerous magnetorotronic states, which are characterized by an extensive set of quantum numbers. Furthermore, we establish that the ground state is determined by a spectral total regulation principle. This finding offers a fresh perspective on the quantum Hall effect and provides a fresh avenue for exploring it. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to other quantum many-body problems. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this approach by examining the fractional quantum Hall effect in graphene. Our results indicate that the Rydronic basis proves highly effective for this specific system. Moreover, the fractional quantum Hall ground state in graphene exhibits a unique structure, arising from the significant overlap between magnetron and Rydronic components. Consequently, this reveals a previously unrecognized feature of the fractional quantum Hall ground state in graphene. We anticipate that this feature will be experimentally verified. Finally, we believe our findings will inspire further research into the quantum Hall effect. This study was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11974370). This paper introduces a geometric approach to the network outbreak problem, which involves identifying a grouping of nodes that minimizes both the initial number of infected nodes and the expected duration of the outbreak. The proposed algorithm relies on the concept of "cutting" a network, defined as the count of edges linking a node to its $k$ nearest neighbors. This method is grounded in a theorem stating that if a node's cutting value does not exceed a specific limit, then grouping that node with its nearest neighbors will result in no increase in the total number of infected nodes. We demonstrate the application of this algorithm to both static and dynamic networks. For static networks, we utilize established metrics such as degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality to determine a node's neighbors. In contrast, for dynamic networks, we employ a time-based metric to identify neighbors. The effectiveness of this algorithm is validated through simulations on both synthetic and real-world networks. Furthermore, we compare our proposed method against existing algorithms, including degree-based, betweenness centrality, and closeness centrality approaches. The results indicate that the network outbreak problem is NP-hard, and our algorithm achieves superior performance compared to these alternative methods. Finally, we discuss the algorithm's limitations and suggest potential directions for future research. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/GNO. This study examines the behavior of pixelized maps derived from the most probable angular power spectra of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), with a specific focus on the impact of a bright foreground source. We demonstrate that the map's peak aligns with the source's true position, while the pixel immediately adjacent to this peak exhibits an anomalously high intensity. This artifact arises because the maximum probability spectrum retains a slight excess power at the source location, which translates into a small but non-negligible intensity in the map. This phenomenon is particularly problematic for point sources, where the nearby pixel's intensity can significantly exceed the source's true intensity. We provide a general framework to quantify the likelihood of such artifacts and their influence on the map's probability distribution. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward method to mitigate this issue: simply shifting the identified peak away from its original position. This approach effectively eliminates the spurious intensity in the neighboring pixel, thereby removing the associated probability bias. Finally, we apply this method to the Planck 2015 CMB maps, showing that it successfully mitigates the problem for several prominent X-ray sources. The corrected maps are available for download. Additionally, we have developed a Python package, `mpmap`, to facilitate the creation of maximum probability maps and the application of our proposed mitigation strategy. The package can be installed via `pip install mpmap`. The source code and a demonstration notebook are accessible at https://github.com/leopoldo-gonzalez/mpmap. This study investigates the multi-body Coulomb interactions within bilayer graphene using the renormalization group method. By analyzing the flow of interaction vertices, we identify a specific fixed point characterized by strong interaction strength. At this point, the interaction flows exhibit distinct behaviors: they increase with momentum transfer in the forward direction but decrease in the backward direction. Furthermore, the renormalized velocity and gap demonstrate power-law scaling with respect to the cutoff. These findings indicate that interaction-driven superconductivity is feasible in bilayer graphene. Additionally, the calculated interaction strength aligns with experimental data, and the observed phenomena are consistent with prior theoretical predictions. Finally, we explore the potential for inducing superconductivity in bilayer graphene through external fields. These results provide a foundation for future experimental research into superconductivity within this material. Additionally, the methodology employed can be applied to other graphene systems. The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, encompassing a vast array of devices that are expected to grow from approximately 16 billion in 2017 to 229 billion by 2022. These devices are typically resource-constrained, possessing limited processing power, memory, and energy. Consequently, the security mechanisms they rely on must be both robust and highly efficient. This paper examines the security challenges inherent to IoT devices and evaluates the efficacy of lightweight cryptographic algorithms in addressing these issues. It further explores the application of these algorithms within the LoRaWAN protocol, detailing the specific security services LoRaWAN provides to IoT devices. Finally, the paper assesses the performance of lightweight cryptographic algorithms in delivering these services, analyzing their computational and energy costs. Through this analysis, the study identifies the most suitable algorithms for LoRaWAN and offers recommendations for future research. The paper concludes by outlining potential research directions, such as developing new lightweight algorithms, optimizing existing ones, and enhancing the security architecture of LoRaWAN. Additionally, it proposes investigating the integration of machine learning with lightweight cryptography to bolster IoT security. The authors intend to pursue these opportunities, with a specific focus on investigating the application of machine learning to improve the security of LoRaWAN. Rapidly evolving experimental conditions necessitate adaptive strategies to maximize data quality. A prominent instance of this need arises in Ramsey interferometry, where environmental factors like temperature fluctuations can compromise measurement precision. This study introduces a sequential Bayesian adaptive algorithm designed to adjust measurement parameters in real-time, ensuring optimal outcomes. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through both simulations and experimental data. Furthermore, we show that this method can be broadly applied to optimize various measurement protocols. By dynamically selecting the most effective settings at each step, the proposed approach achieves a substantial improvement in data quality. Specifically, simulations indicate that optimizing both interrogation time and integration time can enhance signal-to-noise ratios by up to 20%, a significant gain that translates to more precise measurements. This work establishes a versatile framework for adaptive measurements, offering a pathway to achieve higher precision across diverse experimental contexts. Additionally, the code is publicly accessible to facilitate its application in other settings. This paper introduces Gromov importance, a novel metric for assessing network node centrality. By leveraging the Gromov product, it offers a geometrically intuitive approach to centrality that utilizes triangle inequality surplus. The Gromov product quantifies the relative position of a point within a metric space by measuring the deviation from the assumption that the point lies on the shortest path between two other points. Gromov importance is defined as the aggregate of these deviations across all pairs of nodes. The study demonstrates that Gromov importance exhibits a strong positive correlation with established centrality measures, including degree, betweenness, and eigenvector centrality. Furthermore, it establishes a theoretical link to the betweenness centrality proposed by Borgatti and Everett. Finally, the paper examines the computational complexity of calculating Gromov importance and presents a method to derive it from betweenness centrality matrices. The authors conclude that Gromov importance serves as a multi-layer metric for network centrality, providing both geometric and graph-theoretic perspectives. This metric is particularly valuable for elucidating the geometric significance of centrality and for enhancing the interpretability of centrality results. Additionally, Gromov importance can be derived from betweenness centrality matrices, thereby reducing computational complexity. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions. We introduce a novel gravitational theory, termed the Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity (AUGT), which adheres to the principle that physical laws must remain invariant under any rotation within the azimuthal plane. This framework is constructed using the azimuthal four-rotation, defined as the component of the space-time four-rotation perpendicular to this plane, alongside the radial four-vector, which points directly away from the azimuthal plane. AUGT posits that the azimuthal symmetry of the universe's large-scale structure generates a specific symmetry in physical laws, thereby necessitating an additional field known as the azimuthal four-potential. This new field is determined by solving a Poisson equation with a source term derived from matter density. The theory's validity is demonstrated through its successful derivation of Kepler's laws and its ability to accurately predict the precession of Mercury's perihelion. Furthermore, AUGT provides a precise explanation for the anomalous precession of binary pulsars and aligns with the observed redshifts of galaxies. In this initial paper, we outline the fundamental principles of AUGT and present these initial validation results. Subsequent publications will explore the theory's broader implications. Additionally, we will examine the relationship between AUGT and General Relativity, noting that both frameworks yield identical results when applied to systems exhibiting azimuthal symmetry. Consequently, AUGT offers a distinct approach to modeling the universe's large-scale structure, one that simplifies the description of matter distribution and streamlines the calculation of gravitational effects. Ultimately, AUGT provides a viable alternative to General Relativity for describing the universe's large-scale behavior. We introduce a novel, efficient method for representing distances in planar graphs on an augmented structure known as a Tree of Clusters, which we demonstrate to be a graph with bounded treewidth. This reduction enables the application of dynamic programming techniques to solve numerous optimization problems on planar distance graphs that were previously resistant to such methods. Our findings are extended to minor-free graphs, which can be represented with distances preserved through a constant number of vertex duplications.

The core of our approach relies on a planar separator theorem that recursively partitions a graph into disconnected components of nearly equal size. We show that this theorem can be executed in linear time for planar graphs and in $O(n \log k)$ time for $K_k$-minor-free graphs. Furthermore, we establish that the separator construction for $K_k$-minor-free graphs can be performed in $O(n \log^2 k)$ time.

Our primary technical advancement is a novel algorithm that converts the recursive separator decomposition into a Treewidth representation. This method runs in $O(n \log^2 k)$ time for $K_k$-minor-free graphs and produces a Tree of Clusters where each cluster contains $O(n/k)$ vertices. We also provide a straightforward linear-time algorithm to convert this representation into a standard Tree of Clusters format.

We validate the utility of this representation by solving two major problems in quadratic time for planar graphs: (1) computing the maximum number of vertex-disjoint paths between two specified vertex sets, and (2) determining the minimum number of vertices to remove to disconnect a graph into $k$ components of equal size. Both problems are known to be solvable in quadratic time for general graphs. Additionally, we present a linear-time algorithm for the first problem in $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graphs and a polynomial-time algorithm for the second problem in $K_{4,4}$-minor-free graphs.

Finally, we examine the complexity of planarizing graphs by adding edges. We prove that deciding whether a graph can be planarized with at most $k$ added edges is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by $k$. This result extends to the problem of identifying a vertex set of size at most $k$ that, upon duplication, yields a planar graph. We further demonstrate that the separator construction for $K_k$-minor-free graphs can be adapted to the class of graphs with bounded genus.

We introduce a broad framework encompassing many discrete-interval dynamical systems, including all monotonic interval systems and a wide range of set-valued maps. We demonstrate that within this framework, a strongly monotone map exhibits behavior analogous to nonhyperbolic interval maps, specifically the Newhouse phenomenon and shadowing of pseudo-orbits. Furthermore, we prove that a $C^1$ map defined on a compact set experiences Newhouse behavior precisely when a periodic orbit with a positive Schwarzian derivative exists within its closure. These findings extend the work of Barreira and Valls (2005) and their associated results. Additionally, we establish that for a set-valued map where every element is strongly monotone, the existence of a periodic orbit with a positive Schwarzian derivative is both necessary and sufficient for Newhouse behavior. Finally, we explore how these results apply to various sets of set-valued maps, such as those arising in control theory. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) represent a promising method for solving complex problems on near-term quantum hardware. However, their practical utility is currently constrained by the limited number of trainable parameters and the resulting susceptibility to local minima. This study introduces a qubit-excitation-driven adaptive VQA (qAVQA) designed to address these limitations. The approach utilizes qubit excitations as a metric for the significance of individual terms, enabling the dynamic addition of relevant trainable parameters. We demonstrate the application of qAVQA to the preparation of symmetry-adapted wavefunctions for the Helium atom, showing that it can achieve high accuracy with a minimal quantity of parameters. Furthermore, we outline a general framework for applying qAVQA to various quantum chemistry problems. Our findings indicate that this adaptive strategy is effective for systems with low excitation levels, offering a pathway to overcome VQA limitations in near-term quantum chemistry applications. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package that implements the qAVQA algorithm and supports its application to diverse quantum chemistry challenges. Recent investigations into low-frequency gravitational wave (GW) backdrops have revealed a potential signal within the NANOGrav 15-year dataset. This study examines the implications of this detection for the GW strain spectrum, $h(f)$, and its connection to cosmological models. We explore a specific scenario where the GW strain is amplified by a factor of $A$ at frequencies below $f_{\rm{ampl}}$ and remains rigid (unaffected) above this threshold. We analyze the consequences of this model for both NANOGrav and Advanced LIGO-Virgo observations, deriving constraints on the parameters $A$ and $f_{\rm{ampl}}$. Our findings indicate that the NANOGrav 15-year data restrict the amplification factor to $A \lesssim 10^4$ and the transition frequency to $f_{\rm{ampl}} \lesssim 10^{-3}$ Hz. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hubble strain, a low-frequency GW background generated by inflation, can be enhanced by a factor of $A$ at frequencies under $f_{\rm{ampl}}$ while retaining its original form above them. We show that this rigid-amplified Hubble strain aligns with the NANOGrav 15-year results, provided the parameters fall within the same limits. Additionally, we find that the Hubble strain is detectable by Advanced LIGO-Virgo when $f_{\rm{ampl}} \lesssim 10^{-2}$ Hz and $A \gtrsim 10^5$, a range that is excluded by NANOGrav. Consequently, future observations from both Hubble and Advanced LIGO-Virgo will be essential for further constraining the Hubble strain and the rigid-amplified model. Ultimately, this work underscores the significance of multi-messenger astronomy in cosmology. We conclude by discussing the potential for detecting the Hubble strain and its amplified variants using both current and upcoming GW observatories. Finally, we outline the future prospects for amplifying the Hubble strain, including the development of space-based detectors and the deployment of space-based GW antenna systems. This study reports the first interferometric observations of cometary gas emissions using a submillimeter array, specifically targeting the cometary atmosphere of C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS). The data were gathered using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's Atacama Compact Array (ACA) at a frequency of 350 GHz, achieving an angular resolution of 1.5 arcseconds. The ACA's extensive field of view allowed for the detection of gas emissions extending up to 100,000 km from the nucleus. The observed emission distribution aligns with a cometary model that incorporates both intrinsic and induced outgassing. Notably, the emission of CS (3-0) was detected at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3.5, marking the first identification of this molecule in a cometary atmosphere. These findings suggest that the CS observed in PanSTARRS may have a distributed origin, potentially formed within the comet's atmosphere or in the interstellar medium prior to its incorporation into the parent body. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that ACA observations can effectively map the spatial distribution of cometary gas emissions, a capability that could be leveraged to investigate the origins of various cometary volatiles. This study introduces a straightforward and efficient method for unsupervised speech generation. Our approach utilizes a novel sequence-to-sequence model that leverages the unsupervised training of a phoneme-level acoustic model to derive latent phoneme sequences. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in real-world applications, yet they are notoriously difficult to solve due to their inherent complexity. This study introduces a hybrid approach that integrates two established methods: NSGA-II, a well-known multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, and Branch and Bound, a robust technique for handling discrete variables. The proposed method employs NSGA-II to generate high-quality approximate solutions for the continuous relaxation of the MO-MINLP problem. Subsequently, these solutions are refined by rounding the continuous variables to their nearest integer values. Finally, the Branch and Bound algorithm is utilized to explore the solution space, branching from the rounded solutions to identify the global approximate solution. The efficacy of this methodology is validated through numerical examples, with results demonstrating its effectiveness. The paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for future research. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AmirHosseinGhorbani/NSGAII_BB.

The accessibility of high-quality data is fundamental to the progress of data-driven biomedical research. However, current data exchange methods are often inefficient and prone to security risks, as they rely on direct access to individual researchers' file systems. This paper introduces a novel approach to data exchange that leverages web-based portals to manage data access and transfer. By utilizing these portals, researchers can securely share data without granting direct file system permissions. We have developed a prototype implementation that integrates with existing cyberinfrastructure data management tools. Our findings indicate that this portal-based method offers a more secure and efficient alternative to current exchange practices. Furthermore, we outline the necessary steps to deploy this implementation in production environments. We anticipate that this solution will serve as a foundation for future biomedical data exchange infrastructure. While recent studies have leveraged pre-trained language models (PLMs) for this purpose, they typically rely on fine-tuning PLMs that have undergone pre-training solely for sentiment analysis. SentGCL employs two key mechanisms: first, it performs masked aspect-emotion prediction to strengthen the understanding of their inter-relationships; second, it implements a guided contrastive learning approach that generates positive and negative pairs of aspect-emotion pairs to refine their semantic representations. In epidemiological research, case-control designs are frequently employed to investigate causal relationships. When a sampling design is not randomized, it is crucial to account for the selection mechanism to ensure valid inferences. This study focuses on the standard case-control design involving a binary outcome, a binary exposure, and a binary mediator, with the goal of determining if the exposure influences the outcome through the mediator. We demonstrate that a naive analysis ignoring the sampling design can yield biased estimates of direct and indirect effects. To address this, we propose a statistical framework that integrates the sampling design into the analysis. This approach utilizes a weighted regression method to estimate these effects and a model-based approach to assess their significance. We evaluate the performance of these methods through simulation studies and apply them to a case-control dataset from the Women's Health Initiative. The simulation results indicate that our methods offer superior performance compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, the application to the Women's Initiative data illustrates how these methods can be utilized to evaluate whether a specific exposure affects a disease outcome via a particular pathway. Ultimately, our methods enable researchers to determine whether a binary exposure impacts a binary disease through a binary mediator. By incorporating the sampling design into the analysis, we ensure that the resulting estimates are unbiased. Additionally, our methods are computationally efficient and can be readily implemented using standard statistical software. The R code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1992/Mediation. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has provided the first in-situ data from the inner heliosphere, enabling a new perspective on solar wind dynamics. This study examines the energy density of the solar wind across three distinct components: plasma, protons, and protons plus plasma. By analyzing these metrics, we identify the kinetic and thermal energies that dominate each regime. The research further explores the transition from the subsonic to the supersonic solar wind, revealing that this shift is marked by a notable increase in the energy of protons plus plasma. Additionally, the probe's ability to detect structures smaller than its 0.25-second sampling interval is addressed. We conclude that the observed energy density of protons plus plasma serves as a robust indicator of the PSP's heliocentric distance. These findings are supported by comparisons with in-situ measurements from the Ulysses and Wind spacecraft. Ultimately, the results indicate that the dominant energy component in the inner heliosphere is plasma energy at subsonic speeds, shifting to proton energy at supersonic speeds. These conclusions are reinforced by a simulation of the Parker Spiral magnetic field. These insights offer valuable context for interpreting the Parker Solar Probe's data. Finally, the implications of these findings for future Parker Solar Probe missions are discussed. This work was conducted as part of the 2020 Summer Research Program at the University of Michigan. This paper introduces the concept of a noncommutative countable principal bundle, derived from covering objects within the category of C*-algebras. This framework encompasses both classical countable principal bundles and quantum principal bundles featuring discrete structure groups. We demonstrate that any free and minimally amenable action of a countable group $G$ on a unital C*-algebra $A$ naturally generates such a bundle. Furthermore, we establish that these bundles admit associated classifying maps into an appropriate generalized Bunce-Deddens system. Finally, we provide multiple examples of noncommutative countable principal bundles arising from free and minimally amenable actions on specific notable C*-algebras. Additionally, we investigate actions on AF-algebras, proving that under certain conditions, their crossed products are isomorphic to irrational rotation algebras. We also examine actions on irrational crossed products, showing that specific actions on irrational rotation algebras yield isomorphic crossed products with the Jiang-Su tensor product $T \otimes \mathcal{Z}$. These findings offer new instances of countable principal bundles with discrete structure groups and contribute to the ongoing effort to classify them. Ultimately, we propose that the study of noncommutative countable principal bundles may hold significant promise for advancing our understanding of C*-algebras. As a preliminary step, we introduce a novel class of C*-algebras termed "noncommutative countable principal bundle algebras," which includes both irrational rotation algebras and irrational crossed products as special cases. We demonstrate that these algebras possess the strong self-absorption property, a characteristic that may facilitate their classification. We anticipate that this property will play a crucial role in future research concerning the classification of noncommutative countable principal bundles. Finally, we outline several open questions regarding the classification of these algebras and their connections to the Elliott program. We hope that this work will inspire further exploration into the classification of noncommutative countable principal bundles and their associated C*-algebras. Ultimately, we believe that the investigation of these objects may significantly contribute to the broader endeavor of classifying C*-algebras. This research investigates the impact of $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetry on the spectrum of a two-body rotor system featuring two independent rotors, each composed of two rigid bodies linked by a massless rod. The rotor components are modeled as bosonic and fermionic quark-antiquark pairs, while the R-parity of the fermionic quarks is examined in detail. We demonstrate that R-parity is spontaneously broken in the ground state, resulting in a massless fermion and a massive boson. This phenomenon is characterized as an adverse R-parity scissors mechanism, which contrasts with the standard supersymmetric scissors mechanism found in the one-body Double-Rotors Model. The text also outlines the specific conditions required for this adverse mechanism to occur. Furthermore, we show that the R-parity scissors mechanism can be reversed by introducing a small perturbation to the system. Finally, we outline the necessary modifications to the Lagrangian to incorporate this adverse R-parity scissors mechanism. These adjustments involve adding a term to the Lagrangian that couples the R-parity odd ground state with an R-parity even excited state. This addition restores R-parity symmetry and generates a mass gap between the R-parity odd ground state and the R-parity even excited state. The paper concludes by discussing the physical implications of these findings. These results suggest that the adverse R-parity scissors mechanism could play a significant role in the study of the QCD vacuum and the structure of hadrons. This study introduces a neural network method designed to address both hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs). The approach employs a cell-mean-based framework that divides the spatial domain into a structured grid. Within each cell, the solution is approximated using a polynomial basis, while a neural network is utilized to model the unknown coefficients of these polynomials. This network is trained using the residual of the PDE over the entire domain. The proposed technique demonstrates robust performance across various hyperbolic PDEs, including the advection equation, Burgers' equation, and the shallow water equations. Furthermore, it achieves promising results when applied to the Helmholtz equation and the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. Notably, the method successfully recovers the lift coefficient for a NACA0012 airfoil in the latter application. The framework is also adaptable to three-dimensional PDEs. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to deliver accurate results even with a relatively coarse mesh. Additionally, the method exhibits strong stability and convergence properties. The paper concludes with a comprehensive discussion of the technique's strengths and potential areas for future development. Finally, the study provides a detailed comparison of the proposed method against other existing approaches in the literature. The ALICE experiment at the LHC has established itself as a premier facility for heavy-ion physics, offering exceptional particle identification capabilities down to transverse momenta of a few hundred MeV/c. This advantage stems from a specialized detector configuration designed to maximize the identification of charged hadrons, particularly pions, kaons, and protons, across momenta up to a few GeV/c. These findings are crucial for exploring the quark-gluon plasma and its connection to low-energy nuclear physics. The upcoming LHC Run 3 and the subsequent Run 4 and Run 5 periods will enable ALICE to investigate these phenomena with unprecedented precision, utilizing data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions. This presentation will outline the scientific goals of ALICE for these upcoming runs, detail the detector upgrades planned to achieve them, and discuss the associated challenges. Furthermore, it will highlight the significant role of the ALICE collaboration in the broader LHC upgrade initiative. The talk will conclude by presenting a new proposal to enhance ALICE's capabilities beyond the standard LHC Run 4 and Run 5 upgrades. This initiative aims to further advance the study of heavy-ion physics and its relationship to low-energy nuclear physics, while also addressing the growing demand for high-precision data in proton-proton collisions. This proposal is intended to serve as a foundation for future discussions regarding ALICE's participation in the LHC's major upgrade program. Consequently, this allows for the detection of the temporal Unruh effect without requiring particle detection. We investigate tidal features and merger rates for early-type galaxies (ETGs) within the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) Wide-Field Survey. Utilizing deep imaging data, we identified 1,000 massive ETGs (absolute magnitude $M_r < -21.5$) across a redshift range of $0.01 < z < 0.15$. We extracted flux profiles from these images and applied a novel tidal analysis method to quantify tidal characteristics. Our results indicate that the tidal properties of HSC-SSP ETGs align with those of massive ETGs in the nearby Virgo cluster, suggesting that tidal features in massive ETGs are established early in their evolution. Furthermore, we estimated merger rates for these galaxies using their tidal properties and found that the rates for massive ETGs in HSC-SSP are comparable to those in the Virgo cluster. These findings suggest that tidal features in ETGs are formed through major mergers, with the majority of such features appearing after the first major merger. Additionally, we observed that the flux ratio of tidal features in HSC-SSP ETGs is lower than in Virgo ETGs, implying that the tidal features in HSC-SSP ETGs are more recent compared to those in Virgo ETGs. These conclusions are supported by simulations of major mergers between galaxies with similar mass ratios. Finally, we conclude that the tidal features of early-type galaxies are established early in their evolution, and that the majority of these features result from major mergers occurring after the first event. This implies that the first major merger in the history of HSC-SSP ETGs occurred more recently than the first major merger in Virgo ETGs. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the red sequence in the HSC-SSP field was established at $z \sim 1$. Furthermore, we suggest that the flux ratio of tidal features can serve as a valuable tool for estimating the timing of major mergers. This study represents the first application of tidal analysis to early-type galaxies in a wide-field survey. This paper introduces a novel gravitational theory, the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation (ASGT), which posits that bipolar ejections function as a gravitational repellent. In ASGT, the gravitational potential is modeled as a superposition of monopole and dipole components. While the monopole term aligns with Newtonian gravity, the dipole term generates a bipolar ejection field. This phenomenon is characterized by a continuous, outward radial flow of matter from the source, accompanied by a simultaneous outward flow of gravitational energy. This energy flux adheres to a modified form of the energy conservation law. Furthermore, ASGT offers a new framework for understanding the dynamics of bipolar jets observed in various astrophysical systems. The theory also provides a fresh perspective on the gravitational interaction between celestial bodies, such as the Earth and Sun, by deriving a new expression for the gravitational force acting on a test particle within a rotating source. This expression incorporates a centrifugal term that opposes the attractive Newtonian force. Additionally, ASGT yields a revised expression for the gravitational field of a rotating source, which includes a dipole component. This component generates a dipole field with a negative dipole moment, effectively acting as a gravitational repellent. The implications of this dipole field for astrophysical phenomena are explored. Finally, the theory is applied to the analysis of the Pioneer anomaly. The resulting conclusions suggest that ASGT offers a viable alternative to the standard model of gravitation. Overall, ASGT provides a unified framework for describing gravitational phenomena across a broad spectrum of scales, from planetary systems to galaxies. It is anticipated that this theory will stimulate further research into the nature of gravity and its role in the evolution of the universe. The origin of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) remains unresolved, with a leading hypothesis suggesting they stem from the magnetospheres of magnetars. This model necessitates the postponement of optical emission from the central engine until after the FRB is released. We conducted a targeted search for concurrent or postponed optical counterparts to the most energetic FRBs, utilizing the ZTF and Pan-STARRS1 optical telescopes. Our analysis examined 100 of the brightest FRBs, observing 17 of them during the ZTF's initial burst alert phase and 83 during the subsequent extended burst alert phase. We detected no optical counterparts in any of the 100 events. Furthermore, we searched for postponed optical emission up to 10 days post-burst using Pan-STARRS1 data, finding no evidence of such signals. These null results impose stringent limits on the energy and luminosity of any concurrent or delayed optical emission associated with the FRB central engine. Specifically, we establish an upper limit of $L_{opt} \lesssim 10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$ for concurrent optical emission and $L_{opt} \lesssim 10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ for postponed optical emission. These constraints are significant because they rule out the possibility that the optical emission originates from the FRB engine itself. Consequently, any observed optical signals linked to FRBs must arise from a separate population of objects, such as the host galaxies or other astrophysical sources. This finding underscores the critical need for future optical follow-up observations of FRBs to better understand their origins. Additionally, we present a new catalog of 100 well-defined FRBs, which will be valuable for the scientific community in conducting follow-up studies. Our results also suggest that the optical emission observed in some FRBs may instead be caused by the interaction between the FRB and the interstellar medium. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the magnetar hypothesis. We conclude that if the magnetar hypothesis is correct, the optical emission must be postponed by at least 10 days, and the optical luminosity of the magnetar must be extremely low, with $L_{opt} \lesssim 10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$. These constraints are particularly stringent for young magnetars, which are the most likely candidates for producing FRBs. Our findings also suggest that the optical emission from magnetars is likely dominated by radio emission.

This thesis presents design methodologies, enhancement strategies, and reconstruction techniques for high-power laser systems. It begins by detailing the development of a multi-physics simulation framework that integrates ray tracing, thermal analysis, and stress calculations to model laser performance. The work examines thermal effects on laser crystals, specifically addressing thermal lensing and stress-induced depolarization in Nd:YVO4 crystals operating at high power levels. Furthermore, it explores the fabrication of high-damage-threshold laser crystals by reverse-engineering existing components and implementing innovative manufacturing processes. Finally, the study investigates the design and fabrication of high-power, all-solid-state fiber lasers utilizing large-mode-area (LMA) double-clad fibers. These findings offer valuable insights and guidance for the future design, optimization, and fabrication of high-power laser systems.

We introduce Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature framework designed for privacy-preserving payment systems. This approach substantially lowers computational demands for both signing and verifying transactions, making it especially beneficial for verifiers. By leveraging the concept of a succinct set signature, our method ensures that verifier computation remains independent of the ring size. We have successfully deployed this system in a real-world application and benchmarked it against existing ring signature schemes, demonstrating significant performance gains. Specifically, we observed up to a 100-fold reduction in verification time and a 10-fold reduction in signing time. Furthermore, we have integrated this solution into Monero, enhancing its Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS) consensus mechanism. We anticipate that Delegated RingCT will inspire further research into more efficient and practical privacy-preserving payment solutions. Our hope is that this work will encourage the cryptocurrency community to adopt this technology, thereby accelerating the development of faster, more efficient, and practical anonymous payment systems.
