Soft robotics is a rapidly evolving field that leverages the inherent flexibility of its components to create machines capable of adapting to dynamic environments. These robots are typically actuated pneumatically or hydraulically, utilizing their compliant structures to perform tasks traditionally handled by rigid robots. The model-driven control approach has emerged as a promising control strategy for such systems, offering the ability to predict robot behavior and generate control inputs that achieve desired outcomes. This method is particularly advantageous for soft robots because it can compensate for their complex dynamics and enable the use of control techniques originally designed for rigid robots. This paper reviews the model-driven control approach in soft robotics, examining both the current state of practice and open research issues. It begins by defining model-driven control and outlining the necessary steps to implement it. Subsequently, it surveys existing literature, categorizing studies based on the type of models employed and the specific control problems addressed. Finally, the paper identifies key challenges and opportunities for advancing model-driven control in soft robotics. By synthesizing these aspects, the review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the field and guide future research efforts. The source code for the experiments conducted is available at https://github.com/softcontrol. The authors anticipate that this review will offer a clear summary of the current landscape and inspire further investigation into model-driven control for soft robotic systems. Keywords: Soft Robotics, Model-Driven Control, Control Theory, Robotics.

The authors previously introduced a novel concept of "authenticity" for maps into the Jacobi bundle, defining it through the authentic composition property. This paper demonstrates that the authentic Jacobi bundle, as defined by this concept, is unique and corresponds exactly to the "twisted sum of the position and momentum bundles" previously identified by J. Vajda. Furthermore, it is shown that this authentic bundle provides a natural framework for interpreting the E. Cartan connection. Finally, the paper establishes the equivalence between this authentic Jacobi bundle and D.J. Saunders' "natural bundle" J^2Q, which arises from the second-order jet functor applied to position maps. These findings offer a fresh perspective on authentic extensions and clarify the relationships among various "Jacobi bundle" constructions found in the literature. Additionally, the results facilitate the development of a new geometric framework for analyzing second-order ordinary differential equations. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the "twisted sum of position and velocity bundles," which is equivalent to the velocity bundle and represents the most prevalent construction among various "Jacobi bundle" definitions. We introduce TABLEDIS, the inaugural benchmark for table disintegration tailored to table-oriented fact validation. This resource comprises 1,000 instances drawn from 200 queries requiring disintegration, alongside 2,000 instances needing no disintegration. Furthermore, we present and assess various baseline methods, including rule-based, retrieval-based, and LLM-based approaches. Our findings indicate that even the most effective model achieves only 40% accuracy, highlighting the substantial difficulty of the task. We also observe that LLMs are prone to hallucinating table structures during disintegration. To address this, we propose a prompt engineering strategy that leverages in-context examples, which boosts LLM performance by 25%. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive analysis of the challenges LLMs encounter in this domain. We anticipate that TABLEDIS will serve as a valuable benchmark for developing robust models capable of accurately and reliably disintegrating tables. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/table-disintegration.

Phase samplers are compact oscillators that generate a phase signal, which is then integrated and sampled to produce a frequency signal. This paper examines the impact of phase sampler architecture on the sampling of high-frequency, low-duty-cycle square waves. We evaluate two distinct architectures and their corresponding sampling techniques, analyzing how sampling errors affect the representation of square waves. Furthermore, we introduce a method to estimate these sampling errors and apply it to compare the two approaches. Finally, we validate our findings through experimental results. Our findings indicate that the proposed sampling technique for phase samplers effectively reconstructs square waves, and that the error estimation method offers a rapid and accurate means of predicting sampling errors. Additionally, the experimental results demonstrate that the second approach outperforms the first, yielding a superior reconstruction of square waves. We introduce a resilient distance tagging scheme designed for general graphs, specifically targeting planar graphs, which enables the recovery of shortest paths following failures. This scheme relies on a data structure that assigns a distance tag to every edge, allowing the identification of edges belonging to shortest paths even after failures occur. For planar graphs, this structure operates with $O(n)$ space complexity and ensures that each edge's tag can be retrieved in $O(1)$ time. Consequently, the data structure can locate a shortest path from a source to any destination in $O(m)$ time, where $m$ represents the number of edges. Furthermore, the system is capable of identifying all edges on shortest paths between any two nodes within $O(m)$ time. The proposed data structure is straightforward to implement and does not require any preprocessing steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that the data structure can be enhanced to function in a fully dynamic environment, remaining resilient to both insertions and deletions of edges and vertices. In this dynamic setting, the algorithm can recover shortest paths in $O(m)$ time, with the guarantee that each edge is processed at most once. Finally, we establish that the data structure is optimal by presenting a lower bound of $\Omega(m)$ for the time complexity required to recover shortest paths. This lower bound applies to any algorithm that recovers shortest paths upon the failure of a single edge. Our approach is particularly significant for scenarios involving the failure of a single edge, as it achieves a lower time complexity than all existing methods. We also provide a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ for the space complexity of any distance tagging scheme that recovers shortest paths following the failure of a single edge. This lower bound holds true even when the failure is known in advance. Our results are derived from a novel application of the cutset lemma, which we believe will be a valuable tool for future research. We also present a new lower bound for the number of tags needed in distance tagging schemes, which is tight for planar graphs. This lower bound is established through a new graph construction technique that we believe will be useful in other contexts. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to advancements in resilient routing. Our lower bounds are also expected to be valuable for future research endeavors. This study examines two-entity correlations within a lossy Bose-Hubbard framework subjected to an external driving force. The model is analyzed using a moment-domain approach, where correlations are represented through the spectrum-domain form factor. This representation is defined by a density-density correlation function and a current-current correlation function, the latter being derived from the former via a Ward identity. The resulting two-entity correlations are expressed through the spectral properties of a non-Hermitian matrix. To validate the method, the analysis is applied to a ring of $N$ sites featuring nearest-neighbor hopping and loss, both with and without a driving term. In the absence of a driving term, the system exhibits a single eigenvalue with a large imaginary component, indicating a quasi-particle with a short lifetime. When a driving term is present, the matrix displays a semi-circular distribution of eigenvalues, a signature of the random matrix ensemble. Furthermore, the model demonstrates a transition from a superfluid to an insulating phase as the inter-particle interaction strength increases. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations. The methodology employed is applicable to a broad range of open quantum systems. Finally, the implications of these results for the development of quantum simulators are discussed. This study introduces a framework for modeling the tail probabilities of a random variable using Gaussian Processes (GPs). By representing these probabilities as random functions, we can effectively capture their evolution over a domain, thereby extending GP capabilities to out-of-sample detection tasks. We demonstrate the utility of this approach within two specific frameworks: (1) a GP model for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a random variable, and (2) a GP model for the quantile function of a random variable. We evaluate these frameworks using both synthetic data and a real-world dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Our results indicate that GP models for the quantile function surpass existing methods in estimating the CDF, while also showing that GPs can be effectively employed for out-of-sample detection. Furthermore, we show that these models can be integrated with other GPs to learn the conditional distribution of a target variable, even when the target's support is unknown. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of the proposed CDF-based GP model. This work highlights that GP models for the quantile function offer a promising avenue for future research into CDF estimation, and it establishes GPs for the CDF as a viable solution for out-of-sample detection. Additionally, the CDF-based GP model can be utilized to infer the distribution of a target variable when its support is unknown. This result holds particular significance in the study of the Alexandrov–Calabi conjecture. Furthermore, we derive a new local Hölder estimate for the Alexandrov–Calabi equation, which is applicable to various geometric evolution equations. The proof relies on a newly developed technique termed the "blow-up method." Additionally, we provide a new proof of the classical enhanced Alexandrov maximum theorem by L. Nirenberg, which yields the uniform Hölder estimate for classical solutions of the Monge–Ampère equation. This alternative approach offers a distinct perspective on the original proof and may prove valuable for other applications. The paper also includes a discussion of related literature. Finally, we present a counterexample illustrating that the classical enhanced Alexandrov maximum theorem by L. Nirenberg does not hold in unbounded domains. The conjecture asserts that for any smooth function $f$ on $\Omega$, a unique solution $\varphi$ exists if and only if a particular integral inequality involving $f$ is met. Optical clocks represent the most precise timekeeping instruments available. While current research predominantly focuses on repetitive clocks that operate continuously, this study examines non-repetitive clocks, which generate a single optical pulse at a specific, unpredictable moment. We analyze these clocks by modeling their timing and amplitude fluctuations as independent processes. The proposed statistical framework is validated through experiments involving mode-locked lasers, which function as non-repetitive optical clocks. Our findings indicate that the model accurately characterizes the observed fluctuations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the timing of these clocks follows a Poisson process, a result confirmed by both theoretical analysis and experimental data. This insight enables the calculation of the clock's average rate and the quantification of timing fluctuations using the Fisher information. Additionally, we show that the Fisher information regarding the clock rate is directly proportional to the number of recorded events. Finally, we establish that the model's predictions align with experimental results concerning the impact of amplitude fluctuations on clock performance. These results are expected to facilitate the development of new applications for non-repetitive optical clocks. For instance, we illustrate that the model can be utilized to determine the optimal measurement duration for characterizing optical clocks. This approach is applied to two scenarios: first, to identify the optimal duration for measuring the stability of a single clock, and second, to determine the optimal duration for comparing two clocks to detect a relative frequency shift. In both cases, the model proves effective in optimizing measurement strategies. Consequently, this work provides a robust foundation for the design and implementation of experiments involving non-repetitive optical clocks. The methodology is broadly applicable to any system where events occur at random times with random amplitudes. Ultimately, this research paves the way for leveraging non-repetitive optical clocks in diverse fields, including quantum physics, quantum information, and quantum metrology. These advancements could lead to the creation of new quantum sensors and quantum-enhanced metrological techniques. For example, the proposed method could be employed to design experiments aimed at detecting gravitational waves. In this context, quantum metrology can be applied to optimize the measurement strategy for comparing two quantum optical clocks. This approach could enhance sensitivity by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ compared to classical methods. Such an improvement would enable the detection of weaker signals and extend the range of observable sources. This advancement could be realized using existing technology, such as the optical lattice clocks currently under development for the European Space Agency's Space Optical Clock mission. This study introduces a fog-assisted Software Defined Network (SNN) designed to address Service Chain (SFC) provisioning challenges. The proposed architecture incorporates a Fog Assisted Service Chain Provisioning (FASCP) module that utilizes a Collaborative Failure Recovery (CFR) mechanism to restore network services following failures. Additionally, the FASCP module integrates Fault Mitigation (FM) and Energy-efficient Asset Management (EEM) to enhance SNN performance. To evaluate this approach, the authors developed a Fog Assisted Service Chain Provisioning (FASCP) simulator, which was benchmarked against an existing simulator. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed simulator outperforms the existing solution in terms of SFC Quality of Experience (QoE), reliability, fault tolerance, and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the FASCP simulator is implemented in Python and made available as an open-source tool for the research community. We introduce a novel holographic error correction protocol, termed Hyper-MERA, which extends the standard MERA framework by incorporating hyperbolic associations. This method achieves an even more efficient code than MERA, maintaining a code dimension of $2^L$ while reducing the number of physical qubits from $2^{L+2}$ to $2^{L+1}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Hyper-MERA surpasses both HaPPY and MERA codes in terms of minimum distance. Finally, we establish that the error threshold of Hyper-MERA scales with the system size $L$ as $p_c \propto 1/L^{\frac{1}{1+\alpha}}$, where $\alpha$ represents the decay exponent of the error correlation function. This scaling exponent is determined by the competition between the geometry of the holographic code and the decay rate of error correlations. Additionally, we show that this behavior can be recovered in spin chain models by appropriately selecting the Hamiltonian parameters. This finding suggests that ground states of local Hamiltonians can be encoded within a holographic framework, thereby enabling the study of quantum phase transitions in the thermodynamic limit. Our results also provide a new perspective on the relationship between holography and tensor network approaches. Finally, we propose that the observed scaling of the error threshold may offer a new method for defining and characterizing criticality in quantum phase transitions. This study examines the spatial distribution of Galactic Core Fibers (GCFs) by analyzing the distance between them. The analysis utilizes a catalog of 100 GCFs selected from the 200 GCFs originally identified by the authors in their first paper. Distances are calculated between the closest points of each pair, using the 3D coordinates of GCFs derived from the method described in the first paper. The selection of the 100 GCFs is based on the criterion that they must be separated by at least 100 parsecs. The resulting distribution of distances between adjacent GCFs is modeled using a log-normal distribution. The mean distance between neighboring GCFs is found to be 120 parsecs, with a standard deviation of 100 parsecs. This observed mean distance is approximately 10 times larger than the typical scale of Galactic Core stars, which is about 10 parsecs. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings. The results suggest that GCFs are not merely stars that have been gravitationally perturbed by the Galactic Bar; instead, they appear to be a distinct type of stellar object. These segments are composed of clusters of stars, where the clusters are spaced roughly 120 parsecs apart. The size of these clusters is approximately 10 parsecs, consistent with the scale of Galactic Core stars. The paper also addresses the issue of identifying the true center of the Galaxy. This paper introduces a novel Ideal Conservation Voltage Reduction (ICVRD) framework designed for primary-secondary integrated distribution networks. The primary objective of ICVRD is to lower energy consumption by reducing voltage levels at primary buses, which in turn decreases the power required by secondary feeders. To address the intricate coupling between primary and secondary networks, we develop a distributed ideal ICVRD (DICVRD) scheme. This approach utilizes a distributed optimization method to identify the optimal voltage setpoints for primary buses, thereby minimizing total power loss across the entire network. Furthermore, we propose a distributed control strategy that enables feeder transformers to autonomously and optimally regulate secondary feeder voltages in response to changes in primary bus voltages. Simulation results demonstrate that DICVRD successfully identifies the globally optimal voltage setpoints for primary buses and promptly adjusts secondary feeder voltages to achieve these targets. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against communication delays and data inaccuracies. Ultimately, DICVRD offers a promising solution for distribution networks to reduce power losses and enhance energy efficiency. This study examines a non-stationary bandit problem featuring arm-dependent lags, where pulling an arm temporarily removes it from selection for a specific duration. We introduce a specialist algorithm that leverages these lags to enhance performance. We demonstrate that this method achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, which is nearly optimal, provided the number of arms $K$ is constant. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{KT})$ for any algorithm, indicating that our approach is off by only a factor of $\sqrt{K}$. Finally, we propose a simple modification to the Exp3.I algorithm that also reaches the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ regret bound. Our analysis relies on a novel technique for handling arm-dependent lags, which we believe has broader applications. Additionally, we present numerical results comparing our algorithms against baselines.

Text-based social media platforms are now common, yet most existing systems rely on pre-existing user data, limiting their ability to generalize to new communities. This paper introduces a new framework called LEARNING ENHANCED AUTO-REGRESSIVE HUMAN TEXT (LEATHER), which combines a generative model with a reinforcement learning component to master dialogue within unseen communities. We evaluate LEATHER across various social media datasets, demonstrating that it can acquire skills to produce human-like text in these novel dialogue environments. Our results indicate that LEATHER surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both generating diverse responses and achieving social rewards. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the reinforcement learning process, revealing that the agent successfully identifies and adheres to community-specific rules. These findings highlight the potential of LEATHER for creating human-like dialogue in dynamic online communities. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/LEATHER.

This document serves as a review of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) based on the Lattice approach, with a specific focus on non-zero temperature and chemical potential. It begins by outlining the theoretical foundations of the QCD Lagrangian within the lattice framework. Subsequently, it examines the primary challenges associated with QCD simulations, including the sign problem, the necessity of reweighting, and the application of improved actions. The discussion then shifts to results derived from these lattice calculations, covering the transition temperature, the behavior of quark number density and susceptibility near this transition, the chiral condensate, and the mass spectrum of light hadrons. Finally, the text concludes with an outlook on future research directions. This material is intended to be accessible to graduate students and researchers new to the field of Lattice QCD. Whenever feasible, references to the original literature are provided. Additionally, an appendix is included to offer a concise overview of the relevant theoretical background. This appendix is particularly useful for those who may have already encountered some of the topics discussed in the main text. All content herein is original and has not been published previously. While efforts have been made to ensure accuracy, the author does not guarantee that the information is error-free. Any remaining errors are the sole responsibility of the author. Furthermore, no financial or other conflicts of interest exist. Finally, the author acknowledges the valuable discussions with colleagues and friends, which have been instrumental in shaping this work. Special thanks are extended to Dr. Sumanth Kumar for his assistance with LaTeX formatting. The author also wishes to express gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their time and for providing constructive comments and suggestions. Finally, the author hopes that this work will be of interest to readers. Thank you.

This study introduces a linked Gaussian process (LGP) model designed to simulate the probabilistic relationship between turbulent offshore wind speeds and structural loads on wind turbines. By modeling the conditional mean and covariance of target loads as functions of proxy variables, the framework captures the joint distribution of these proxies and loads through linked Gaussian processes. This approach offers a computationally efficient alternative to high-fidelity physics-based models for characterizing the statistical dependencies between proxies and loads. The methodology is validated using synthetic data and an open-source dataset from the NREL 5MW offshore wind turbine. Results indicate that the LGP model achieves high accuracy in predicting target load statistics, with a mean absolute error of 0.001% relative to the load's standard deviation. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robust performance across varying turbulence intensities and significant reductions in computational time compared to physics-based approaches. These findings suggest that the LGP framework is a promising tool for probabilistic structural reliability assessments of wind turbines. Additionally, the code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/linked-gp. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Keywords: linked Gaussian processes, proxy modeling, wind-turbine loads, probabilistic modeling, stochastic modeling. MSC 2020: 62P12, 62P30, 62F15, 62F12, 62F10.

This study investigates the Izmir earthquake that struck Turkey on October 30, 2010, by analyzing Twitter data. We gathered 1,000 tweets from that day and categorized them into three groups: Earthquake Information, Earthquake Rumors, and Other. Our analysis reveals that the majority of the collected tweets were not related to the earthquake. Furthermore, we observed that the tweets containing actual earthquake information were predominantly posted by users from the Izmir region. These findings are significant for developing future systems designed to automatically detect and filter earthquake-related information within Twitter streams. To support this objective, we also introduce a dataset of 1,000 manually labeled tweets from October 30, 2010, which can be utilized to train and evaluate such automatic detection systems. We have made this dataset publicly available for research purposes. Finally, we present several experimental results demonstrating the performance of various machine learning algorithms on our proposed dataset. The source code and the dataset are accessible at: http://www.cs.uaf.edu/~muratd/Research/EarthquakeTweetClassification.html. This study examines the $R_\infty$ property within classes of generalized Baumslag-Solitar (GBS) groups and GBS-like groups. Specifically, we analyze infinitely generated nilpotent quotients of GBS groups, demonstrating that the $R_\infty$ characteristic for these quotients is not invariably constant. Furthermore, we investigate finite nilpotent quotients by deriving an explicit formula for the $R_\infty$ characteristic of a non-nilpotent GBS group and proving that this characteristic is invariably constant for certain families of nilpotent quotients. Finally, we extend these findings to the $R_\infty$ characteristic of monodromy representations associated with nilpotent quotients of GBS groups. In this context, we establish that the characteristic is invariably constant for specific families of monodromy representations, while simultaneously providing examples of invariably constant groups and non-constant group families where this property does not hold. Additionally, we offer a partial solution to an open problem posed by Chen and Wang regarding the $R_\infty$ characteristic of nilpotent quotients of the Heisenberg group. Our findings indicate that the $R_\infty$ characteristic is invariably constant for the Heisenberg group over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ when $p=2$, and for specific families of Heisenberg groups where this is not the case. We also present a method to calculate the $R_\inq$ characteristic for these quotients, which further illustrates this variability. Finally, we demonstrate that the $R_\infty$ characteristic for the $Q_8$ group is invariably constant. Throughout this work, we employ the technique of replacing generators with polynomials in non-commuting variables, a method introduced by Chen and Wang. This approach facilitates the computation of the polynomial inverse monodromy representation, allowing us to derive the $R_\infty$ characteristic for nilpotent quotients of GBS groups. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the $R_\infty$ property for nilpotent quotients of the Heisenberg group in terms of the nilpotent quotient itself. Finally, we generalize the concept of the $R_\infty$ characteristic to the $R_\inq$ characteristic for any positive integer $q$. Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for tracking how molecular structures and dynamics evolve. However, extracting this information from experimental data is difficult because the inversion problem is ill-posed, often resulting in unstable solutions. This paper introduces a new approach that combines forward optimization with a novel trajectory framework to generate robust reconstructions of time-dependent molecular properties. The method is validated using simulated data from a simple molecule, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, it is applied to analyze terahertz spectroscopy experiments on the peptide Ala3, successfully distinguishing between two proposed models of its conformational dynamics. The study concludes that this technique is broadly applicable to time-resolved spectroscopy across various domains, including molecular spectroscopy, ultrafast electron diffraction, and pump-probe experiments. It offers a general framework for solving the challenging problem of reconstructing time-dependent molecular behavior from time-resolved measurements. Additionally, the code is publicly accessible via a GitHub repository. These findings were published in *Physical Review Research* (2021).

This paper introduces SceNDD, a naturalistic driving dataset collected in Spain, comprising 10 hours of video footage recorded by dashcams mounted on vehicles. The data includes 800 video clips, each annotated with driving contexts and featuring 360-degree spatial context. The study evaluates two state-of-the-art scene classification methods—Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNN) and Deep Learning-based Contextual Embedding (DLE)—and reports their performance metrics. Additionally, the paper outlines the data collection methodology, the annotation process, and the classification benchmarks, while also discussing potential future research applications. The dataset and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/fernando-ruiz/SceNDD. The findings were presented at the 2021 International Conference on Intelligent Systems and Control (ISC).

Boundary entropy entropy is defined as the boundary analogue of entropy, representing the residual entropy that persists even when a system reaches its ground state. This concept is significant for investigating the entanglement entropy of black holes and their associated thermodynamic properties. In this study, we examine the behavior of reflected entropy within interface conformal field theories (ICFTs) and boundary entropy (bEE) in boundary conformal field theories (BCFTs). We derive the bEE and establish the monotonicity of bEE, demonstrating that it serves as a biconcave function of temperature. Furthermore, we calculate the reflected entropy for both BCFT and ICFT models, proving that it adheres to the strong subadditivity inequality. Finally, we explore the relationship between reflected entropy and bEE, showing that the former can be derived from the latter. These findings offer valuable insights for analyzing the entropy of black holes. Additionally, we provide the corresponding Python code for the reflected entropy at the end of the paper. This work is part of a series; Part I can be found in arXiv:2209.00009. The Python code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-2000/reflected-entropy. Keywords: Conformal Field Theory, Entanglement Entropy, Black Holes. arXiv: 2209.00009v1 [hep-th] 30 Aug 2022. This paper introduces a novel channel estimation framework designed for RIS-assisted OFDM systems that addresses hardware imperfections and operates with a reduced number of subcarriers and a shortened cyclic prefix. The proposed method integrates a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a linear minimum mean square error (LMMSE) estimator. Initially, the MLP is trained to reconstruct the cascaded RIS-Channel-User response from a limited set of pilot symbols. Subsequently, the estimated cascaded response is fed into an LMMSE estimator to generate channel estimates for data symbol locations. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms existing methods in terms of estimation accuracy while simultaneously reducing computational complexity and signal processing time. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against various hardware imperfections, including non-linearities, phase quantization errors, and DC offset. Finally, the study explores the potential of this approach for real-world deployment. This study introduces a non-invasive experimental approach to validate the IFt in biological systems, specifically examining the energy efficiency of the molecular ratchet driving RNA polymerase movement along DNA. By applying a magnetic field to the DNA, we manipulate the energy consumption of RNA polymerase without disrupting its function. This technique enables the verification of the IFt while preserving the natural dynamics of the molecule. Our findings indicate that the energy consumption of RNA polymerase is minimal, with an average value approximately 100 times lower than that of the heat engine driving a colloidal Brownian particle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the IFt can be verified without perturbing the system's dynamics. These results suggest that the energy consumption of RNA polymerase is negligible, a conclusion that may extend to other biological molecular machines. This work examines the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons defined on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. We demonstrate that, unlike in the case of instantons associated with closed $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures, the deformation complex does not rely solely on the exterior derivative and Hodge star operator. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a unique $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-Einstein manifolds for every connection. These findings extend previous research conducted by the authors and T. Walpuski regarding torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures and provide additional insight into nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures. Additionally, we offer an alternative derivation of the existence theorem for $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons due to J. Nordström. Finally, we explore the relationship between the deformation complex and the associated Dirac operator. As an application, we prove that the moduli space of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on a nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-Einstein manifold is smooth. This result contrasts with findings by J. Nordström, who showed that for torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-Einstein manifolds, the linearization of the curvature map at an $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton is not surjective. The paper concludes with an outline of the moduli space of torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons. To achieve this, we construct a family of explicit torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons and analyze their deformation properties. Our results indicate that the moduli space is non-compact and contains elements that are not self-dual. This outcome stands in contrast to the moduli space of torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-Einstein manifolds, which is known to be empty. The primary tool employed is a specific class of normal forms applicable to torsion-free $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures. We also present a version of this normal form tailored specifically for nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures. Finally, we provide a comprehensive list of references and resources for further study. The Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) has caused a global pandemic, prompting numerous nations to deploy contact tracing applications to curb its spread. This study evaluates the privacy safeguards of the Brazilian app Coronavírus-SUS, specifically regarding the confidentiality of user data. We introduce a novel attack model termed the "Partial Knowledge Attack," which leverages partial information about a target's contacts to infer private details. Our findings indicate that this attack successfully compromises the privacy of 50% to 90% of users within the Coronavírus-SUS application. Furthermore, we propose a mitigation strategy to enhance the app's privacy protections. The source code for our simulation is made available to facilitate reproducibility. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of conducting rigorous privacy assessments for COVID-19 digital solutions. Quantum machine learning represents a rapidly evolving field that holds the promise of surpassing classical methods in specific scenarios. This study examines a hybrid architecture utilizing a quantum neural network layer, analyzes its training dynamics, and demonstrates that the layer's output is a probabilistic mixture of binary sequences. We show that this layer can be trained to generate quantum data, a phenomenon we term "quantum data collapse." Furthermore, we illustrate that this behavior can be effectively modeled by a Bayesian network. Finally, we explore the implications of this quantum data generation for training quantum classifiers. Our research indicates that when training data consists of quantum data, the quantum classifier's performance is significantly enhanced. Additionally, we demonstrate that the quantum data generated by our network can be interpreted as a valid quantum state. These findings underscore the critical role of quantum neural networks in advancing the field of quantum machine learning. We present a code-creating function within the ACL2 theorem prover that translates ACL2 programs into correct-by-construction C code. Our approach involves a straightforward, superficial embedding of C into ACL2, where every C term corresponds directly to a specific subset of valid ACL2 terms. This method enables the automatic generation of verified C code from ACL2 programs. We have implemented this code creator as a library and integrated it into the ACL2 distribution. We demonstrate its utility by applying it to verify various C programs, including those written in standard libraries. Our findings indicate that, despite the inherent complexity of C, the proof generating the correct C code is relatively concise and accessible. Additionally, we have developed a user-friendly interface for the code creator that supports interactive refinement, allowing users to interactively construct correct C code by refining initial ACL2 programs. We have also created a checker that verifies the correctness of the generated C code. Finally, we have established a toolchain integrating our code creator, the checker, and a C compiler into the ACL2 distribution. This distribution also includes a C compiler frontend, a C type checker, and a C pretty-printer. We showcase the entire workflow by verifying a C program for a Caesar cipher. We conclude by discussing the tool's limitations and outlining potential future research directions. Our primary objective is to facilitate the verification of C programs using ACL2. We believe this work represents a significant step toward that goal, as it enables the automatic verification of C programs based on their high-level specifications. Furthermore, we aim to extend this research to support more complex C features, such as pointers and arrays, in future endeavors. To achieve this, we plan to develop a more sophisticated embedding of C into ACL2. We also intend to investigate methods for automatically verifying C programs that utilize these complex features. Finally, we will explore ways to make the code creation process more efficient and scalable. We believe this work marks a crucial milestone in our broader goal of enabling the automatic verification of C programs using ACL2. By allowing high-level specifications to automatically generate correct C code, we can significantly reduce the effort required to verify C programs. Moreover, this approach can help ensure the correctness of C code in safety-critical systems. We hope this work will inspire further research in this area and contribute to the broader field of formal methods. In conclusion, we believe this work represents a significant step toward the automatic verification of C programs using ACL2. By enabling high-level specifications to automatically generate correct C code, we can greatly simplify the process of verifying C programs

This study investigates the resonance fluctuations affecting the (39991) Iochroma group. By analyzing the orbital elements of 1,000 asteroids from the group, we determined that the asteroid (39991) Iochroma occupies a stable region within the 3:1 mean motion resonance. Furthermore, we identified that the group's center of mass is situated at a distance of 2.4700 ± 0.0005 AU from the Sun. Our findings indicate that the group exhibits a strong 3:1 mean motion resonance with Jupiter, and the resonance fluctuations of the group members are primarily driven by the Kozai-Lidov mechanism. Additionally, we observed that the group displays a significant obliquity concentration at approximately 90°. Finally, we conclude that asteroid (39991) Iochroma is likely a primordial object that has remained dynamically stable for billions of years. These results offer valuable insights for future research on the group. The data utilized in this work can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stad1200. The Hurwitz Zeta function, denoted as $\zeta(s,a)$, is defined by the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n+a)^s}$ for $\Re(s)>1$ and $0<a<1$, and can be extended to the entire complex plane via analytic continuation. This extension yields the relation $\zeta(1,a)=-\psi(a)$, where $\psi$ represents the digamma function. In 1916, S. Ramanujan demonstrated that the odd zeta values $\zeta(2k+1)$ for $k=1,2,3,\ldots$ can be expressed using the digamma function evaluated at rational points $\frac{p}{q}$. This note presents a generalization of Ramanujan's findings by expressing these values through the digamma function with arguments based on quadratic irrationals. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the Ramanujan-Schatten identity and the Hurwitz Zeta function. Additionally, we derive a novel identity for the Ramanujan $B$-function, which is defined as $B(z)=\frac{\zeta(1-z)}{\zeta(z)}$. Finally, we provide a new proof of a result by J. Borwein regarding the linear independence of $\pi^m$ and $e^{\pi\sqrt{d}}$ over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$. These findings offer a fresh perspective on the work of J. Borwein, who originally utilized the Wronskian determinant of the functions $f_1(x)=1$, $f_2(x)=e^{\pi\sqrt{d}}$, and $f_3(x)=e^{-\pi\sqrt{d}}$ to derive his identity. Our approach circumvents the need for the Wronskian determinant, thereby providing a more straightforward proof of Borwein's identity. Our results also offer a new perspective on the identity concerning the Riemann Zeta function at negative integers, $\zeta(-n)=\frac{(-1)^nB_{n+1}}{n+1}$, where $B_n$ denotes the $n$-th Bernoulli number. This is achieved by examining the special values of the Ramanujan $B$-function at negative integers, which are defined as $B(-n)=\frac{\zeta(1+n)}{\zeta(-n)}$.

This work calculates the complex circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces by applying a novel technique for equivariant K-theory. This technique leverages the relationship between equivariant K-theory and the representation rings of circle subgroups, a connection that also facilitates the computation of circle-equivariant K-theory for spheres. The study subsequently extends these findings to the complex projective spaces $\mathbb{C}P^1$ and $\mathbb{C}P^2$ within the realm of circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology. Furthermore, the text introduces a new framework for elliptic cohomology based on equivariant families of gerbes, which offers an alternative method for determining the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of $\mathbb{C}P^1$ and $\mathbb{C}P^2$. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. This project was undertaken under the supervision of Dr. David Gepner and Dr. David Higham. Additionally, the author acknowledges the significant contributions of the EPSRC and the University of Oxford to their education and research. The author also wishes to thank their parents for their unwavering support and encouragement. Finally, the author expresses gratitude to all friends and colleagues who have shared in this journey.

A primary objective of algebraic topology is identifying algebraic invariants that characterize topological spaces. These invariants are valuable for analyzing complex systems across mathematics, physics, and data science. This study demonstrates the application of a machine learning framework to derive such invariants for simplicial complexes. Leveraging the high-dimensional, non-linear, and complex nature of these complexes, we employ a graph convolutional neural network (GCN) to generate algebraic invariants for simplicial complexes of varying dimensions. Our approach utilizes simplicial homology to represent these complexes and learns algebraic features that capture their topological properties. We evaluate the learned representations by assessing their ability to classify simplicial complexes and by examining the learned morphisms. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's effectiveness in modeling real-world data by learning representations for simplicial complexes constructed from the 305-galaxy galaxy survey. Finally, we explore the application of simplicial cohomology within machine learning contexts. The accompanying code repository includes implementations of simplicial homology, cohomology, and classification tasks. This work holds significance for physics, as it enables the learning of representations for simplicial complexes that retain physical information. Additionally, the proposed framework offers a pathway to uncovering algebraic features in high-dimensional data, a capability that holds promise for advancing machine learning applications in physics. This research was conducted within the Machine Learning for Physics initiative, a collaboration between the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences, the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics, and the University of Potsdam. The initiative aims to investigate the intersection of physics and machine learning, with a specific focus on leveraging algebraic topology for physics-related tasks. The findings presented here offer a foundation for future research into applying algebraic topology in physics. This study investigates the angular distributions of $J/\psi$ mesons produced in $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ reactions near $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV, incorporating both initial- and final-state QCD corrections. We analyze the ratios of cross sections, $\sigma(J/\psi+\eta_c)/\sigma(J/\psi+\Upsilon)$ and $\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{cJ})/\sigma(J/\psi+\Upsilon)$, as well as the polarization ratios, $P_{\parallel}(J/\psi)+P_{\perp}(J/\psi)$ and $P_{\parallel}(J/\psi)/P_{\perp}(J/\psi)$, where $P_{\parallel,\perp}$ represent the longitudinal and transverse polarizations of the $J/\psi$. Our findings indicate that next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD corrections significantly alter these ratios, with the $\chi_{c1}$ case exhibiting the most pronounced effects. Furthermore, we examine the potential impact of these NLO corrections on the experimental observation of the peak in the $\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{c1})/\sigma(J/\psi+\Upsilon)$ ratio at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. Additionally, we explore the possibility of detecting the NLO contribution to the $P_{\parallel}(J/\psi)/P_{\perp}(J/\psi)$ ratio through measurements of the azimuthal angle between the planes of the $J/\psi$ and $\chi_{c1}$ in the process $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{c1}$. Finally, we compare our predictions with existing Belle data. Our results suggest that the experimental upper limit on the ratio $\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{c1})/\sigma(J/\psi+\Upsilon)$ is consistent with NLO QCD predictions, while the measured value of $P_{\parallel}(J/\psi)/P_{\perp}(J/\psi)$ aligns well with the predicted range. Although Signal is a widely adopted messaging application, its registration process requires users to provide a phone number and a six-digit personal identification number (PIN). We conclude by proposing specific recommendations for the Signal development team. This research is the first to explore user perspectives on Signal PINs, and the insights gained are expected to be valuable for the Signal team and other application developers. This study introduces a new approach for integrating functions of the form $f(x)\max(0, \Phi(x))$, where $\Phi(x)$ represents the normalized cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a probability measure $\phi(x)dx$. This method is particularly valuable for problems involving solar energy, as $\max(0, \Phi(x))$ models the fraction of daylight relative to the day-night cycle. We propose a novel Gaussian quadrature technique that yields a quadrature formula with a specific number of points, achieving any desired level of accuracy. The effectiveness of this solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature is demonstrated through various test cases. Furthermore, we establish a general theorem that enables the calculation of associated node values and weight values for these quadrature formulas. Finally, we illustrate the application of these formulas by computing the mean insolation for a given latitude. Additionally, we show that these formulas can be applied to determine the day length and sunrise/sunset times for any specific date. This approach offers a precise and efficient method for solving solar energy problems, surpassing the accuracy of previous methods. This paper introduces the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, a curvature tensor that extends the standard Gauss-Newton matrix to broader contexts. We demonstrate that the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix possesses an explicit low-rank form, enabling the development of a corresponding ViViT network architecture. This new architecture offers a more efficient and interpretable low-rank representation of curvature compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we establish that the curvature entry of a function can be derived from its second-order directional entry, and we prove that the second-order directional entry of a function is low-rank when the function is a polynomial. Additionally, we present empirical evidence indicating that ViViT outperforms current models in both training and inference efficiency. This study examines how Grammatical Gender (GG) influences word representations in a GG-labeling language, specifically Italian. We introduce GG-ROBERTA, a model trained to predict GG labels, and analyze its latent space using the gender prediction task proposed by Devlin et al. (2019). Our findings indicate that the latent space of GG-ROBERTA is highly sensitive to GG, with gendered adjectives and nouns clustering distinctly based on their labels. Furthermore, gendered verbs are grouped according to their agreement with adjectives and nouns. However, despite this sensitivity, the model fails to capture gender stereotypes, and the gendered clusters remain largely impermeable to adversarial attacks. These results suggest that while the model is robust, it lacks the ability to generalize gender associations to novel words. Finally, we explore the potential of GG-ROBERTA for downstream applications, such as detecting gender bias in Italian. We demonstrate that for any locally compact topological group $G$ containing an open compact normal subgroup $K$, the inclusion map $H^1(G, -) \to H^1(G/K, -)$ constitutes a charmability functor. Leveraging this finding, we establish that virtually compact arithmetic subgroups of higher rank exhibit charmability. Furthermore, we prove that uniformly lattices in locally compact second countable groups display rigidity within their cohomology. Additionally, we examine the implications of these results for the Grothendieck conjecture regarding function fields. As an application, we provide a new characterization of charmability utilizing Banach spaces and operator theory. Finally, we outline several questions and conjectures concerning charmability and rigidity. These concepts are significant in the study of profinite completions of arithmetic groups and the investigation of function fields with non-trivial constant fields. The paper concludes with an outline of applications to charmability and rigidity. Keywords: charmability, rigidity, cohomology, arithmetic groups, Banach spaces, Grothendieck conjecture. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for numerous applications, yet it is challenging due to the extensive and sparse nature of traffic data. While existing methods often rely on historical data, they struggle to achieve high accuracy when predicting across all time periods. This paper introduces a novel, data-driven approach that leverages the similarity among time periods to enhance prediction accuracy. The proposed method, called Similarity-driven Attribute Extraction (SAE), utilizes a data-driven attribute extraction technique to identify and model the most significant features of these time periods. By modeling these attributes, SAE can forecast traffic flow for any time period, thereby improving overall prediction performance. Experimental results demonstrate that SAE achieves a substantial reduction in Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) compared to baseline methods. Furthermore, SAE exhibits strong generalization capabilities, maintaining high prediction accuracy even when applied to traffic data from different cities. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Similarity-driven-Attribute-Extraction. The LOFAR Low Frequency Array, situated in Ireland, is a compact radio telescope designed to monitor the sky for transients. Its backend, the LOFAR Real-time Transient Catcher (REALTA), is engineered to detect and record these events in real time. This system has successfully identified and recorded numerous radio transients, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), the most enigmatic of which are millisecond-duration radio bursts originating from distant galaxies. This paper details the REALTA system's initial detections of FRBs, including the first recorded capture of the repeating FRB 180916.J0511+29. Furthermore, we present a new analysis of the burst rate for the repeating FRB 20201124A, revealing that its activity is intermittent and that its burst rate fluctuates by approximately two orders of magnitude over a timescale of roughly 100 days. Additionally, we report the detection of a new repeating FRB, designated FRB 20220111A. Finally, we provide a comprehensive summary of the REALTA system's performance. This work serves as a foundation for future studies utilizing REALTA. The REALTA backend is now accessible to the public via the LOFAR Data Archive (LDA). This study examines the impact of pre-released marketing materials, such as trailers and posters, on a film's box office performance. While prior research has explored this relationship, it has been constrained by limited data regarding these pre-release assets. To address this gap, we introduce a novel dataset that expands upon existing collections by incorporating additional information on current film marketing materials. Utilizing this enhanced dataset, we analyze how various pre-released features influence gross revenue. Furthermore, we observe that the effects of other pre-released features vary depending on the specific film. These insights could prove valuable for both film distributors and producers. Finally, we note that the proposed model is capable of identifying the optimal combination of pre-released features for maximizing revenue. This study examines a frequency-regulated synchronous machine to demonstrate that it can also serve as an auxiliary device for voltage regulation. The device's parameters are tuned to minimize reactive power exchange with the grid, thereby stabilizing voltage levels. The analysis covers both steady-state conditions and dynamic behavior, with a specific focus on systems exhibiting two degrees of freedom. Results indicate that the proposed solution is highly effective in two-variable systems and remains reasonably effective in more complex scenarios. Furthermore, the findings suggest that this approach could be particularly beneficial for integrating renewable energy sources, which often exhibit variable or stochastic output. Finally, the paper outlines potential future research directions. The presented concept and associated mathematical models are applicable to any frequency-regulated machine, including asynchronous generators, rotary energy storage systems, and flywheels. Although the analysis is primarily conducted for a single-machine infinite bus system, the conclusions are expected to hold for larger power systems as well. Additionally, the proposed solution is not limited to specific power system configurations. While the study focuses on synchronous machines, the underlying principles can be extended to other machine types, such as rectifiers and inverters. The paper concludes by identifying potential future research avenues. The convergence of computing and communication technologies has driven the widespread adoption of cyberphysical systems, which are defined by their closed-loop control mechanisms. However, this paper argues that introducing cognition into these systems is both essential and feasible. We identify the primary obstacles to achieving this, specifically the absence of a unified cyberphysical system model and the lack of a standardized communication protocol. To address these challenges, we propose a cognitive computing framework that integrates a unified model and protocol, thereby facilitating the integration of cognitive capabilities into cyberphysical systems. The viability of this approach is demonstrated through a proof-of-concept implementation. Ultimately, we anticipate that this work will establish a foundational framework for the next generation of cyberphysical systems endowed with cognition. Additionally, the proposed cognitive computing framework is expected to serve as a basis for developing cognitive computing platforms, which will provide the necessary infrastructure to support cyberphysical systems with cognitive abilities. This will enable researchers to concentrate on the algorithms and methodologies required to endow systems with cognition. Finally, we believe this framework will foster the emergence of cognitive computing as a distinct and vibrant research discipline. The paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews related work; Section III outlines the challenges in integrating cognition into cyberphysical systems; Section IV presents the cognitive computing framework; Section V demonstrates the framework's feasibility via a proof-of-concept; and Section VII concludes the study. Furthermore, Section III-A specifically examines the challenge of integrating cognition into existing cyberphysical systems. This study revisits the origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess observed in blazar spectra, a phenomenon that remains a contentious issue. We demonstrate that this excess can be attributed to the partial polarization of inverse Compton scattering (IC) radiation emitted by relativistic electrons within the jet, interacting with low-energy photons from the broad-line region (BLR) surrounding the supermassive black hole. To validate this hypothesis, we developed a novel Monte Carlo code, MAPPIES, which is an extension of the previously introduced Monte Carlo Uses for Inverse Compton Scattering (MCISS). MAPPIES incorporates the angular distribution of the linearly polarized BLR photon field and the polarization state of the relativistic electron population. We applied this code to investigate the physical origins of the UV/soft X-ray surplus in blazar spectra. Our results indicate that the polarization of the jet photon field is essential for reproducing the spectral energy distribution (SED) of blazars. Furthermore, we show that the jet polarization fraction must be relatively high, and that the polarization angle of the jet photons aligns with the magnetic field orientation in the jet. These findings suggest that the surplus in UV/soft X-ray spectra arises from the polarization of inverse Compton scattering involving linearly polarized photons from the BLR and polarized electrons in the jet. Additionally, we demonstrate that the magnetic field configuration in the jet can be constrained by comparing the polarization angle of the jet photon field with the polarization angle of the magnetic field. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for blazar physics. The MAPPIES code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tae-kyeom/MAPPIES. This study addresses the problem of distinguishing two pure states that are symmetric with respect to a unitary operator. We demonstrate that this discrimination can be achieved with perfect accuracy by applying a suitable unitary evolution to the input state prior to standard optimal hypothesis testing. Consequently, we establish an efficient constructive method for identifying two pure states that are symmetric under a unitary operator. Furthermore, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition ensuring the existence of an optimal detection strategy that requires no evolution, expressed through the commutation relations between the symmetry operator and the individual elements of the positive operator-valued measure used for detection. Finally, we apply these findings to the task of determining the direction of a light beam using a single-photon input and a polarization beam splitter. In this application, we explicitly construct the optimal unitary transformation to achieve perfect state discrimination. Pulsar timing array (PTA) observations have recently detected a common-spectrum process (CSP) signal, which is widely interpreted as evidence of a gravitational wave background (GWB) generated by a population of supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs). However, the PTA data's sensitivity to GWB sources remains uncertain, as the definitive "smoking gun" signature of SMBHBs has not yet been confirmed. This study investigates the potential of relic magnetic fields within the PTA frequency band to generate a detectable GWB signal. We demonstrate that a stochastic background of magnetar spin-down can produce a GWB that is potentially observable by current PTA systems. Specifically, we show that the amplitude of this magnetic-field-driven GWB signal is contingent upon the population density of magnetars and their spin-down rates. Furthermore, we find that the spectral shape of this magnetic-field-induced GWB signal differs from the standard PTA signal model. Our analysis indicates that the PTA signal could be detected by existing systems within a few years, provided the signal amplitude exceeds $10^{-14}$. Additionally, we propose that future PTA observations should be conducted in the pulsar timing spectrum band to better constrain the spectral shape of the GWB signal. Finally, we outline the prospects for detecting GWB signals arising from magnetar spin-down in the near future. This research offers a novel perspective on GWB sources and establishes a new framework for exploring the stochastic gravitational wave background. The findings may also have implications for understanding the evolution of magnetars and their role in the broader astrophysical context. Small-Region Estimation (SRE) is a critical method for generating reliable estimates in areas with limited sample sizes, a common challenge in many developing nations. This study examines the performance of various SRE techniques using real-world data from Nepal's 2011 census. We evaluated multiple approaches, including the direct model, the Fay-Hartigan model, the Fay-Hartigan model with fixed variance, the Fay-Hartigan model with a lower bound, the Fay-Hartigan model with a variable lower bound, the Fay-Hartigan model with a variable lower bound and a fixed prior mean, the Fay-Hartigan model with a variable lower bound and a fixed prior mean with a lower bound, and the Fay-Hartigan model with a variable lower bound and a fixed prior mean with a lower bound and a prior variance. Additionally, we introduced a novel model- and design-focused approach termed the "Fay-Hartigan model with a variable lower bound and a fixed prior mean with a lower bound and a prior variance with a prior variance with a lower bound." This new method incorporates a lower bound for the prior variance of log-relative risks, which is derived from the sample variance of the same metric. We assessed these models using two metrics: the coefficient of variation (CV) and the mean absolute error (MAE). Results indicate that the model-focussed approach yielding the lowest CV and MAE values is the "Fay-Hartigan model with a variable lower bound and a fixed prior mean with a lower bound and a prior variance with a lower bound." Furthermore, this paper explores the application of the empirical Bayes method for small-area estimation in the context of the Nepal census. The proposed model-focussed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more robust framework for small-area estimation. This enhanced model can be readily adapted for future censuses and other surveys. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights for practitioners and researchers engaged in small-area estimation. I argue that Pontryagin dualism offers a more robust framework for understanding continuous reasoning than the view that reasoning operates on a circle. While the latter perspective is intuitive, it struggles to extend to reasoning about multiple variables or of higher order. In contrast, Pontryagin dualism provides a more general foundation that naturally accommodates multi-variable and higher-order continuous reasoning. Furthermore, I outline a proof demonstrating that the dual of a compact abelian group is itself compact, and the dual of a discrete group is compact as well. This proof draws upon concepts from measure theory and topology. Although the argument is rigorous, it is not entirely free of hand-waving, as it relies on the dual of a locally compact abelian group being locally compact—a fact that itself requires a substantial proof. Consequently, I hope that readers with a background in measure theory and topology will find this exploration both enjoyable and enlightening. Additionally, I have endeavored to elucidate the proof's core intuition without excessive technical jargon. Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning approach that enables training on locally held data while safeguarding user privacy. This method is particularly valuable for sensitive datasets, such as those in healthcare, where data remains on-premise and is shared only in the form of model updates. However, the privacy of these updates is not guaranteed. This study demonstrates that FL-trained models can inadvertently disclose private information, a phenomenon we term "update leakage." We illustrate this risk using a medical imaging dataset, showing that even with encryption, FL models can reveal sensitive details about individual patients. Furthermore, we reveal that FL can lead to unfairness by exposing the labels of minority class samples, thereby compromising the confidentiality of these groups. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce a novel framework that combines differential privacy with secure aggregation to mitigate both update leakage and unfairness. Our results indicate that this approach effectively protects individual privacy and ensures fair treatment across all classes. Additionally, we propose a new metric to quantify the differential privacy guarantee of FL, which can be applied to any FL configuration. We also explore the trade-off between privacy and utility in FL, demonstrating that while privacy can be enhanced, it often comes at the cost of reduced model utility. Finally, we examine the impact of various FL hyperparameters on both privacy and utility. Our findings offer a comprehensive perspective on the privacy and fairness challenges inherent in FL, providing a foundation for developing more robust and equitable systems. Relation GANs are a class of generative adversarial networks designed to synthesize images by modeling relationships between pixels. They achieve this by employing a connection network that links pixels based on their relational data. While the connection network can be trained using various supervised techniques, such as triplet loss, this paper demonstrates that integrating it within a GAN framework yields superior results. We illustrate this approach using a simple yet effective example: training Relation GANs with connection networks to reconstruct images from the Caltech-101 dataset. Our findings indicate that this method produces higher-quality image reconstructions compared to other training approaches for the same connection network. Additionally, we show that Relation GANs can generate new images that closely resemble the training set, whereas the connection network alone fails to do so effectively. We introduce a twin-field quantum key exchange (TFQKEX) protocol that operates without requiring phase synchronization. In this approach, phase modulation is substituted with a straightforward on-off keying scheme, thereby eliminating the need to encode phase information. We demonstrate that the security of this method remains comparable to the original TFQKEX, which depends on phase encoding. This advancement significantly simplifies the system architecture, making TFQKEX more viable for practical implementation. Furthermore, we show that TFQKEX can achieve long-distance quantum key distribution without relying on quantum repeaters. Additionally, we prove that the protocol is secure against general coherent attacks, ensuring unconditional security. Finally, numerical simulations indicate that TFQKEX can establish keys over distances up to 1,000 km under realistic conditions. These findings suggest that TFQKEX holds great promise for real-world applications. Our research has been published in *Physical Review A*, Volume 104, Article 042410 (2021). We introduce a novel method for identifying objects with open lexicons, utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations. Unlike conventional supervised approaches that rely on fixed sets of predefined categories, our method learns to map visual inputs to a continuous space of novel object classes. Specifically, we propose a new training objective that trains a model to predict a continuous embedding for each object class alongside a bounding box, using only class-agnostic bounding boxes as input. This class-agnostic bounding box serves as a pseudo label, enabling the model to learn a continuous embedding space where objects of the same class are localized accurately and clustered together. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Pascal VOC dataset, which features a limited number of predefined categories. The resulting model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, achieving high average precision on novel object classes that were never seen during training. Furthermore, we show that our model can be easily adapted to a wider range of categories through fine-tuning with a small set of examples. To our knowledge, this is the first method to effectively address open lexicon object identification without requiring pixel-level annotations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/visipedia/pseudo-box-supervised-continuous-cls.

This study evaluates two factor models designed to capture the time-varying nature of mortality rates. The first model, an extension of the Lee-Carter framework, allows factor loadings to vary over time. The second model, inspired by principal component analysis, assumes constant loadings. Both approaches are applied to predict mortality rates for the United States and United Kingdom. Results indicate that the PCA-based model with constant loadings outperforms the Lee-Carter model, while a further extension of this approach—allowing for stochastic loading changes—achieves even greater predictive accuracy. Additionally, the constant-loading specification demonstrates superior out-of-sample stability compared to the time-varying alternative. These findings hold true for both the United States and United Kingdom datasets. Finally, the study calculates life expectancies and analyzes their evolution. Although the constant-loading model produces slightly lower life expectancy values, it remains highly effective at reproducing historical trends. Overall, the constant-loading specification proves to be the most suitable for mortality prediction. These results are also validated using data from France and Germany.

This study examines the optimal pricing and purchase timing for a lottery ticket within a model featuring risk-averse agents. We introduce a novel "smart" lottery framework where winning probabilities are dynamically adjusted based on the number of active participants. Furthermore, we propose an alternative valuation metric that accounts for the purchaser's temporal position relative to draw events. Our analysis of a representative agent reveals that optimal lottery design involves setting prize amounts to a moderate level and pricing tickets at a low point. Additionally, we identify that an optimal purchase strategy may involve waiting until a later stage, specifically when the price per ticket is at its peak. These findings are supported by numerical illustrations. Ultimately, our results suggest that maximizing the value of a lottery mechanism requires careful calibration of prizes and pricing, alongside strategic consumer behavior regarding timing. In two-dimensional materials, electron-phonon interactions are significantly amplified, profoundly influencing valley dynamics. This study employs a first-principles approach to investigate these interactions in graphene, borophene, and silicene. We identify two novel valley-dependent electron-phonon coupling mechanisms: first, a direct coupling between electrons and phonons, and second, an indirect coupling mediated by electrons within non-valley degenerate bands. Our findings indicate that while the direct mechanism is negligible in graphene and borophene, it becomes substantial in silicene. Conversely, the mediated mechanism is significant in graphene and borophene but is suppressed in silicene. These results offer critical insights for designing efficient valley filters and valleytronic devices. Furthermore, our methodology is broadly applicable to other two-dimensional materials. Finally, the derived analytical expressions for these mechanisms are expected to be valuable for advancing theoretical research into electron-phonon interactions. These expressions have been made available to the community via the open-source code \texttt{PhononValley}. Our work establishes a foundation for the development of efficient, low-power valleytronic technologies. Additionally, the methodologies employed are anticipated to facilitate the design of novel materials with robust valley degrees of freedom. We introduce a novel method for visualizing high-dimensional data on a sphere, leveraging the Riemannian manifold structure inherent to spherical data. By integrating the concept of a Laplacian with the embedding of spherical data, we develop a Laplacian-based algorithm that generates a low-dimensional representation while maintaining the local neighborhood relationships of the original high-dimensional space. This approach is demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our primary contributions are twofold: first, we propose a new spherical embedding algorithm that preserves local neighborhoods and reveals the intrinsic structure of the data; second, we demonstrate that this method effectively handles a synthetic dataset where points are drawn from a von Mises-Fisher distribution. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art spherical embedding techniques. Furthermore, we show that the method is robust to noise and remains effective even when the data distribution is non-uniform. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed method can be applied to visualize data points in a way that enhances human interpretability. By extending the method to second-order perturbation theory in the interaction strength, we achieve high precision for weak to intermediate couplings. Our results align well with existing weak-coupling perturbation theory and numerical renormalization group findings. Furthermore, we employ a finite-size scaling analysis to forecast interaction energies at strong coupling, revealing a notable dependence on system size. This observation suggests that the Fermi polaron exhibits finite-size effects even in the strong-coupling regime, a phenomenon potentially attributable to a finite correlation length. Additionally, we explore the possibility of a quantum phase transition from a Fermi polaron to a bound pair state. Finally, we compare our computed interaction energies with those derived from the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) framework. While the DMFT polaron energy accurately reflects the weak-coupling behavior, it fails to capture the correct interaction energy in the strong-coupling regime. This discrepancy indicates that the DMFT self-energy, which is derived from an infinite-volume limit, may be unsuitable for describing the Fermi polaron under strong coupling conditions. These findings underscore the necessity of developing new theoretical approaches capable of describing the polaron in the strong-coupling limit. Our study demonstrates that DiagMC is a viable tool for this purpose, offering a complementary perspective to the recent DMFT-based analysis of the polaron. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for future DiagMC investigations into the phase diagram of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron.
