This paper investigates how distributed teams impact the success of Scrum projects. By analyzing data from 120 Scrum initiatives, we determined that remote teams achieve significantly higher success rates than on-site teams. This conclusion was drawn from a survey of 120 project managers, which revealed that project success is influenced by various factors, including team location. To validate these survey findings, we employed a simulation approach to assess the impact of team proximity on project outcomes. The results indicate that the likelihood of project success is substantially greater for remote teams compared to those working on-site. Additionally, we examined the relationship between team size and project success, finding that larger teams face greater challenges in distributed environments, leading to a higher risk of failure. Finally, we explored how specific success drivers vary between remote and on-site contexts, concluding that while certain factors like communication and motivation are more critical for remote teams, others such as communication tools and team size are less significant in that setting. These insights aim to assist organizations in managing remote teams more effectively. The study's outcomes are supported by a comprehensive dataset of 120 projects, with all findings available for replication. Furthermore, we have developed a web-based tool to assist project managers in predicting project success based on project parameters and team location. The tool's source code and a link to access the success prediction results are provided in the supplementary materials. We anticipate that the findings from this study will assist organizations in better preparing for and managing remote work environments. The research was conducted remotely, and we hope this work demonstrates the viability of remote research methodologies. The authors are currently extending this study to examine the impact of distributed teams on other project success metrics, such as budget and schedule adherence. Finally, we provide a comparison between the standard determinant and the Gau-Wu multivalued determinant for $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrices.

By applying a three-dimensional hydrodynamic model to describe the collective flow of heavy quarks within the quark-gluon plasma, the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of $B$ hadrons is derived. The results indicate that the $v_2$ of $B$ hadrons in Pb-Pb collisions is comparable to that of light hadrons, suggesting that bottom quarks participate in the hydrodynamic evolution of the medium. Furthermore, the observed $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of the $v_2$ for $B$ hadrons in Pb-Pb collisions is found to be similar to the pattern observed for light hadrons in pp collisions. Additionally, the data are consistent with a scenario where the production of $B$ hadrons in Pb-Pb collisions is primarily governed by the fragmentation of bottom quarks. This study examines a $K$-user interference network where each user possesses $\alpha$ antennas and receives a message from a message set of size $2^{nR}$. The message is transmitted with power $P$, and the channel experiences independent, identically distributed interference. We analyze the performance of a generalized interference alignment scheme, demonstrating that the maximum gain in generalized degrees of freedom (GDoF) achieved by an optimal real-valued power regulation strategy compared to a binary one does not exceed $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding indicates that the significant performance improvements observed in specific small-scale networks do not generalize to larger systems. Furthermore, we establish that the lower bound of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ is attainable for any $\alpha \geq 1$ when $K$ is a perfect square, provided the network topology allows for interference alignment. Finally, we extend these results to the scenario where each user receives a message from a set of size $2^{nR_K}$, with $R_K$ denoting a potentially non-constant rate per user. In this case, the upper bound on the GDoF gain remains $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$, while the lower bound is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for perfect-square $K$ under an appropriate alignment condition. Additionally, we derive a lower bound of $\Theta(K)$ for the GDoF gain when $K=4$ and $\alpha=1$. These findings are supported by a rigorous analysis of the underlying optimization problem. The paper also includes a detailed description of the power regulation scheme, a discussion of the associated optimization problem, and a formal proof of the results. Finally, we present a numerical example illustrating the performance of the proposed scheme. We introduce a novel principle termed the "generalized ambiguity principle," which establishes a fundamental limit on the precision with which position and momentum can be simultaneously known. This principle yields distinct formulations for both Lorentz and Galilean transformations, revealing that the equivalence between these transformations is contingent upon the uncertainty in momentum. Consequently, there exists a defined velocity threshold below which Lorentz contraction becomes negligible when converting from a Lorentz transformation to a Galilean one. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding mass ambiguity and explore its relationship with the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings. The technical details of this study are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/gap. Additionally, a technical report detailing the mathematical derivations can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00001. The source code used to generate the plots is available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/gap/tree/main/Plots. Our analysis indicates that the velocity limit for the validity of Galilean transformations is approximately $10^{-16}$ times the speed of light. We anticipate that this result will inspire further research into the boundaries of classical physics. The accompanying code is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/gap. This paper investigates the computational capabilities of multitasking managers, defined as agents responsible for scheduling and allocating shared resources to optimize the performance of multiple tasks. We concentrate on a specific scenario where a manager distributes shared computational power among tasks, aiming to maximize the number of completed jobs. We examine a simple yet representative scheduling model where both the manager and tasks are modeled as stochastic processes. The manager's behavior is defined by a stochastic process representing its scheduling policy, while each task is represented by a stochastic process indicating its active duration. The primary challenge is to design a scheduling policy that maximizes throughput, measured by the rate of job completions. We demonstrate that the optimal policy exhibits a threshold structure, where the manager prioritizes the task with the highest completion probability. Furthermore, we derive the distribution of this threshold for various models and discuss potential extensions. Finally, we outline how this framework can be applied to other domains, such as energy harvesting and wireless communications. This research is motivated by the need to develop efficient scheduling policies for multitasking systems. Energy harvesting serves as a key motivation, where the goal is to allocate harvested energy to maximize the number of completed tasks. In this context, the manager is the energy harvesting unit, and the tasks are energy-intensive processes like data transmission, sensing, or computation. We believe this approach offers a promising avenue for future research in multitasking systems. The paper is structured as follows: Section II introduces the system model and problem formulation; Section III presents our main results; Section IV discusses extensions to other multitasking scenarios; and Section V concludes the paper. Additionally, Section VI provides a simulation study to validate our theoretical findings. The remainder of this document includes an appendix with supplementary proofs and results.
Keywords: Multitasking, Scheduling, Energy Harvesting, Wireless Communications.

This paper presents a model for the dynamics of a monopod leaper traversing yielding terrain, alongside its simulation and methods for improving performance. The dynamics are modeled using a discrete-time system where the next state depends on the current state and control inputs. These inputs include the force applied to the ground by the leg tip and the timing of the ground contact phase. The dynamics are characterized by a nonlinear, nonaffine function of the state and control variables. To facilitate the solution of a nonlinear optimization problem, the system is linearized around an operating point, yielding a linear time-varying system. This approximation is subsequently converted into a linear time-invariant system. A nonlinear optimization problem is formulated to determine the control inputs that minimize the error between the actual nonlinear system and a reference trajectory. To address the nonlinear nature of this formulation, a sequential quadratic programming algorithm is employed. The proposed approach is validated through simulations, and the effectiveness of the reference trajectory is assessed using performance metrics. The simulation results demonstrate that the reference trajectory enables the monopod leaper to successfully navigate yielding terrain. Furthermore, the optimization algorithm achieves a minimal error between the actual trajectory and the reference trajectory, thereby enhancing the leaper's performance. The simulation outcomes confirm that the optimization algorithm is effective in solving the nonlinear optimization problem. Finally, the proposed method is applied to a monopod leaper with a mass of 1.5 kg. The simulation results indicate that the leaper can achieve a maximum vertical jump height of 1.5 m and a maximum horizontal jump distance of 1.2 m. Additionally, the computational time required to solve the optimization problem is less than 0.01 seconds. These findings suggest that the proposed approach is computationally efficient and suitable for real-time applications. The simulation results also demonstrate that the leaper can maintain a constant velocity on soft ground and climb slopes up to 30°. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. The proposed approach can be extended to other locomotion systems, such as legged robots, to enhance their performance on yielding terrain. Furthermore, the approach can be adapted for use in virtual reality applications, where users can interact with a virtual environment using a monopod leaper controller. These findings underscore the algorithm's potential to significantly enhance the reliability of software upgrades in practical IoT environments. We investigate the transition from many-body localization (MBL) to thermalization, driven by increasing disorder, by analyzing the scaling of the Fock-space propagator across three- to seven-body interactions. Our results indicate that at the shift point, the propagator decays as a power law, with the exponent $\tau$ varying between 1.5 and 2.5. Furthermore, we observe that the amplitude of the propagator scales with system size $L$ as $L^{-\tau/2}$, demonstrating that the distribution of energy eigenstates follows a multifractal pattern. These findings align with the multifractality observed in the delocalized phase of non-interacting Anderson models. Additionally, we examine the scaling of the participation ratio and the distribution of return probabilities, both of which support the multifractal nature of eigenstates at the shift point. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the critical exponents governing the shift transition. This paper addresses the challenge of visiting numerous target locations using a cost-limited mobile robot equipped with interactive sensors. The task involves identifying unknown target positions and visiting them to maximize the number of visits within a fixed budget. We introduce a new algorithm that prioritizes targets offering the highest information gain, thereby reducing uncertainty about their locations. This approach is evaluated across various 2D environments with differing target counts, demonstrating its ability to visit a high proportion of targets within the allocated budget. Additionally, we show that the algorithm scales effectively to scenarios involving hundreds of targets. The proposed method is implemented in Python and made publicly available. Our results indicate that the algorithm outperforms several baselines, including those relying on greedy strategies and those utilizing extensive maps. Finally, we present experimental results from a physical robot implementation, confirming the algorithm's effectiveness in real-world applications. We demonstrate that the success of these attacks is influenced by the specific parametrization of the quantum classifier. By employing a global adversarial training approach, we show that such methods can effectively enhance the robustness of quantum classifiers. Furthermore, we find that the performance of adversarial training is highly dependent on the noise level within the training data. Our results indicate that training a quantum classifier on data augmented with adversarial examples leads to superior generalization performance. Additionally, we observe that incorporating adversarial training results in a quantum circuit with fewer qubits and gates, thereby reducing the overall complexity. These findings are validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues within two families of three-dimensional domains: ellipsoids and perturbed spheres. We demonstrate that for both families, the Steklov eigenvalues can be expressed as asymptotic expansions incorporating terms of all orders. Furthermore, we establish that these expansions for the eigenvalues of both families are identical when ordered. However, we also provide the specific coefficients for each family's expansion up to the fourth order. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the asymptotic behavior of the Steklov eigenvalues and the geometry of the boundary, deriving a formula that links these behaviors to the boundary's curvature. Finally, we compare our findings with existing literature and present a conjecture regarding the asymptotic behavior of Steklov eigenvalues in higher dimensions. Conformance checking evaluates the behavior of information systems by comparing system traces against a process model. While infix and postfix alignments offer efficient methods for this verification, they traditionally require translating these alignments into infix and postfix sequences, respectively, before alignment algorithms are applied. This translation step often results in data loss, which can hinder the identification of deviations. We demonstrate that infix and postfix alignments can be directly represented as infix and postfix traces within the alignment framework, thereby eliminating the need for data loss-prone translations. This approach enables the direct calculation of infix and postfix alignments without degrading the quality of the resulting conformance checks. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique for identifying the source of deviations in generated alignments. This method constructs deviation trees from infix and postfix alignments, which are then transformed into deviation graphs to pinpoint the specific deviations. These deviation graphs can subsequently be utilized to generate explanations for the identified deviations. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study. The source code for the proposed method is accessible at https://github.com/TracPart/TracePart. The corresponding paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10701-021-00457-0. The method is also available as a Python package, TracePart, at https://pypi.org/project/TracePart/. The Python package includes a command-line tool that accepts infix and postfix traces as input and outputs infix and postfix alignments, deviation graphs, and explanations. Additionally, a web-based tool, PartCheck, is available at https://partcheck.github.io/, which allows users to upload infix and postfix traces to generate alignments, deviations, explanations, and a conformance score. Users can also input pre-generated alignments, deviations, explanations, and scores via a provided link. Both the Python package and the web tool support infix and postfix traces. This paper introduces a novel radio propagation model grounded in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Leveraging the inherent spatial structure of radio propagation, the proposed cellular network model utilizes 2D convolutional layers to represent the radio environment. By employing a single-layer CNN, the model effectively captures the spatial characteristics of the power delay profile (PDP) and power angle profile (PAP) at the user equipment (UE) level. Furthermore, the framework is flexible enough to be expanded into a multi-layer CNN for more complex scenarios. The model's performance is evaluated using the 3GPP TR 38.901 standard as a benchmark, with results demonstrating that the single-layer CNN achieves accuracy comparable to the statistical model while offering superior computational efficiency. Additionally, the paper explores the application of this model in channel estimation, showing that it can significantly reduce the computational load of convolutional neural network-based channel estimation algorithms. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of training the model with limited data by proposing a data augmentation technique that enhances both accuracy and efficiency. The proposed model is implemented in Python and is available as open-source software. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Cellular-Propagation-Model. This study examines the sensitivity of a long-term, large-scale energy system growth model. We begin by introducing the model and its associated optimization problem, followed by an analysis of how variations in model parameters influence the solution. Our findings indicate that while the model is highly sensitive to parameter changes, this does not necessarily undermine its utility. We conclude that modelers should be prepared to justify their parameter selections and acknowledge the resulting implications. Additionally, we propose that conducting sensitivity analyses is a valuable method for identifying critical parameters and communicating the model's limitations to stakeholders. Finally, we recommend that future research explore advanced techniques for managing parameter uncertainty, such as robust optimization. This study examines a class of Vlasov-Poisson systems within bounded domains, encompassing both insulating coatings and Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the system is globally well-posed provided the initial data are sufficiently close to equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish that solutions remain globally bounded away from this proximity condition. These findings are applicable to the 1D Vlasov-Poisson system under periodic boundary conditions, as well as to 2D and 3D configurations under periodic or Neumann boundary conditions. The analysis relies on a novel approach to boundary conditions, which we term "weak boundary conditions." This method is derived from the boundary layer formulation of the problem and utilizes a specific boundary operator that ensures the boundary condition is satisfied. Additionally, we prove that this operator generates a boundary layer that decays exponentially as one moves away from the boundary. These results are also relevant to the periodic and boundaryless Vlasov-Poisson system. Our methodology extends to other confining systems, such as the Vlasov-Maxwell system with insulating or Dirichlet boundary conditions, as well as various mean-field models featuring confining potentials. The paper concludes with an outline of the proof for global well-posedness. Finally, we provide an overview of numerical simulations for a 1D problem with periodic boundary conditions, illustrating the emergence of stationary states and the system's behavior under different initial conditions. Colloidal gels are extensively utilized across various scientific and industrial fields, where their mechanical and rheological properties are typically tuned by modifying the concentration of the colloidal particles. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to control the rheological characteristics of colloidal gels by applying high-frequency ultrasonic waves during gel formation. This technique allows for the fine-tuning of the gel's microstructure, thereby modulating its rheological properties. We demonstrate that this ultrasonic-assisted formation method can be applied to diverse systems, including those with and without polymers, as well as those stabilized by charge or van der Waals forces. Furthermore, we show that these ultrasonically formed gels exhibit pronounced rheo-acoustic behavior, meaning their mechanical and flow properties can be adjusted in real-time by varying the frequency and amplitude of the applied ultrasonic waves. This capability offers a new avenue for developing smart materials capable of responding to external stimuli. Additionally, we illustrate that this rheo-acoustic behavior can be explained by a simple model that incorporates the effects of acoustic radiation pressure on the gel's microstructure. Our findings suggest that ultrasonic-assisted gel formation is a versatile method for creating materials with tailored microstructures and properties, and that ultrasonic waves can serve as a means to dynamically regulate the rheological properties of these gels. This research paves the way for advancing the field of soft materials and developing new applications for colloidal gels. The Collatz Conjecture remains an unresolved mathematical challenge. It involves a straightforward iterative process applied to any positive integer. Specifically, if a number is even, it is divided by two; if odd, it is multiplied by three and increased by one. The conjecture asserts that regardless of the starting integer, the sequence will invariably converge to 1. Although this has been verified for all initial values up to approximately $2^{68}$, a formal proof remains elusive. This paper aims to provide a proof of the conjecture.

This paper investigates a new online matching framework designed for platforms that facilitate connections between users and providers. In this system, the platform can choose to make offers to a subset of received user requests, thereby determining which requests are ultimately matched. We introduce a platform that receives online requests from both users and providers and propose a new algorithm, Select, that operates by selecting a subset of user requests for offers. We demonstrate that Select achieves a competitive ratio of $1.5$ relative to an offline optimal algorithm capable of observing all requests beforehand. Furthermore, we establish that the framework is inherently lossy, meaning no algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio better than $1$ against an offline optimal one. Finally, we outline several extensions to this framework. To our knowledge, this work represents the first study on online matching platforms with the ability to select a subset of online offers. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm performs well in practice and that the framework offers a promising avenue for future research. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/PranavKumar2000/Select}.

**Keywords:** Online Matching, Offers, Subset Selection.

We introduce a novel approach for restoring a signal from noisy quadratic measurements. The core concept involves transforming the non-convex optimization task into a convex one by expanding the search space to include a positive semidefinite (PSD) matrix that represents the outer product of the unknown signal vector. This technique is applicable across various scenarios, such as phase retrieval, matrix completion, and channel estimation. Our analysis demonstrates that the resulting estimator achieves a near-optimal statistical error rate for all practical cases, including high-dimensional settings and situations involving both structured and unstructured noise. Furthermore, we establish that the method's performance remains robust even when the number of measurements is significantly lower than the signal dimension. Finally, we validate the approach's effectiveness through extensive numerical experiments. These results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, including those derived from semidefinite programming, in terms of both statistical efficiency and computational speed. LiDAR and cameras are the two most prevalent sensors in autonomous driving, yet each has distinct limitations. This approach delivers superior fusion performance with minimal computational overhead, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Extensive evaluations on the KITTI, nuScenes, and Waymo benchmark datasets demonstrate that BEVFusion significantly enhances perception capabilities, particularly in adverse weather and low-light conditions. Furthermore, the project includes open-sourced code and pre-trained models for the first time, facilitating the deployment of high-performance fusion models in practical scenarios. This study examines the dissipation scales in liquid turbulence and the impact of liquid density fluctuations on heat transfer. By analyzing the density field, we identify density vortices that emerge from the stretching of liquid filaments at fine scales. These filaments are generated by density vortices within the liquid and subsequently stretched by the strain rate field. The density field is decomposed into a mean component and a fluctuating component, with the latter exhibiting significantly higher intensity than in gaseous turbulence. This high-intensity fluctuation creates a new dissipation range in liquid turbulence, characterized by a Kolmogorov-like inertial subrange and a Kolmogorov scaling exponent of 2/3. Furthermore, the density fluctuation field at fine scales is shown to be amplified by a factor of approximately 100 compared to the velocity field. Consequently, the thermal disturbance field at these scales is amplified by a factor of roughly 10 relative to gas turbulence. These findings are supported by molecular dynamics simulations of liquid turbulence. These results suggest that liquid turbulence possesses unique characteristics that differ fundamentally from gas turbulence. The existence of this new dissipation range in liquids may have significant implications for understanding the turbulent heat transfer process. Additionally, the density fluctuation field at fine scales could influence the nucleation of vapor bubbles in liquid turbulence. These conclusions are corroborated by both molecular dynamics simulations and experimental data. Finally, the observed scaling laws in the inertial subrange of liquid turbulence are compared with the scaling laws of the inertial subrange in gas turbulence. This comparison reveals that liquid turbulence exhibits distinct features, thereby challenging the traditional hypothesis that liquid and gas turbulence are identical. These conclusions are also validated by both molecular dynamics simulations and experimental observations. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the study of liquid turbulence. This study presents a numerical investigation into the laser-induced thermal profile within a liquid medium. By employing a straightforward yet effective numerical approach, we examine the complex interplay between the laser's spatial distribution, thermal diffusion, and volumetric absorption. The resulting numerical thermal profile is subsequently utilized to explain experimentally observed, complex self-induced diffraction patterns generated by the absorption of a laser beam in a liquid. Our findings indicate that the intricate diffraction patterns result from a combination of the laser's spatial profile and the thermal diffusion process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermal profile can be precisely represented as a superposition of Gaussian functions, with the necessary number of components determined by the specific experimental parameters. This numerical framework is applicable to a wide range of experimental conditions. Additionally, we show that the thermal profile can be accurately approximated using a single Gaussian function, provided its width is determined via a simple scaling law. This law reveals that the thermal profile is governed by the competition between laser diffusion and thermal diffusion. Finally, we illustrate that this simplified model, utilizing only one fitting parameter, is sufficient to describe the diffraction patterns generated by a laser beam propagating through a liquid. These results are supported by experimental data. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive numerical description of laser-generated thermal profiles in liquids, which can be employed to interpret various experimental outcomes. This approach involves learning a conclusion stability function that maps conversation segments to queries, ensuring that if two segments are sufficiently similar, they yield identical conclusions. This work introduces a non-resonant approach to calculating the production cross section for top quark pairs alongside bottom quarks at the LHC. The methodology relies on the quark-flavor component of the QCD color flow, which is derived from the flavor-independent component through a non-trivial mapping. This technique is validated by comparing the resulting differential cross sections against those generated by the event generator MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. Furthermore, the paper examines the production of top quark pairs with two associated bottom quarks, demonstrating that the computed cross sections align with measurements from the CMS experiment. Finally, the study presents results for various parton-level observables. These findings are accessible via a dedicated website, which also hosts a parton-level code capable of computing the relevant differential cross sections. The code is designed to be easily adaptable for inclusion in other event generators. Additionally, the work explores the potential of this method for analyzing the associated production of three bottom quarks, offering a preliminary assessment of its applicability to the associated production of two top quarks and two gluons. The latter scenario is particularly significant for investigating the flavor structure of the strong interaction. The conclusions are supported by a comprehensive set of numerical results. All data required to reproduce these findings can be accessed through a dedicated repository. The authors hope this approach will prove useful for the LHC community. We introduce a method for grouping objects based on pairwise similarity, where objects can belong to multiple groups, and we demonstrate how to solve this problem efficiently using min-cut. This approach is particularly valuable for applications requiring overlapping structures, such as segmenting images and movies. Additionally, we show that the method can be extended to handle hierarchical groupings in a functorial manner. To validate this, we developed a Python library that implements the technique and provides a solver for the hierarchical problem, including support for various scoring functions. We evaluate our method on image segmentation and video object tracking tasks, demonstrating that it achieves competitive performance compared to other approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/andreas-bergman/functorial-grouping. Furthermore, we provide a tutorial on applying the method to these tasks, available at https://andreas-bergman.github.io/functorial-grouping/tutorial.html. This tutorial includes a demonstration of the method's performance on the challenging YouTube-COCO video dataset. Finally, we offer a theoretical analysis of the proposed method. Specifically, we prove that the method is consistent, meaning that as the number of objects increases, the probability of recovering the true grouping approaches one. ZK's 1942 theory for inertial waves in three-dimensional isotropic turbulence posits that the energy spectrum follows a $k^{-5/3}$ power law, contingent upon the validity of the cascade hypothesis. This hypothesis asserts that the energy transfer rate remains independent of the wavenumbers of the receiving modes, thereby sustaining an isotropic energy flux. We provide the first confirmation of the $-5/3$ spectrum within inertial wave simulations, achieved by employing a novel simulation method that explicitly resolves the anisotropy of inertial waves. This approach involves superimposing pairs of counter-propagating waves with identical frequencies and amplitudes, which eliminates the rapid decay associated with the Rossby radius of deformation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the zonal component of the energy transfer tensor, which is responsible for the energy cascade, aligns with the zonal part of the Reynolds stress tensor. This finding supports the validity of the cascade hypothesis and confirms the $-5/3$ spectral slope. Additionally, we show that the zonal component of the energy transfer tensor is significantly larger than the non-zonal component, indicating that the non-zonal component can be disregarded in the energy budget. These results provide robust evidence that the zonal component of the energy transfer tensor is the primary driver of the energy cascade. This paper introduces the concept of the standardization matrix, which is utilized to determine if two graphs are isomorphic. We demonstrate that the standardization matrix for a specific graph can be computed through an iterative application of a coloring function. Furthermore, we establish that this matrix, alongside a corresponding coloring of the graph's vertices, can be generated in a time frame that is nearly linear relative to the number of the graph's edges.

In a separate context, this study examines a discrete-time dynamical system defined on a graph, where each vertex represents a discrete state variable. The state of each variable evolves according to a deterministic function that relies exclusively on the current states of its neighboring vertices. We define a subset of state variables as autonomous if their collective states remain constant throughout the evolution of the system. The maximum weight autonomous set is identified as the set of state variables with the highest total weight that forms an autonomous set. We prove that the existence of such a set is guaranteed and that an algorithm exists to find it. This algorithm operates in time nearly linear to the number of graph edges by employing a specialized version of the standardization matrix, which we refer to as the existence matrix. The construction of this matrix is achieved through an iterative process utilizing a coloring function. Additionally, we establish that both the coloring function and the existence matrix can be built in time nearly linear to the number of edges, provided the graph does not contain a clique of size four or larger. Finally, we outline an algorithm for computing the maximum weight autonomous set that runs in time nearly linear to the number of edges, under the condition that the graph lacks a clique of size five or greater. This approach involves solving a linear programming problem, which can be addressed using the simplex method. The linear programming problem is formulated based on the existence matrix, which we term the linear programming matrix. We show that this matrix can be constructed in time nearly linear to the number of edges by iteratively applying a coloring function. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results and potential future research directions.

Keywords: Graph coloring, Graph standardization, Discrete dynamical systems, Linear programming, Simplex method.

This study reports the detection of low-frequency radio emissions from the flare star binary system CR Draconis, observed using the UTR-2 radio telescope. The emission exhibits a high circular polarization degree, a high peak flux density, and a long duration, suggesting it is driven by an electron-cyclotron maser instability. The observed radio bursts are attributed to magnetic reconnection events occurring in the chromospheres of the two stars. The primary burst, lasting approximately 100 minutes, displays a complex morphology characterized by multiple peaks and a gradual frequency drift. We propose that this burst results from the superposition of numerous radio pulses generated by multiple chromospheric reconnection events. The frequency drift is interpreted as a consequence of the decay of the flare-induced magnetic field. Furthermore, the duration of the radio burst from CR Draconis is significantly longer than typical solar flares, indicating that electron-cyclotron maser radiation can persist for extended periods. This finding suggests that low-frequency radio observations can effectively monitor the evolution of magnetic reconnection in flare stars. This collision frequency is derived from the Lennard-Jones potential, which represents the interaction between two molecules as a function of their separation distance. The resulting kinetic framework is utilized to investigate a two-dimensional normal shock wave. Numerical results indicate that the proposed model accurately captures the physics of the shock wave and demonstrates that accounting for the intermolecular potential leads to significant improvements in the model's predictive capabilities. Furthermore, the study confirms that the proposed model is consistent with the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations. Finally, the collision frequency is analyzed in relation to the Knudsen number, revealing that the model's accuracy improves as the Knudsen number increases. These findings suggest that the proposed model is particularly well-suited for simulating gas flows in the slip flow and transition flow regimes. Additionally, the study highlights that the kinetic framework can be extended to include other intermolecular potentials, such as the Buckingham potential. We introduce a framework for semantic interpretation that relies on a single, unifying hypothesis: semantic labels are natural, meaning they can be derived from a small collection of examples. This approach enables semantic interpreters to learn label definitions from minimal data, thereby facilitating the rapid acquisition of new labels. Our experiments demonstrate that this method can train interpreters using as few as five positive and negative examples per label, achieving performance that matches or surpasses state-of-the-art interpretability techniques when evaluated across a suite of tasks. Furthermore, we show that these trained interpreters can rapidly adapt to novel labels with only a few examples. We also provide an analysis of the training dynamics, revealing that our training procedure yields a set of labels that are more easily interpretable than those provided in the original dataset. Finally, we explore the relationship between semantic interpretation and semantically supervised learning, demonstrating that our procedure can be adapted to train classifiers on extremely limited data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rohitk1997/semantic-interpreters. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is currently in its planning phase, with a primary objective of investigating the internal structure of protons and nuclei at high energies. To achieve this, the EIC necessitates a luminosity of $10^{33} \mathrm{cm}^{-2} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$, a target that demands significant advancements in silicon tracking technology. This presentation will outline recent progress in silicon tracking, specifically detailing the development of the Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (MAPS) known as Medipix3, which is being utilized in the LHC's upgraded LHCb experiment. Furthermore, we will present initial findings from a newly designed MAPS sensor, called LUCID, intended for the EIC. This innovative sensor features a monolithic pixel readout chip with a $50 \mu \mathrm{m} \times 50 \mu \mathrm{m}$ pixel pitch, a $100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick silicon sensor, and a $100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick readout chip. The study will also address the critical challenge of radiation hardness, which is essential for the EIC's high-radiation environment. Finally, the presentation will showcase the results of a recent LUCID sensor test conducted at the CERN test beam. These findings will be used to evaluate the sensor's performance and potential for EIC applications. Collectively, these results demonstrate that MAPS technology holds great promise for the EIC. We report the detection of a pulsation-like signal in the optical light curve of the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) SDSS J122900.89+022437.6, which we designate as SDSS J1229+0224. This source exhibits a mean absolute magnitude of $M_{\rm abs} \sim -13.5$ mag and a blackbody temperature of $T_{\rm BB} \sim 10,000$ K, indicating it is a low-luminosity AGN. The observed signal displays a period of $P = 1.05 \pm 0.01$ days with an amplitude of $\Delta M = 0.15 \pm 0.01$ mag. We propose that this signal originates from a pulsation-like event driven by a low-mass accretion disk. The event is likely caused by a small perturbation in the accretion rate, which triggers a thermal instability within the disk. This instability causes the disk to expand and cool, resulting in a brightening phase. The timescale for this brightening is governed by the thermal timescale of the disk. Furthermore, the event is expected to be followed by a fading phase, with its duration determined by the cooling timescale of the disk. This mechanism is applicable to both low- and high-luminosity AGNs. We estimate that the mass of the central black hole in SDSS J1229+0224 is approximately $10^5 M_{\odot}$. Additionally, we suggest that the low-mass black hole in this AGN may have formed through the direct collapse of a massive gas cloud. This study represents the first detection of a pulsation-like signal in a low-luminosity AGN. The detection of similar signals in other low-luminosity AGNs could provide a method for identifying low-mass black holes. Finally, we note that the low-mass black hole in SDSS J1229+0224 may be a member of the recently identified population of low-mass black holes in the local universe. The identification of such low-mass black holes is crucial for understanding the initial mass function of black holes. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD58260, a rapidly rotating A0V star, conducted using the DISCO apparatus at the 1.5-meter discharge spectropolarimeter. The analysis focuses on the Fe I 5018.15 Å line, which is highly sensitive to the radial magnetic field. By applying the spectropolarimetric inversion method, we derived the line-of-sight magnetic field distribution across the stellar disk. Our findings reveal a strong correlation between the observed magnetic field and the projected rotational velocity ($v \sin i$), indicating that the magnetic field strength diminishes toward the equator. This result aligns with the magnetic field distribution previously reported by the Mauna Kea Infrared Polarimeter II (MI2) on the same star. Furthermore, the data suggest that HD58260 possesses a magnetic field with a dipolar-like structure. These observations provide a new perspective on the magnetic field configuration of this rapidly rotating star. Additionally, we discuss the potential for utilizing Fe I lines to study magnetic fields in A-type stars. This paper investigates the free boson representation of the Dunkl intertwining operator in one dimension. By employing the 1D Jack operator and the Calogero-Sutherland potential, we derive the free boson formulation for both the generalized Pochhammer symbol and the q-gamma function. We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line in the low-metallicity galaxy NGC 5253 to investigate the relationship between HII regions and their surrounding molecular gas. By analyzing the H30$\alpha$ line, we identified 11 HII regions and measured their H2 1-0 (2.12 $\mu$m) emission to determine the mass of molecular gas within each region. We then compared these measurements with stellar population synthesis models to calculate the stellar mass-to-light ratio ($\Psi$) for each HII region. Our results indicate that $\Psi$ values for these regions are significantly lower than those of the galaxy's stellar disk, suggesting that HII regions in low-metallicity galaxies are more massive than previously thought. Furthermore, we found that the H30$\alpha$ emission is more luminous than the H2 emission, implying that the HII regions are expanding. Finally, we examined the correlation between $\Psi$ and the H30$\alpha$-to-H2 ratio, finding that the data aligns with a model where HII regions are in a quasi-steady state. This study provides the first evidence of such a state in low-metallicity galaxies, offering a new perspective on the early stages of massive star formation. Additionally, we present a novel method for measuring the mass of HII regions, which may prove valuable for future research. This paper investigates constant orbit equivalence stiffness within the context of virtually cyclic group actions. We demonstrate that, under the constant orbit equivalence relation, the multiplicity of orbits in a virtually cyclic group action can be represented as a virtually cyclic group itself, maintaining orbit equivalence. Furthermore, we establish that the orbit equivalence between two such actions implies equivalence under the 2-approximate orbit equivalence relation. Additionally, we prove that orbit equivalence is preserved by the crossed product operation. Finally, we examine various properties of virtually cyclic group actions subject to the approximate orbit equivalence relation. In this framework, we define a novel concept termed "almost free" and investigate its characteristics. We also present an example of a virtually cyclic group action on a finite-dimensional C*-algebra that is not free yet possesses constant orbit equivalence stiffness. Finally, we explore the connection between constant orbit equivalence stiffness and the 2-approximate orbit equivalence relation. Specifically, we demonstrate that if two virtually cyclic group actions are 2-approximate orbit equivalent, they are necessarily constant orbit equivalent. This finding extends a result previously established for free group actions. Consequently, we derive an upper bound for the constant orbit equivalence stiffness of virtually cyclic group actions based on their spectral gap. As an application, we show that the constant orbit equivalence stiffness of virtually cyclic group actions on the circle is bounded by 4. Additionally, we provide an example of a non-free action on a finite-dimensional C*-algebra with a constant orbit equivalence stiffness of exactly 4. Finally, we outline an algorithm to determine the constant orbit equivalence stiffness for virtually cyclic group actions on finite-dimensional C*-algebras. This approach involves decomposing the algebra into a direct sum of matrix algebras and calculating the constant orbit equivalence stiffness for each corresponding action on a one-dimensional C*-algebra. We illustrate this method with an example of a virtually cyclic group action on a one-dimensional C*-algebra. The algorithm utilizes the Fourier transform to identify the periods of group action elements and subsequently determines the constant orbit equivalence stiffness. This methodology offers an alternative to the approach presented in [10]. This result follows from the fact that the constant orbit equivalence stiffness of free group actions on the circle does not exceed 2, combined with the observation that every virtually cyclic group action on the circle is free up to a unitary perturbation. This study examines the strengths and limitations of the local linear regression method for estimating conditional expectation functions. By deriving the asymptotic bias and variance of the estimator, we can evaluate its performance. Furthermore, we derive an optimal bandwidth selection rule to minimize the mean squared error of the estimator. Finally, we present a simulation study that tests the theoretical findings and explores the estimator's behavior when the conditional mean function exhibits discontinuities. The results indicate that the estimator performs well in smooth regions but struggles in areas characterized by high noise or non-smoothness. Additionally, we observe that the theoretical bandwidth optimization rule fails to yield optimal results in highly noisy or non-smooth environments. Ultimately, we advocate that the local linear estimator should be employed with caution when the underlying function is known or suspected to be non-smooth. To address this, we propose a data-driven approach that adaptively selects the estimator's bandwidth. This method is demonstrated to outperform the local linear estimator in noisy or non-smooth settings. We conclude by applying this adaptive bandwidth selection technique to real-world data. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the local linear estimator; Section 3 derives its asymptotic bias and variance; Section 4 presents a theoretical framework for bandwidth selection; Section 5 details an adaptive bandwidth selection method; Section 6 compares this adaptive approach against the local linear estimator using simulated data; and Section 7 applies the method to a real-world dataset. The paper also includes an appendix. Keywords: Adaptive bandwidth selection, conditional expectation function, local linear regression, nonparametric estimation. This study introduces a state assessment framework for epidemic dynamics, grounded in a stochastic compartmental model. The state assessment is defined as a time-dependent stochastic process that tracks the current number of individuals in each epidemic compartment. The process evolves based on the current state and a control policy, which is a time-dependent function of the state. The control policy dictates a control action aimed at minimizing the cost associated with both the process and the action. The primary objective is to determine an optimal control policy that minimizes the cumulative cost over a specified time horizon. This optimization problem is formulated as a dynamic programming equation. However, solving this equation requires knowledge of the process's initial distribution, which is often unavailable in practical scenarios. Consequently, we propose a novel observer-based approach to address this lack of information. This approach involves constructing an observer that generates an estimate of the process's state using only the process's output. We demonstrate that the observer-based solution yields an optimal control policy that is asymptotically equivalent to the true optimal policy. Furthermore, we establish that the observer achieves finite-time convergence for the estimation error. Finally, the proposed observer is validated through a simulation of the epidemic dynamics. The results indicate that the observer performs effectively in estimating the number of individuals across various epidemic compartments. Additionally, the observer demonstrates robustness against parameter uncertainties. These findings suggest that the proposed observer-based approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of epidemic models. To our knowledge, this research represents the first application of state assessment to epidemic dynamics. The developed observer-based approach offers a new perspective for designing control strategies in epidemic management. The associated dynamic programming equation provides a foundation for formulating and solving control problems in this domain. Ultimately, the optimal control policy derived from this equation can serve as a valuable tool for decision-making in managing epidemics. This study thus offers a fresh perspective for epidemic control, with potential applications in controlling the spread of the virus and mitigating the impact of lockdowns. The proposed observer-based approach is also extensible to other infectious diseases. The results herein can contribute to the development of new methods for epidemic control. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the state assessment framework for epidemic dynamics; Section 3 develops the observer; Section 4 presents the observer-based solution; Section 5 provides a simulation example; and Section 6 concludes the study. This study investigates the stability of Kerr-lens mode-locking in a Ti:sapphire laser by applying ABCD matrix formalism to a resonator equipped with two cylindrical lenses. By analyzing the eigenmodes, we derived closed-form expressions for the spot size and beam waist location. Furthermore, we established stability criteria for the resonator and determined the stability region as a function of the angle between the cylindrical lenses. These findings are supported by specific experimental results. Additionally, we have developed a computational tool to determine fundamental experimental parameters, which is accessible at the following link: https://github.com/ultrafastlab/cklm. This tool enables users to explore the stability region and calculate the spot size location and magnitude for various configurations. We anticipate that the results and this tool will prove valuable for designing and optimizing Kerr-lens mode-locking lasers. The tool's source code is available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/ultrafastlab/cklm. Finally, we acknowledge the valuable discussions with Prof. A. V. Sokolov. This paper introduces a new asynchronous online federated learning framework designed to address nonlinear regression tasks where data is continuously streamed to multiple clients. The primary innovation lies in its ability to manage diverse computational resources across these clients. To achieve this, we propose a novel asynchronous online learning algorithm that integrates a distributed sliding window with a dynamic update rule. This mechanism enables the global model to adapt to varying computation speeds by automatically adjusting the frequency of updates received from each client. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed framework, establishing bounds on both sublinear regret and average risk. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our approach effectively handles heterogeneous computation capabilities and surpasses existing methods in terms of prediction accuracy. We introduce a three-dimensional photonic band gap (3D-PBG) photonic crystal (PhC) structure designed to function as a back reflector for thin-film solar cells. This PhC-based reflector redirects both direct and diffuse incident light into silicon layers thinner than the standard diffusion length for minority carriers. By leveraging the PhC's 3D-PBG property, the structure reflects a broad spectrum of light back into the silicon layer. We demonstrate that a 3D-PBG PhC slab is more effective than a conventional metallic back reflector at trapping light within thin silicon layers. Furthermore, we show that a PhC slab with a periodicity of approximately 100 nm can achieve near-complete light absorption in silicon layers as thin as 10 nm. This capability is attributed to the PhC slab's ability to couple incident light into the topological edge states located at the interface between the slab and the surrounding medium. Additionally, we illustrate that the PhC slab can be engineered to support multiple topological edge states, thereby extending the spectral range over which the PhC slab acts as a back reflector. Finally, we demonstrate that the PhC slab can be designed to support topological edge states at oblique angles of incidence, enabling the reflection of light incident at oblique angles. These findings suggest that 3D-PBG PhC structures offer a promising avenue for developing high-efficiency, low-cost solar cells. Our results are supported by comprehensive numerical simulations. This paper introduces a new formula for tetration and provides a detailed derivation. We demonstrate that, given a complex number $z$, the expression $f(z)$ exhibits asymptotic periodicity with respect to $\log(z)$ as the real part of $z$ increases. Furthermore, we establish that $f(z)$ displays asymptotic homogeneity of degree zero regarding the variable $\log(z)$. Leveraging these two asymptotic properties, we derive a formula that offers an alternative perspective on the tetration problem. Additionally, we present a method for calculating the fractional iterate of any entire function, provided its Taylor coefficients decrease rapidly enough to ensure the convergence of a specific series. Finally, we apply this methodology to address the problem of calculating the fractional iterate of the function $e^z - z$. In this specific instance, we obtain an explicit solution for the function $F(z)$, which represents the $1/2$-th iterate of $e^z - z$. We also provide numerical values for the coefficients of the Taylor series of $F(z)$ and compare them with those of the function $G(z)$, whose coefficients were computed using the method described in our earlier publication, "An Algorithm for the Computation of the Fractional Iterate of an Entire Function." The comparison reveals that the coefficients of $F(z)$ are significantly smaller in magnitude than those of $G(z)$. This finding suggests that the approach proposed in this paper may be more effective for computing the fractional iterates of entire functions with rapidly growing coefficients.

The study investigates the magnetic properties of the centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$, a material characterized by strong quasi-two-dimensionality. Using a combination of experimental data and theoretical modeling, we determined the magnetic structure and analyzed the temperature dependence of key parameters, including the Néel temperature ($T_N$), magnetic moment, and anisotropy. We demonstrate that the magnetic structure arises from the competition between two exchange interactions, $J_1$ and $J_2$, which are derived from the hopping integrals $t_1$ and $t_2$. Furthermore, we show that the hopping integral $t_2$ is highly sensitive to the ionic radius of the A-site ion, a factor that significantly influences the magnetic behavior. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the broader class of centered honeycomb antiferromagnets. The experimental findings are supported by density functional theory calculations. This paper introduces a model designed to estimate the power of nonlinear distortions in two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) formats. This study examines the influence of coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole modes on these excitations in $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg. Utilizing the random phase approximation, we calculated the energy and strength of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance (IGMR) for both nuclei. The results indicate that the IGMR energy in $^{28}$Si is 13.56 MeV, which is 1.1 MeV lower than the experimental value of 14.6 MeV. Conversely, in $^{24}$Mg, the calculated IGMR energy of 15.0 MeV aligns well with the measured value of 15.1 MeV. Furthermore, we computed the E0 strength distribution for both nuclei and observed that the IGMR strength is significantly depleted in $^{28}$Si compared to $^{24}$Mg. This depletion is attributed to the mixing of IGMR strength with quadrupole strength, a phenomenon that is more pronounced in $^{28}$Si than in $^{24}$Mg. Consequently, the study underscores the critical role of coupling between giant monopole and quadrupole resonances in determining IGMR properties. Additionally, we calculated the E2 strength distribution for both isotopes and found that the E2 strength is substantially reduced in $^{28}$Si relative to $^{24}$Mg. This reduction is attributed to the mixing of quadrupole strength with monopole strength, which is more significant in $^{28}$Si than in $^{24}$Mg. Finally, we conclude that the coupling between giant monopole and quadrupole excitations is essential for accurately describing the properties of the IGMR. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled systems featuring Coulomb resistance. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, the closed-loop system's behavior can be mirrored by a hybrid system, enabling the application of hybrid system theory to analyze the open-loop system. Furthermore, we establish that local exponential convergence to a periodic trajectory is achievable through a stabilizing feedback regulation law. These theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations. The proposed methodology is applicable to various mechanical systems, including those with hysteretic friction, where the stick-slip dynamics are modeled as hybrid systems. Additionally, the results hold significance for hybrid feedback control design, where control laws are synthesized using hybrid system techniques. The paper begins by presenting a mechanical example to illustrate the analysis and synthesis results. Subsequently, we outline the methodology for analyzing stick-slip and periodic trajectory convergence in feedback-regulated systems with Coulomb resistance. Finally, we present a feedback control law designed to achieve local exponential convergence to a periodic trajectory. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the motivating example; Section 3 addresses the analysis of stick-slip and periodic trajectory convergence; Section 4 details the synthesis of a feedback control law for local exponential convergence to a periodic trajectory; and Section 5 concludes the study.

Keywords: Stick-slip, hybrid systems, feedback control, periodic trajectory convergence.

This paper introduces a new risk management framework grounded in Bellman equations, which we term the Profound Bellman Risk Management (PBRM) approach. By extending the scope of risk measures, this method offers a more comprehensive solution to risk management challenges. The study begins by defining the Profound Risk Measure (PRM) and its associated density function. It subsequently demonstrates that the density function serves as a risk measure itself, thereby establishing a recursive property for PRM. Leveraging this recursion, the paper develops a Bellman equation-based solution to address the Markov Decision Process (MDP) problem. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to validate the proposed method. The results indicate that the approach yields solutions comparable to traditional methods while simultaneously managing risk. Additionally, the application of this framework to portfolio optimization is explored. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the proposed Bellman equation-based solution provides an effective means for risk management. Sequential recommender systems are widely used to suggest the next item based on a user's purchase history. However, these systems often overlook the fact that items are purchased for specific purposes, which can be inferred from the sequence of intent-driven acquisitions. This paper introduces the Hidden User Intent (HUI) framework, which models a user's purchase history as a Markov chain where the observed item sequence is driven by an underlying Markov chain of latent user intents. We demonstrate that the HUI framework is mathematically equivalent to a specific type of hidden Markov model (HMM) and can be efficiently solved using the forward-backward algorithm. Furthermore, we find that incorporating latent intents into sequential recommenders significantly enhances performance. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of the HUI framework through experiments on a real-world dataset. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1995/HUI. This paper investigates the double confluent Heun equation (DCHE) within the context of one-dimensional quantum mechanics. We demonstrate that the equation's singularity structure can be derived from the Coulomb problem by applying a specific canonical transformation in phase space. This transformation induces a symmetric unfolding of the DCHE's outset, transforming it into a flat configuration. Furthermore, we establish that the canonical momentum corresponding to the unfolded outset functions as a quantum number. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for the integrability of the problem. These results are anticipated to be applicable to other instances of the DCHE. Additionally, we explore the connection between our approach and the recently proposed "canonical unfolding" method. Finally, we outline a potential application of these findings to the construction of a solvable model for a one-dimensional quantum dot. Throughout this work, we adhere to the $\hbar=1$ convention. We examine the statistical evaluation of a rank-one matrix $M^*$ under the null hypothesis that its entries are independent and identically distributed with mean zero. This analysis focuses on scenarios where the matrix exhibits groupwise heterogeneity, meaning the non-zero mean signal is confined to specific sub-blocks. We derive the fundamental limits for any estimator that remains invariant under permutations within these sub-blocks. These limits are expressed as a function of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the relative sizes of the sub-blocks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these limits are achievable by a plug-in estimator that utilizes the optimal rank-one solution under the respective groupwise heterogeneity assumptions. Finally, we apply these findings to the problem of detecting groupwise heterogeneity in bipartite networks. In this context, we show that the fundamental limit for the optimal detector remains identical regardless of whether the network is assumed to be homogeneous or to possess groupwise heterogeneity. Additionally, we prove that a simple plug-in estimator can achieve this optimal detection rate. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations. The study of topological materials has traditionally been confined to systems possessing specific symmetries, such as time-reversal, particle-hole, and chiral symmetries. This article introduces a new topological framework for materials that lack these conventional symmetries. By employing a generalized unitary transformation, we demonstrate that the absence of standard symmetries does not preclude the existence of topological structures. We define a novel topological invariant known as the winding number and establish its connection to the Chern number. Furthermore, we investigate topological models under these new conditions, revealing that the winding number can be altered through the breaking of spatial symmetries. Finally, we propose a topological representation of the wave function that remains valid even without any symmetries. These findings are validated through numerical simulations. Our research expands the scope of topological material research beyond symmetry-protected systems and offers a fresh perspective on the field. Additionally, the proposed topological representation of the wave function may find applications in quantum information science. Our results are anticipated to be valuable for advancing the study of topological materials. This paper introduces a decentralized regulation strategy for linear multi-channel networks that ensures stability, robustness, and disturbance attenuation. The proposed solution enables each channel to operate independently with its own local feedback loop, maintaining distributed stability and robustness even when channels are interconnected. This distributed regulation framework is applicable to a wide range of continuous-time linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, including those that are non-minimum phase, unstable, or unstable delay systems. The paper provides a geometric characterization of the set of regulators capable of achieving these objectives and outlines a distributed algorithm to compute them. Furthermore, an explicit parameterization of the set of distributed regulators is derived, which allows for the selection of a specific regulator to meet a prescribed $H_{\infty}$ performance level. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a numerical example involving a multi-channel network. Additionally, the methodology is extended to discrete-time LTI systems, with corresponding geometric characterizations and algorithms developed for both discrete and continuous cases. Finally, the paper presents a numerical example featuring a discrete-time multi-channel network. The significance of this work lies in its ability to achieve distributed regulation for systems that were previously considered unregulable under distributed control schemes. The resulting regulators are computationally efficient, enabling their implementation in real-time applications. The primary motivation for this research is the need for distributed control in large-scale systems, such as power grids and communication networks, where centralized control methods are often impractical due to scalability constraints. By utilizing distributed control, these systems can be regulated effectively while remaining robust to communication failures and capable of adapting to changes in system topology. The paper concludes by discussing potential applications of the proposed regulators in various domains. In epidemiological research, missing data frequently necessitate assumptions to ensure valid inferences. While researchers often assume data are missing completely at random (MCAR), this assumption is often untenable. When data are missing not at random (MNAR), the likelihood function must be adjusted to account for the missingness mechanism. This paper introduces the E-value, a Bayesian approach designed to quantify sensitivity to the assumption of randomness in absences. The E-value represents the minimum multiplicative increase in the probability of the data required to render an MCAR assumption plausible. We demonstrate the E-value's utility through a simulation study and a real-world application involving the association between maternal smoking during pregnancy and preterm birth. Furthermore, we outline a method for estimating the E-value using a Monte Carlo approach. This framework is implemented in the R package `bayesens`, which is available at https://github.com/andrewjg/bayesens. The package includes a simulation function, a real-world example, and an estimator for the E-value. We conclude by discussing the E-value's advantages and limitations. Ultimately, the E-value offers a quantitative metric to assess the impact of non-random missing data on study conclusions. By enabling researchers to evaluate how sensitive their findings are to the MCAR assumption, the E-value facilitates more robust and reliable conclusions. Additionally, it provides a framework for communicating the influence of missing data to a broader audience. Ultimately, the E-value serves as a valuable tool for evaluating the validity of inferences drawn from studies with absent data. This study examines the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane, deriving its full set of $q$-deformed linear symmetries that constitute the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. We introduce WORTH, a system designed to automatically generate large-scale, fine-grained, and geospatially localized tags for urban environments. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging has long been a cornerstone of computational linguistics, serving as a vital tool for language analysis. However, historical collections present unique challenges, as the meaning of words often shifts over time, rendering modern taggers ineffective without substantial adaptation. While previous research has explored adapting taggers using either static or dynamic training data, this study evaluates the performance of POS taggers trained on static corpora versus those trained on temporally evolving corpora. The findings indicate that taggers trained on dynamic data achieve significantly higher accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a novel forecasting approach that predicts the most probable taggers for specific time periods, thereby enhancing the reliability of the resulting taggers. This method offers a dependable solution for annotating historical collections, enabling researchers to efficiently conduct diachronic analyses. The proposed system is fully automated and accessible at https://pos-fcst.org. The associated code and data are available at https://github.com/mauricio-garcia/pos-fcst. Our results demonstrate that taggers trained on dynamic corpora outperform those on static ones, and the introduced forecasting method improves the reliability of annotated historical texts. These contributions provide a robust foundation for the annotation of historical collections and facilitate diachronic analysis. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 outlines the methodology; Section 4 presents the experimental results; and Section 5 concludes with a discussion of the findings. This paper investigates two distinct non-smooth regularity frameworks for partial differential equations. The first framework addresses a broad category of non-smooth functions defined on open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are differentiable almost everywhere and whose non-differentiable points are confined to a closed set of Hausdorff dimension $s < n-1$. We demonstrate that if the non-differentiable set possesses a non-differentiable measure of dimension strictly less than $s$, these functions satisfy the same local properties—such as the chain rule, product rule, and integration by parts—that they would in smooth settings. The second framework applies to non-smooth vector fields exhibiting a non-integrable cross product structure, which are prevalent in various physical contexts. We establish that these vector fields are integrable in a generalized sense, enabling the application of Stokes' theorem and the formula for the divergence of a cross product within specific domains. These findings are utilized to derive novel non-smooth regularity results for specific non-linear partial differential equations. The study employs a unified approach grounded in geometric measure theory, which we believe is applicable to a wide array of non-smooth functions and non-smooth vector fields. Consequently, this methodology offers a versatile tool for analyzing non-linear hyperbolic conservation laws and related physical systems. The work is highly technical, with the majority of proofs deferred to the appendix. Additionally, we present a series of illustrative examples and non-examples to elucidate the theory and demonstrate its application to specific conservation laws. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential avenues for future research. This work is a collaborative effort by the authors. The development of smart cities is driven by the need to enhance citizens' quality of life. To ensure these initiatives meet user needs, it is essential to gather and analyze citizen expectations, subsequently designing and implementing solutions that address them. This paper introduces a formal specification approach for requirements, utilizing a technique that transforms natural language into formal specifications through a series of structured questions. We have developed an automated technique to facilitate this process and created a smart assistant application to support requirement engineers in analyzing user requirements. This application assists in converting natural language expectations into formal specifications by prompting developers with a sequence of questions. The proposed method was validated through a case study involving the development of a smart parking solution. The results demonstrate that the approach is effective, efficient, and capable of generating formal specifications that are both accurate and complete. Furthermore, the questions generated by the technique are intuitive and easy for non-expert developers to understand and answer. Finally, the questions are designed to be independent of specific formal languages, allowing developers to choose any language to represent the specifications. Consequently, this method is well-suited for smart city projects, which typically involve developers lacking formal specification expertise. Additionally, the approach is highly adaptable to various development scenarios and can be easily extended to other domains. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SmartAssis/SmartAssistant. This work was conducted within the SmartCity4Dev research project, which focuses on developing smart city solutions through a collaborative effort between academia and industry. The project's primary objective is to create a framework that enables the development of smart city applications by a diverse range of actors, including domain experts, software developers, and hardware engineers. This framework aims to facilitate the analysis, specification, and development of applications that improve citizens' quality of life. The questions generated by the SmartAssistant are derived from the SmartCity4Dev framework, which is detailed in our previous research. This framework is a formal specification language that supports the analysis and specification of requirements, design, and development activities. It is both domain-independent and formal language-independent, allowing developers to select any language to express specifications. The framework has been successfully applied in various contexts, including the development of smart parking solutions, smart lighting systems, and smart waste management systems. Concealing errors within quantum circuits is a recognized strategy for lowering the error rate of concealed operations. This study introduces a novel method called the concealed inverse protocol, which utilizes concealed errors to eliminate other errors within superconducting quantum circuits. The protocol is specifically tailored for superconducting quantum devices, with its implementation analyzed in the context of the IBM quantum apparatus QASM-14. Our findings demonstrate that this approach can diminish the error rate of concealed inverse operations by up to 80%. Furthermore, we illustrate that applying this method to multi-qubit gates, such as the Toffoli gate, can achieve comparable error reductions. These results indicate that the concealed inverse protocol serves as an effective error reduction technique for superconducting quantum devices. Additionally, the protocol can be integrated with other methods, including quantum error correction, to further enhance the performance of superconducting quantum systems.
