This paper investigates the conditions under which a regular category admits a faithful and exact functor mapping into Set, which would represent preorder structures via cocartesian diagrams. We examine these conditions within the framework of locally multiplicative categories, defined as categories where every pullback is a product. Our findings demonstrate that in this specific context, the existence of such a functor is contingent upon an equivalence connection between the multiplicative and cartesian structures. This concept was originally proposed by M. Makkai and has recently been applied in the study of regular categories within a many-sorted setting. We provide a detailed analysis of this notion and its connection to equivalence of categories, followed by an exploration of various examples and counterexamples. Finally, we establish that any multiplicative category where all pullbacks are products possesses an equivalence connection, thereby proving that the question of representing preorders via cocartesian diagrams of objects and morphisms is meaningful in the context of multiplicative categories. Additionally, we present a novel construction of such a functor for any multiplicative category where pullbacks are products, utilizing a recently developed concept of a "weak multiplicative functor." This approach offers a new perspective on the relationship between multiplicative and cartesian structures. We further show that this construction can be adapted to the many-sorted setting, yielding a multiplicative graph as an alternative to the many-sorted category previously employed in this context. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our work and the theory of distributive categories, specifically regarding the existence of a strong functor from preorders into cocartesian diagrams within multiplicative categories. We conclude by outlining several open problems. The present work extends the author's doctoral thesis, which was supervised by M. Makkai. Maritime and offshore sectors rely on extreme environmental data to evaluate the safety and resilience of structures against rare events. To address this, we introduce a new method for estimating extreme sea states by combining the multivariate spatial conditional peaks (MSCP) model with the generalized Pareto distribution. This approach is validated using a real-world dataset of significant wave heights and peak wave directions from the North Sea. The resulting estimates provide detailed profiles of extreme sea states, including significant wave height, wave direction, wave period, and spectral width. Furthermore, the method enables the calculation of return levels for these variables at various locations, offering a more comprehensive understanding of extreme conditions than previous techniques. These findings are crucial for risk assessment and the design of infrastructure within the maritime and offshore industries. The R package `spatial.conditional` is available to facilitate the implementation of this methodology. The code and data required to replicate the analysis can be found at https://github.com/JulianKneib/SPC_Paper. Current vision-language models (VLMs) typically rely on image-text pairs for training, where text descriptions are generated based on images. However, these models often suffer from inaccurate descriptions that introduce noise into the learning process. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that generates visual-directed text descriptions to enhance VLMs. Specifically, we leverage a text-to-image model to create images from prompts, which are then paired with existing image-text pairs to train the VLM. This framework, named VT-CLIP, leverages the visual information within the generated images to guide the VLM in learning more precise representations. Extensive experiments across various VLMs demonstrate that VT-CLIP significantly boosts performance, achieving up to a 1.8% improvement on zero-shot classification tasks. Furthermore, our method proves effective even when using synthetic image-text pairs derived from object detection and segmentation tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/lyg1999/VT-CLIP. We introduce a quantum algorithm designed to invert an arbitrary matrix $A$ acting on $\mathbb{C}^d$, which is provided as a black box. This method achieves an $O(\log d)$ improvement in complexity compared to the state-of-the-art technique by Childs and Wood. The approach is applicable to noisy matrices that are effectively simulatable, such as those arising in quantum chemistry. Our procedure involves preparing a specific state using $O(\log d)$ additional qubits and subsequently applying a sequence of $O(\log d)$ operator switches. The primary complexity metrics are the count of queries to $A$ and the number of quantum gates required. We demonstrate that for matrices $A$ satisfying these criteria, the query complexity is $O(\kappa_A \epsilon^{-1/2} \log d)$ and the gate complexity is $O(\kappa_A \epsilon^{-1/2} \log^2 d)$, where $\kappa_A$ represents the condition number of $A$ and $\epsilon$ denotes the target success probability. Furthermore, we establish that any algorithm utilizing $O(1)$ extra qubits cannot achieve a complexity better than $O(\kappa_A \epsilon^{-1/2})$. Our findings are supported by a rigorous analysis of the algorithm's behavior within the presence of noise. Additionally, we present a numerical simulation of the algorithm's performance on the IBM quantum computer, IBMQ\_Santiago. This simulation indicates that the algorithm is viable for current noisy hardware, provided the matrix $A$ possesses a sufficiently low condition number. Finally, we discuss the algorithm's potential utility in the context of the quantum-enhanced linear system solver. We demonstrate that the compact Hilbert polynomial of a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ serves as an invariant for its completion $\widehat{R}$, provided that $\widehat{R}$ possesses a positive dimensional irreducible minimal prime. This finding yields a novel characterization of $F$-regular rings within the context of positive characteristic. Specifically, we establish that for a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ of positive characteristic, $R$ is $F$-regular if and only if, for every $\mathfrak{q} \subsetneq \mathfrak{m}$, the compact Hilbert polynomial of $R/\mathfrak{q}$ exhibits strictly positive leading coefficients. Furthermore, we provide an explicit example of a local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ where the completion $\widehat{R}$ is $F$-regular, yet $R$ itself is not $F$-regular. Finally, we offer an alternative proof of the fact that the completion map preserves $F$-regularity for local rings. Additionally, we present an example of a local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ where the completion map transforms $R$ into a ring that is both $F$-regular and Cohen-Macaulay, despite $R$ lacking the Cohen-Macaulay property. These examples are constructed using determinantal rings. The discussion concludes with an exploration of the relationship between the compact Hilbert polynomial and the Hilbert polynomial of the associated graded ring of a local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$. In particular, we construct a local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ where the associated graded ring $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)$ is Cohen-Macaulay, yet the completion $\widehat{R}$ fails to be Cohen-Macaulay. This example also illustrates a scenario where the compact Hilbert polynomial of $R$ differs from that of $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)$. The examples utilized in this paper are derived from toric rings. To facilitate this approach, we develop a method for computing the compact Hilbert polynomial of a toric ring $\mathrm{Spec}(R)$ given the fan $\Sigma$ and the lattice polyhedron $P$ defining $R$. This technique is also applicable to toric rings of positive dimension.

The framework supports the encoding of annotations across various imaging modalities, including 2D images, 3D volumes, and segmentation masks. Additionally, it provides a specialized API for handling machine learning results, such as classification scores and bounding boxes, which are common in these fields. The surface chemistry of ultrathin films is a critical factor influencing their electronic properties. This study investigates the surface composition and its impact on the electronic structure of epitaxial V$_2$O$_3$ films grown on SiO$_2$(100) substrates. By employing X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and low-energy electron diffraction (LEED), we identified oxygen vacancies at the surface, which were subsequently passivated through annealing in an oxygen atmosphere. Low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM) and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) revealed that these vacancies induce a metal-insulator transition in the bulk vanadium oxide. Furthermore, we observed that oxygen vacancies generate a surface state within the bulk band gap. These findings offer valuable insights into the surface chemistry of vanadium oxides and the mechanisms driving the metal-insulator transition. Ultimately, this research underscores the pivotal role of surface composition in governing the physical properties of ultrathin films. This work investigates the connection between conjugate connections on Lie algebras and the associated Lie-Poisson structures. We demonstrate that any conjugation automorphism on a Lie algebra induces a corresponding Poisson diffeomorphism on its dual. Furthermore, we examine the Chevalley conjugation on real forms of simple Lie algebras and establish that it generates specific Poisson diffeomorphisms on the duals of these Lie-Poisson manifolds. As applications, we explore how these findings relate to the Lie-Poisson formulation of the classical rigid body problem and its Lie-Poisson dual. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between the classical Lie algebraic $R$-matrix and the classical Riemannian $L$-operator derived from a bi-invariant metric on a Lie group. Finally, we highlight the role of Chevalley conjugation in the Lie-Poisson description of the classical Lie algebraic $R$-matrix. These results offer new perspectives on the classical rigid body problem and the topological structure of the adjoint orbit. The paper concludes with an appendix detailing the Chevalley conjugation for all simple Lie algebras. This paper introduces a compressible Navier-Stokes solver designed for applications in fluid dynamics, aerodynamics, and combustion. The development leverages several principles from the managing conservation principles, including a finite volume scheme, a thermodynamic equilibrium model, and a finite-time exact Riemann solver. Additionally, a finite difference approach is employed to compute viscous and heat flux terms. The study details the implementation of these concepts and presents various numerical test cases to demonstrate the solver's capabilities. These examples cover a range of scenarios, from incompressible flows to shock waves, as well as thermodynamic equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. The results indicate that the solver performs effectively and efficiently across all tested scenarios. Furthermore, the numerical experiments confirm that the method is highly accurate, with all test cases passing the respective order of accuracy tests. This study evaluates various machine learning algorithms to forecast whether a bank loan will default. We gathered a dataset of 10,000 NPL (Non-Performing Loan) cases from a bank in the Middle East. After preprocessing the data and selecting relevant features, we applied feature selection techniques to identify the most significant variables. Additionally, we analyzed feature importance to determine which variables most strongly influence loan defaults. This research offers valuable insights for both data scientists and bank management, enabling the development of predictive models that can prevent future loan defaults. This paper introduces a new image identification architecture designed to leverage orientation information within image features. The proposed Orientation Convolutional Architecture (OCA) integrates a novel orientation convolutional layer that accepts tensors as input and produces tensors as output. We demonstrate that OCA surpasses traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in identifying images from the Caltech-101 dataset. Furthermore, we show that OCA exceeds the performance of a specialized architecture, known as the orientation convolutional neural network (OCNN), which was originally developed to utilize orientation features. Additionally, we establish that OCA achieves these results with reduced computational complexity. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of OCA's ability to extract orientation features and outline potential applications for future research. We introduce a novel trace formula that connects the twisted trace of the relative Langlands-Sharkey operator with the trace of the super-Dolbeault-Laplace operator on a product of Riemann surfaces. This operator is defined on a specific interval situated on a geodesic curve within a Teichmüller space of a surface of revolution. We subsequently derive formulas for both sides of this equation and examine the asymptotic behavior as the trace on the left-hand side tends toward infinity. Finally, we explore the asymptotic dynamics of the trace on the right-hand side, demonstrating that it adheres to a novel type of relative trace equation. This new equation can be regarded as a non-linear extension of a previously established trace relation by Li and Zudilin. Furthermore, we establish a link between this novel equation and a specific second-order differential equation with a regular singular point at zero. In the appendix, we provide a concise overview of the background of the relative trace equation. This work serves as a sequel to the paper \cite{KKSZ2020}. We establish that the precision of the top quark mass determination from the 2011 CMS Run 1 data is limited by substantial flavor dependencies in both the cross section and $p_T$ spectra of top quarks. These dependencies, which are not adequately addressed in the analysis, stem from higher-order QCD corrections. Consequently, the current uncertainty of 1.1 GeV in the top quark mass is significantly larger than the statistical precision of 200 MeV. We propose that the mass should be derived from the ratio of the cross section to the $p_T$ spectrum, a method that eliminates these higher-order effects. Applying this approach to the CMS Run 1 data yields a top quark mass of $m_t = 173.2 \pm 0.3$ GeV. This result is robust against variations in the renormalization and factorization scales, as well as the parton distribution functions. Furthermore, the uncertainty is reduced by a factor of four compared to the CMS collaboration's published value. We also demonstrate that this method can be applied to the LHCb experiment. Utilizing LHCb data, we extract a forward rapidity $p_T$ spectrum for top quarks, which exhibits a strong dependence on the flavor of the incoming quark. This dependence is also attributed to higher-order QCD corrections. By combining the LHCb $p_T$ spectrum with the CMS rapidity distribution, we obtain a top quark mass of $m_t = 173.2 \pm 0.3$ GeV. This value is consistent with the CMS result and shows agreement with the ATLAS measurement of $m_t = 172.1 \pm 0.9$ GeV. Our findings suggest that the ATLAS uncertainty is similarly limited by flavor dependence, indicating that the top quark mass can be measured with a precision of 0.3 GeV using either CMS or LHCb data. This represents a significant improvement over the current ATLAS precision of 0.9 GeV. We conclude that the top quark mass is a well-defined observable that can be extracted from the CMS and LHCb data. However, we emphasize that the extraction method must account for higher-order QCD corrections to ensure the accuracy of the result. A graph $G$ is defined as nearly regular if the disparity between its maximum and minimum degrees does not exceed one. This paper investigates edge-coloring properties specific to such graphs. We demonstrate that for any integers $r$ and $k$ where $r \geq k \geq 2$, every connected nearly regular graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta(G) = \Delta(G)-1 \geq k$ admits a proper edge-coloring using $r$ colors such that every vertex $v$ possesses at least $\min\{n-1, \frac{n-1}{r}\}$ colors incident to it. Furthermore, for the specific case of $k=2$, we establish that each vertex $v$ can be assigned at least $\frac{n-1}{r}$ colors in an incident manner, ensuring that the remaining $r-1$ colors are applied to the edges not incident to $v$. These findings lead to the conclusion that for $r \geq 2$, any connected nearly regular graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta(G) \geq 2$ can be properly edge-colored with $r$ colors so that every vertex $v$ has at least $\frac{n-1}{r}$ colors incident to it, and the set of non-incident colors for $v$ forms a consecutive sequence of integers. Additionally, we provide a characterization of nearly regular graphs where $\delta(G)=1$ that are capable of being edge-colored with $r$ colors such that each vertex $v$ has at least $\frac{n-1}{r}$ colors incident to it, and the colors of the edges not incident to $v$ constitute a set of consecutive integers. Finally, we offer a sufficient condition under which a nearly regular graph $G$ with $\delta(G)=1$ admits a proper edge-coloring with $r$ colors where, for every vertex $v$, the colors of the non-incident edges are consecutive integers and the count of these colors is at least $\frac{n-1}{r+1}$. This condition is shown to hold true for all nearly regular graphs $G$ where $\delta(G) \geq 2$. The results presented herein extend and refine findings previously reported in \cite{MR3905000}. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and significant loss of life, prompting the urgent need for rapid and accurate diagnostic methods. While Computed Tomography (CT) scans are a primary tool for identifying lung infections, the high volume of daily requests has overwhelmed radiologists, necessitating more efficient processing techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that LCT-TDCN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an accuracy of 98.5% on the LIDC-IDRI dataset. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness against class imbalance, maintaining consistent performance across different data distributions. This study examines the spatial efficiency of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, which are essential for delivering broadband connectivity to remote areas. We introduce a method for calculating the number of satellites required to cover a specific region, utilizing a geometric model that incorporates the satellites' communication range and orbital altitude. Our findings indicate that for a given location, increasing the communication range results in a non-linear decrease in the required number of satellites. Additionally, we determined that for any specific communication range, there exists an optimal altitude that minimizes the satellite count needed to cover the target area. Finally, we demonstrate that this geometric approach can be extended to estimate the number of satellites needed to cover the entire Earth's surface. We introduce a novel mesh generation algorithm designed to produce coarse quadrilateral grids with elements of uniform size for CAD models. The process begins by creating an initial coarse triangulation, which is then converted into a quadrangulation. To ensure the resulting mesh meets the target coarse size, we formulate a linear optimization problem that maximizes the minimum element size across the entire mesh. By restricting the optimization variables to whole numbers, the solution yields a quadrangular mesh where the variation in element sizes is minimized. This approach is particularly effective for CAD models with intricate geometries, such as those featuring holes, protrusions, and curved surfaces. The method has been successfully applied to various model classes, including aircraft, automobiles, and human figures. Furthermore, we have developed an open-source software tool that implements this optimization-based quadrangulation technique. The software is capable of producing quadrangular meshes for CAD models that are ready for further refinement into high-quality, body-fitted, triangular finite element meshes. Finally, we demonstrate that this generalized theory remains invariant under a novel symmetry known as $U$-duality. In this context, the $S$-matrix is expressed in terms of a generalized charge vector that transforms as a vector under $U$-duality. InAs quantum wells situated on undoped InAs buffers are prone to electron accumulation at the interface between the well and the surface, which can elevate the Fermi level and cause unwanted fixation. This study examines how this fixation influences the photoluminescence (PL) properties of these structures. We demonstrate that annealing in an oxygen atmosphere effectively mitigates electron accumulation, thereby restoring the sample to its original PL characteristics. Furthermore, we show that this accumulation can be modeled using a simple two-level system. Finally, we provide a quantitative analysis of the surface states responsible for this accumulation. These findings are anticipated to be applicable to other III-V semiconductor systems. Additionally, the ability to control surface states offers a potential pathway for developing tunable optical devices. This tunability could be achieved through surface adsorption or by applying an external electric field. We illustrate this concept using a device consisting of a quantum well on a buffer, separated from a metal gate by an insulating barrier. Our calculations indicate that applying a gate voltage of approximately 10 V is sufficient to shift the Fermi level from the mid-gap position to the conduction band edge. Such a configuration could enable the creation of electro-optic modulators with bandwidths reaching into the gigahertz range. Finally, we discuss the potential impact of these results on the development of quantum information technologies. Specifically, we show that the fixation of the Fermi level can restrict the coherence times of quantum dots within the quantum well. However, annealing in an oxygen atmosphere can remove the surface states, thereby restoring the coherence times to their initial values. This underscores the critical importance of managing surface states when working with III-V semiconductor quantum structures. Ultimately, our results suggest that oxygen annealing is a vital step in the fabrication process for achieving high-performance quantum devices. We conclude by outlining several promising directions for future research. These include investigating the impact of surface states on quantum dot properties, exploring new methods for manipulating surface states, and developing novel applications for these tunable surface states. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for computing the optimal transport map between two $N \times N$ Gaussian measures on the plane, achieving both $O(N)$ runtime and quadratic precision. The method samples points from the 2D Gaussian map in a specific pattern: two rows are selected from each dimension, and these points are arranged into a triangular matrix following a collinear transport pattern. The resulting optimal transport map for this map is then used to construct the desired map for the 2D Gaussian. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the error and demonstrates its convergence to 0 as $N \to \infty$. The primary theoretical contribution is the proof that the error of the proposed map is bounded by the error of the collinear transport map. This reduces the problem to a one-dimensional case, which is solved using the 1D precise algorithm from [1]. The error analysis for the proposed algorithm is identical to that of [1]. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical results. The code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1234567890/rapid-sinkhorn.

The young, active M-dwarf AU Microscopii (AU Mic) hosts two known planets, b and c. This study utilizes Far Ultraviolet (FUV) observations from the Hubble Space Telescope to examine the star's chromospheric activity and its impact on the upper atmospheres of these planets. We analyzed 10 HST/STIS FUV spectra of AU Mic, covering a span of 10 years, to investigate the variability of the Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) emission line. Our results indicate that Ly$\alpha$ variability is not solely tied to flaring events; instead, it reflects both a persistent, variable component and transient flaring activity. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between the equivalent width of the Ly$\alpha$ line and the flux of the C IV 1548,167 \AA\ doublet, suggesting that the star's chromosphere is in a state of constant variability. By comparing these findings with the known orbital periods of planets b and c, we conclude that neither planet has a significant influence on the star's chromospheric activity. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the atmospheric evolution of the planets and the potential habitability of the system. This paper introduces a statistical approach to the Closest Neighbor Classification (CNC) problem that accounts for unequal data within groups. The study derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimated conditional distribution function (CDF) and distribution function (DF) under the assumption of balanced sampling, where the proportion of sampled units from each group converges to a constant as the sample size grows. Furthermore, it establishes the consistency of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) for the conditional CDF and CNC for a specific function under balanced sampling. Additionally, the authors develop a novel method termed the "balancing" procedure, which enables the consistent estimation of the conditional CDF even when sampling is not balanced. This is achieved by constructing a pseudo-sample that effectively mimics a balanced sample. The paper also proves the consistency of the NPMLE using this pseudo-sample. Finally, the theoretical findings are validated through a simulation study and an application to a real-world dataset. The results indicate that the balancing procedure performs well in scenarios where the number of observations from each group is small relative to the total sample size. However, the performance of the NPMLE derived from the pseudo-sample is highly sensitive to the sampling fraction in each group. Consequently, the study recommends that, whenever feasible, a balanced sampling design should be employed to ensure the NPMLE remains consistent. We present the second installment of a series identifying the most luminous quasars at high redshifts through the Ultra-bright High-redshift Quasar (UHQ) project. This study leverages the SkyMapper Southern Survey (SMSS) dataset, which covers 12,500 square degrees of the southern sky with a 5th magnitude limit. By cross-referencing SMSS data with the 2017 Quasar Catalogue (QSO-17), we identified 1,000 SMSS sources with no QSO-17 counterparts, subsequently filtering these candidates using multi-wavelength data and spectroscopy. The resulting sample comprises 12 UHQ quasars, including 10 new discoveries. These findings confirm the existence of a radiant "wall" at the extreme luminosity end of the quasar luminosity function, a phenomenon previously noted in the Northern Sky. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the UHQ sample exhibits a significantly flatter luminosity function compared to the broader QSO-17 sample, indicating that the radiant tail is not merely a minor extension of the main population but rather a distinct, separate population. We also report the discovery of a new luminous quasar at $z=6.11$ and a potential candidate at $z=7.08$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the evolution of the quasar luminosity function. The UHQ sample is accessible via the SMSS Data Release 3. We present detection of charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting island mediated by a quantum point, utilizing a gate electrode to sense the dot's electron population. This approach enables the study of tunneling mechanisms within a hybrid system that integrates a purely superconducting qubit with a charge-based qubit. The setup is highly relevant for developing hybrid quantum systems and for investigating fundamental aspects of charge noise in solid-state devices. This work introduces two novel contraction metrics tailored for entropy discontinuities in systems governed by preservation laws. The first metric is constructed using the derivatives of the entropy and the state variables, while the second relies on the derivatives of the state variables alone. We demonstrate that the second metric yields a broader class of discontinuities compared to the first. Furthermore, we establish that both metrics facilitate the derivation of sharp Rankine-Hugoniot conditions and facilitate the design of high-order well-balanced schemes. Finally, these metrics are applied to a specific model problem: a system of balance laws describing shallow water flow over a topography with a single critical point. In this application, the contractions are defined via the derivatives of the water depth and the bed elevation. This paper introduces a framework that leverages data to forecast, improve, and regulate the dynamics of networked processes. The approach relies on a novel, entirely data-driven method for learning the nonlinear dynamics of these processes, specifically targeting networked systems with nonlinear interactions. We demonstrate that this framework can be applied without requiring explicit knowledge of the underlying network structure. The core of the proposed method involves a nonlinear auto-regressive network with exogenous inputs (NARX) model, which is tailored to capture the nonlinear dynamics of networked processes by utilizing a tensor product of a linear auto-regressive model and a vector of linear cross-regressions. This technique is shown to be capable of identifying a nonlinear model that is data-consistent with the true process dynamics. The framework's efficacy is validated through its application to a networked Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method can accurately reconstruct the nonlinear dynamics of the networked SIS model using solely epidemic data, even in the absence of network structural information. Furthermore, the framework is demonstrated to achieve precise prediction of the networked SIS epidemic dynamics and to successfully regulate the epidemic spread by adjusting the infection rate. These findings suggest that the proposed approach holds significant potential for regulating the dynamics of networked processes. Additionally, the method is noted for its computational efficiency, as the learning algorithm can be implemented using standard convex optimization techniques. The paper concludes by outlining the method's limitations and proposing several avenues for future research. Finally, the source code for the proposed framework is made available online. This study examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability governing a liquid layer coating a cylindrical fiber, incorporating both surface tension and slip-augmented viscous resistance. By utilizing the Rayleigh-Plateau dispersion relation, we demonstrate that air slip within the bulk liquid reduces the growth rate of the instability, thereby delaying the formation of drops. Conversely, surface contamination further diminishes the growth rate by increasing the effective surface slip length. We analyze the critical conditions for the instability, accounting for slip-augmented viscous effects, and explore how air slip and surface contamination alter the wavelength of the most unstable mode. Finally, we validate our theoretical predictions against experimental data. The proposed model is applicable to various scenarios involving viscous liquid layers on fibers, including those found in microfluidic systems and biological contexts. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to analyze the instability of liquid layers surrounding other geometries, such as droplets or bubbles. These findings hold significant potential for advancing the design of microfluidic devices and biomimetic systems. Furthermore, the theoretical framework may offer insights into the growth of bacteria and viruses on fiber surfaces. Ultimately, this work advances our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms driving the Rayleigh-Plateau instability in viscous liquid layers. **Background:** Scoliosis is a condition characterized by an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine. Early detection and monitoring of scoliosis are crucial for determining the most effective treatment. Ultrasound (US) imaging has emerged as a valuable tool for diagnosing and monitoring this condition. While US offers a non-invasive, radiation-free method for assessing spinal curvature, it requires skilled operators. To address this limitation, we developed a robotic ultrasound system capable of automatically scanning the spine. This system employs a 2D ultrasound probe mounted on a robotic arm to perform automated scanning, with an integrated vision system guiding the probe to the target area. The system's US images are processed by a deep learning model to generate spinal curvature measurements.

**Objectives:** This study aims to evaluate the dependability of the automatic ultrasound system for scoliosis assessment by comparing its performance against manual ultrasound scanning conducted by experts.

**Methods:** Scoliosis was simulated in a healthy spine using a bending device. Ultrasound imaging was performed on these spines using both the automatic system and by expert operators. The ultrasound images were analyzed by a deep learning model to calculate spinal curvature. The automatic system's results were compared with those from the experts. Additionally, the repeatability of the automatic system was assessed.

**Results:** The ultrasound images obtained by the automatic system were comparable to those produced by experts. The mean absolute error between the automatic system and expert measurements was 1.11° ± 1.01°. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for the automatic system was 0.99, indicating high reliability.

**Conclusion:** The ultrasound images generated by the automatic system are highly comparable to those by experts, demonstrating that the system is a dependable tool for scoliosis evaluation. This system can assist clinicians in performing ultrasound examinations, thereby enhancing the efficiency of scoliosis assessment. Future research will focus on testing the system on patients with scoliosis.

**Keywords:** Scoliosis, Ultrasound, Robotic Arm, Deep Learning, Dependability.

This study introduces a novel, non-statistical approach for generating synthetic speech of varying lengths. The method utilizes a median-driven technique to identify and extract recurring, non-overlapping segments from input audio. These extracted segments are then reused to produce speech with adjustable durations. The findings indicate that this procedure successfully reduces speech duration across a broad spectrum of target lengths. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the quality of the output remains consistent regardless of the desired length. The proposed method is applicable to any speech recognition system, including those based on deep learning, and can be implemented without requiring modifications to the underlying acoustic or language models. Additionally, the approach is versatile enough to handle diverse speech input types, such as continuous or discrete outputs. The study also explores the application of this length adjustment technique in the context of privacy protection. Experimental results confirm that the procedure effectively conceals the original speaker's identity. Finally, the paper examines the impact of different target lengths on both the quality and privacy efficacy of the synthetic speech. The authors conclude that this non-statistical method offers a more efficient solution for length adjustment compared to existing statistical approaches. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/Median-Driven-Length-Adjustment. The paper is available in both English and Hindi. The escalating prevalence of hate speech on the internet has sparked significant concern, prompting numerous research initiatives aimed at mitigating its impact. This paper introduces a novel model designed to detect hate speech by automatically extracting domain-specific features. The model employs a domain-aware dictionary to identify and extract features from target and ideology groups within hate speech contexts. To capture the semantic relationships between these groups and the content, we utilize a feature graph representation. Furthermore, we propose a feature graph attention network that integrates extracted features with original text features to identify hateful utterances. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in detecting hate speech. Additionally, we present a visualized analysis of the learned features and their connections to achieve superior performance. The code and data associated with this work can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/FGA-HateSpeech. Finally, we hope this research will inspire future efforts to develop domain-aware models for hate speech detection. The paper is available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.00202. We introduce a quadrature technique for evaluating the electron density of a molecule across a three-dimensional continuum. The approach begins by defining a set of polyhedra that partition the molecular space. We then identify a series of sites situated on the faces of these polyhedra, ensuring that the electron density at each site can be determined with high precision. Finally, we construct a quadrature formula utilizing these sites and their corresponding weights. This formula is capable of being applied iteratively over a sequence of subdomains within the continuum. The method has been implemented in the program Q-Chem, and we provide performance benchmarks for both isolated molecules and periodic systems. These results demonstrate that the quadrature achieves high accuracy with minimal computational overhead. Furthermore, we show that the proposed approach can be integrated with the quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM) to facilitate the analysis of periodic systems. Specifically, we illustrate how QTAIM can be employed to investigate charge transfer in a series of organic donor-acceptor materials. Our findings indicate that the quadrature method offers a straightforward and efficient means for analyzing electron density in both isolated molecules and periodic systems. Finally, we discuss potential future applications of this technique. The source code for the quadrature method is accessible at https://github.com/qchem/qchem/tree/master/src/continuum. The construction of this framework relies on the Hopf fibration, while its power coordinates are defined using directed areas. We demonstrate that the power coordinates for directed areas satisfy the same algebraic relations as those in the directed line framework, thereby enabling the formulation of quaternion-like formulas for 3D space. Furthermore, we establish that the power framework for directed areas is equivalent to the power framework for oriented projective plane. Finally, we illustrate several applications of this framework, including the representation of 3D space, projective transformations, and the derivation of quaternion-like formulas. Additionally, we show that the power coordinates for directed areas can be utilized to define the power coordinates for oriented points. Hothouse Earth represents a potential future state where elevated greenhouse gas concentrations trigger a self-reinforcing warming cycle, characterized by a significant rise in global mean temperature alongside a marked increase in the frequency of extreme precipitation events. This study examines the mechanisms driving these extremes within a hothouse climate, utilizing a simplified radiative-convective model to represent a Venus-like atmosphere. We demonstrate that the primary driver of extreme precipitation in this regime is the amplification of atmospheric moisture transport, which scales exponentially with temperature. Furthermore, we show that the probability of precipitation extremes follows a power law, with an exponent that decreases as temperature rises. Finally, we analyze the role of cloud feedbacks in shaping these extremes, revealing that while clouds enhance precipitation, they do not alter the power-law exponent. These findings are derived from a framework that integrates the Clausius-Clapeyron law, atmospheric moisture transport, and saturation vapor pressure. Our results indicate that the mechanisms governing precipitation extremes in a hothouse climate differ fundamentally from those in current climates. These outcomes are anticipated to hold true for both Earth and other planetary atmospheres under hothouse conditions. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/RCM. The efficacy of deep learning models is significantly compromised by noisy labels, a challenge that is particularly acute in medical image categorization due to the high cost and time required for expert annotation. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called the Bayesian Analytics Guided Label Restoration Mechanism (BAGLRM), which mitigates label noise through the integration of deep learning and Bayesian analytics. This approach employs a deep convolutional neural network to estimate the posterior distribution of class labels, utilizing a Bayesian analysis module to refine noisy labels based on the confidence levels of individual predictions. Subsequently, a confidence level estimator determines the certainty of each sample, guiding the deep learning model to optimize its loss function using the refined labels. Extensive experiments across three medical image datasets demonstrate that BAGLRM effectively reduces label noise and enhances the performance of various deep learning models. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the proposed framework is both effective and efficient. The results indicate that BAGLRM can improve accuracy by up to 10.1% in medical image categorization tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/BAGLRM. This study introduces a data-informed approach to enhance the predictive capabilities of coherent framework-based models for instantaneous boundary turbulence. The methodology involves modifying the instantaneous model for coherent structures (IMICS) to incorporate a new closure for the production of coherent structures (PICS), utilizing a machine learning algorithm. This algorithm is trained on high-fidelity data derived from direct numerical simulations (DNS) of a canonical wall-bounded flow: a channel flow at a bulk Reynolds number of 5000. The proposed data-informed model demonstrates superior performance compared to the original IMICS model, as evidenced by more accurate predictions of Reynolds shear stress and the mean velocity profile. Furthermore, the model effectively captures the dynamics of coherent structures, including their generation, evolution, and dissipation. The findings indicate that the proposed model holds significant potential for enhancing the prediction of instantaneous boundary turbulence in other wall-bounded flows. Finally, the authors outline several avenues for future research to further refine the model and broaden its applicability. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor George Constantinescu. We investigate the Hofstadter model featuring time-reversal violation via a complex next-nearest-neighbor hopping term. At a specific flux value, $ \Phi = \Phi_0/2$, the system enters a Weyl semimetal phase characterized by two Weyl nodes situated at the Brillouin zone boundaries. By applying a uniform electric field, these nodes shift away from the boundaries along the field direction within the Brillouin zone. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the chiral anomaly manifests as a non-Ohmic current response to the applied electric field. Finally, we examine the stability of the Weyl nodes against perturbations that restore time-reversal symmetry. This framework offers a promising avenue for exploring topological phenomena in artificial lattice systems. Our findings may be realized in various platforms, including superconducting qubit arrays, photonic circuits, and electronic circuits. Additionally, we propose a potential realization using a quantum Hall bar constructed from a two-dimensional electron gas. In this setup, the Hofstadler model is simulated by applying a perpendicular magnetic field to the quantum Hall bar, while the complex hopping term is implemented through a gate voltage applied along a specific direction. By adjusting the gate voltage, the Weyl nodes can be displaced from the Brillouin zone boundaries. This proposal could enable the observation of the chiral anomaly in a quantum Hall bar under a tilted electric field. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of detecting the chiral anomaly through shot noise measurements. Our results may contribute to the realization of topological quantum computing. We introduce a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna designed to convert standard light sources into highly efficient, bright, and unidirectional emitters. This device utilizes a silicon nanopillar integrated with a gold nanosphere to achieve dielectric-plasmonic coupling. The silicon pillar functions as a waveguide, directing incident light into the nanosphere to excite localized surface plasmons. This hybrid plasmonic-dielectric structure generates a strongly confined electromagnetic field at the nanopillar's base, which acts as the primary source of light emission. By adjusting the nanosphere's dimensions, we can precisely control the emission wavelength and directionality. This approach offers a promising pathway for developing new types of unidirectional light sources. Furthermore, the design is compatible with existing silicon photonics technology, making it ideal for integration into photonic circuits. We anticipate that this technology will enable the creation of novel light sources, such as unidirectional LEDs, laser diodes, and laser sources, specifically tailored for silicon photonic applications. Additionally, the ability to control the emission direction of these sources could significantly enhance the performance of various photonic devices. This study investigates the electronic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) using first-principles calculations. We examine how Mn adatoms influence the Dirac cone, band structure, and magnetic behavior of the system. Results indicate that the Dirac cone is suppressed by the adatoms, with the resulting band gap varying based on the configuration. Specifically, a single Mn atom induces a band gap of 0.12 eV, while three co-planar Mn atoms produce a gap of 0.24 eV. Furthermore, the magnetic moments of the Mn atoms are found to be 3.0, 2.5, and 2.0 Bohr magnetons for one, two, and three co-planar atoms, respectively. Finally, the magnetic coupling between the Mn atoms is determined to be antiferromagnetic. These findings suggest that the system holds promise for spintronic applications. Additionally, the research explores the impact of Mn atom positions on the system's electronic characteristics. Finally, we analyze the stability of various configurations by calculating the binding energy per atom. Overall, this study provides a foundation for designing spintronic devices. Multi-label text classification involves assigning multiple categories to a single document, a task that often falters when certain categories are scarce, resulting in imbalanced datasets. This study evaluates various oversampling techniques to address this issue. We introduce a novel oversampling method that integrates multiple strategies, including back-translation. Our findings indicate that combining these approaches yields superior performance compared to individual methods. This study examines the interrelationships between regional news coverage of COVID-19, along with corresponding case counts, fatalities, and viewership metrics. Utilizing data from the NewsD dataset, which tracks over 1,000 U.S. news outlets, the analysis covers the period from March 15 to May 15, 2020. By applying a dynamic factor model, the research identifies and evaluates the correlations among these variables. The findings indicate that coverage volume and audience engagement are positively correlated, whereas COVID-19 case and death rates exhibit only weak or no correlation with either. Furthermore, the study observes that while coverage and audience levels fluctuate in tandem, these fluctuations lag behind changes in case and death rates. These results offer valuable insights for regional news organizations aiming to balance public interest with audience demands during a pandemic. Additionally, the methodology employed is applicable to other contexts involving large volumes of time-series data. The code utilized for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub.

We introduce a straightforward criterion for determining the minimum number of basis functions required to ensure conservation. Additionally, we propose a technique to enhance angular momentum precision without increasing the count of basis functions. These developments are applicable to a broad spectrum of simulations. The methodology is validated using angular momentum states up to $l=100$, and the code is made available for public use. This study examines the transmission of polarization from an initial proton to a final proton during elastic scattering, a mechanism that could enable the extraction of the proton's electric polarizability. The analysis demonstrates that maximizing polarizability sensitivity requires a specific kinematic configuration: an unpolarized electron beam striking a polarized proton beam, with the scattered electron detected at 90 degrees relative to the beam axis. Furthermore, the electron scattering angle is shown to be critical for enhancing sensitivity to polarizability effects. These findings are derived using the complete one-loop $O(\alpha)$ QED and QCD amplitudes for the $e \vec{p} \to e \vec{p}$ process, alongside the corresponding optical theorem sum rule for the proton form factor $G_Q$. The results are presented in a model-independent framework, with explicit calculations provided for the proton as a Dirac fermion. Additionally, the study explores the potential for detecting polarizability effects in the $e \vec{n} \to e \vec{n}$ reaction. Finally, the paper outlines the necessary experimental conditions and achievable precision levels required to observe these effects.

We introduce a digital model for an alkaline spin maser operating on a chip, which functions as a maser with digital control capabilities. This device utilizes a collection of atoms that can be prepared in any desired quantum state via laser excitation. We demonstrate that the maser's gain can be enhanced by preparing the atoms in a squeezed state. Furthermore, we show that the atomic ensemble can be manipulated to function as a quantum memory for maser photons. Our proposed device is compatible with existing technology and could significantly advance maser research. We expect that the novel capabilities of this digital spin maser will inspire both experimental and theoretical investigations. Finally, we highlight that the ensemble of alkaline atoms serves as a versatile platform for exploring various quantum technologies. Specifically, we illustrate that the atoms can be prepared in entangled states using a straightforward protocol. Additionally, we show that the ensemble can act as a quantum interface between optical and microwave domains, a critical component for quantum communication. We anticipate that alkaline atom ensembles will become a fundamental resource for quantum technology. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the model of the digital alkaline spin maser; Section 3 examines maser gain within this framework; Section 4 addresses the use of the atom ensemble as a quantum memory for maser photons; Section 5 examines the ensemble as a quantum resource; and Section 6 provides concluding remarks. In 2018, B. Mohar and C. S. Woodall introduced the concept of thick graphs, which serve as a discrete counterpart to Riemann surfaces. They demonstrated that determining the genus of a thick graph is an NP-hard problem. This paper presents the first method for estimating the genus of a thick graph with an absolute error of no more than 1, proving the method's polynomial runtime. Additionally, the authors propose several conjectures and outline potential future research directions. As an application, the paper calculates the genus for all thick graphs where the number of edges does not exceed 12. This paper introduces a randomized Newton approach for convex optimization within a multi-agent framework. In this setup, a network of agents collaborates to minimize a sum of individual cost functions, where each agent knows only its own function and communicates with neighbors. The proposed algorithm enables each agent to compute a Newton step for its specific cost function using only local data and information exchanged with neighboring agents. Theoretically, the method demonstrates that the expected decrease in the function value is proportional to the current function curvature. Numerical simulations are provided to validate these theoretical findings. Additionally, the paper investigates the convergence properties of the algorithm and its variants under assumptions of non-smoothness and non-convexity. Finally, the agent-based nature of the algorithm is highlighted as a significant advantage for distributed applications. The study concludes by outlining potential future research directions. This work is situated in the fields of multi-agent systems, distributed optimization, and convex optimization. Keywords include multi-agent systems, distributed optimization, and convex optimization. This research examines the efficacy of transfer learning in identifying hate speech within Hindi and Bengali languages. We gathered a novel dataset of 1,000 Bengali comments, which we annotated to create a balanced collection of 500 offensive and 500 non-offensive statements. Following the training of a BERT model on this new dataset, we evaluated its performance as both a monolingual system and through cross-lingual transfer from English to the two Indian languages. The study demonstrates that transfer learning yields superior results compared to models trained exclusively on Hindi or Bengali data. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the experimental outcomes, offering insights into the advantages and limitations of transfer learning applied to hate speech detection. Our findings indicate that while transfer learning enhances performance, it also introduces certain challenges. Time projection chambers (TPCs) utilizing gas detectors as ionization media offer the potential for high-resolution recoil energy measurement. This paper outlines the design and performance of TPCs equipped with multi-gap micro-mesh (MG-Mu) detectors, which deliver low-noise, high-precision charge and timing data. We demonstrate that these systems can resolve individual electron drift times with a precision of 100 ps, enabling the reconstruction of drift trajectories for ionization electrons. This capability allows for precise position determination and the measurement of ionization charge. We illustrate these techniques through examples from a prototype TPC designed for the DARWIN dark matter direct detection experiment. Furthermore, we show that the ratio of measured to expected charge can serve as a powerful discriminator against non-nuclear recoil backgrounds, such as electrons or gamma rays. Finally, we discuss how these methods can be applied to analyze the full three-dimensional trajectory of a dark matter candidate, thereby enhancing sensitivity to such events. These approaches are applicable to a wide range of TPC technologies, including those employing Xe, Ar, or other noble gases. The techniques described here are currently being implemented in the DARWIN TPCs, which are under construction at the European Spallation Source. Additionally, we explore how these methods can be adapted for TPCs utilizing non-noble gases. Machine learning is increasingly being utilized to forecast human performance and behavior. Nevertheless, the deployment of machine learning to forecast human outcomes raises significant ethical concerns regarding its potential impact on human decision-making. This study examines the ethical implications of applying machine learning to predict commercial driver performance. We developed a novel framework for specialist moderation, where an application expert reviews machine outputs to mitigate bias and ensure fairness. This framework incorporates a new metric for evaluating the fairness of moderating machine outputs, defined as the difference between the false negative rate and the false positive rate. Using a dataset of over 10 million trips from more than 1,000 drivers, we demonstrate that specialist moderation can enhance fairness. Our findings indicate that when a machine identifies a driver as high-risk, the specialist typically lowers the risk classification, and conversely, when a driver is deemed low-risk, the specialist often elevates the classification. These results suggest that specialist moderation can significantly influence commercial driving outcomes. Furthermore, we show that our fairness measure effectively captures the effects of moderation, offering a practical tool for specialists to moderate machine outputs with a specific fairness objective. This work introduces a new approach to ethical machine learning that empowers specialists to actively moderate predictions, thereby reducing bias and improving fairness. We believe this framework will be valuable for a wide range of applications involving the prediction of human behavior. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/EquitableML/CommercialDriving. This paper details the findings of a systematic assessment of over 100 methods designed to identify out-of-vocabulary (OOV) or out-of lexicon (OOlX) words. We evaluated these approaches across three distinct tasks: OOlX word segmentation, OOlX word morphological analysis, and OOlX word machine translation. The experiments covered a broad spectrum of techniques, ranging from traditional to state-of-the-art, and were conducted using three OOlX OOV corpora. Our results indicate that methods based on neural networks and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) achieve the highest accuracy. Furthermore, we found that OOlX word morphological analysis is the most challenging of the three tasks, while OOlX word machine translation is the easiest. Finally, we offer several recommendations for future research in this domain. This study represents the inaugural effort to comprehensively compare various algorithms for handling OOlX OOV words. This paper examines the temporal dynamics of the "hot hand" phenomenon in sports, specifically within the NBA. By analyzing shooting patterns across various game contexts, we identify distinct time scales that govern these statistical fluctuations. Our findings indicate that, when accounting for game-specific variables, shooting performance exhibits significant temporal correlation over short intervals. Conversely, this correlation diminishes or disappears at longer intervals. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the observed short-term correlations are not merely artifacts of regression to the mean but instead reflect a genuine "hot hand" effect. These insights are derived from a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,000 games featuring 20 teams and 420 players. The study's methodology and conclusions are broadly applicable to other domains, such as the card game Blackjack. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that understanding the specific time scales of performance is crucial for making informed decisions in both sports strategy and casino operations. This study investigates the impact of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and exchange fields on the transport properties of armchair graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs) connected to ferromagnetic leads, with gate voltage serving as a key tuning parameter. Our findings indicate that while both SOC and exchange fields can suppress conductance, only the exchange field enables regulatable spin-polarized transport. Specifically, conductance is predicted to remain robust in the presence of SOC alone, whereas it is significantly reduced when both SOC and an exchange field are applied. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the exchange field can be tuned to achieve a transition from a metallic to an insulating state, a mechanism that operates exclusively through a Fano resonance. This tunable insulating state is accessible only within a specific range of backgate voltages. Additionally, we observe that the tunable insulating state induced by SOC and an exchange field is primarily driven by a level crossing between the two spin channels. Finally, we note that the tunable insulating state is more readily achieved in wider AGNRs. These results suggest that incorporating exchange fields alongside SOC is an effective strategy for spin manipulation in graphene-based spintronic devices. Additionally, our findings offer a potential pathway to realize a graphene-based spin transistor. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11374147). This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for the weak convergence of sequences of functions mapping from a compact subset $K$ of a Hausdorff topological space into a Banach space ordered by a regular, normal cone. These convergence results apply to sequences of mildly nonlinear monotonic operators and, through specific instances, yield versions of Korovkin's theorem and theorems by Gasanov, Khan, and Puri regarding vector-valued functions. Additionally, the paper examines strong convergence and investigates certain applications, including a generalization of the Chung–Szász theorem concerning Poisson-Charlier polynomials. Furthermore, it presents a generalization of a theorem by Mursaleen and Natesan regarding Walsh series, as well as a generalization of Gasanov's theorem regarding Fourier-Dirichlet series. Finally, the work includes a generalization of a theorem by Mursaleen and Natesan concerning Lagrange interpolation series. In each application, the original theorems are recovered as particular cases. The findings are also extended to mappings defined on open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Notably, the weak convergence theorems for sequences of monotonic operators are applied to establish strong convergence results for sequences of nonlinear operators possessing specific compactness properties. Finally, the authors propose several open problems for future research. This study examines the production of optical hadrons, identified as $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ mesons, in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=200$ GeV. The analysis employs a novel theoretical framework that integrates the dynamics of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) with a hadron transport model. By incorporating a hadron transport component, the model accounts for the regeneration of optical hadrons through charm-anticharm quark pair rescattering within the QGP. The results indicate that this mechanism successfully explains the experimentally observed enhancement in the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$) for both $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ mesons. Furthermore, the framework is applied to isobar collisions, revealing that the ratio of $R_{AA}$ between the two isobar species provides a sensitive probe of the QGP's transport properties. These findings suggest that future measurements of $R_{AA}$ for optical hadrons could serve as a valuable tool for constraining the transport coefficients of the QGP. Finally, the work explores the potential of utilizing optical hadrons as observables to investigate the transport characteristics of the QGP. This study introduces a new approach called the Outside Complicated Scaling (OCS) method, designed to derive scaling laws for atoms and molecules situated in intense direct-current (DC) fields. By applying OCS, researchers can efficiently calculate the scaling laws governing various physical properties of these systems. The method's validity is confirmed through its ability to reproduce scaling laws previously established by other techniques. Furthermore, OCS is demonstrated to be effective for systems involving multiple electrons and multiple atoms or molecules. Its efficiency is illustrated by the rapid computation of DC ionization rates for a diatomic molecule, which is completed in approximately 10 seconds. These findings indicate that the OCS method serves as a valuable tool for investigating the strong-field ionization of atoms and molecules within strong DC regions. Additionally, the paper outlines the potential for extending the OCS framework to alternating-current (AC) environments. Finally, the study discusses the relationship between the OCS method and the adiabatic approximation. We introduce a novel class of chiral optical chambers characterized by unilateral coupling between their constituent modes. These chambers can be constructed using materials exhibiting unilateral optical gain and unilateral optical depth. We explore the optical properties of such structures, demonstrating that they support both nonreciprocal unidirectional propagation and nonreciprocal reflection. Furthermore, we outline specific material requirements and propose potential implementations utilizing optical gain media. Specifically, the proposed unilateral propagation devices offer a pathway to miniaturize optical isolators, while unilateral reflection devices can function as nonreciprocal mirrors. This paper introduces GUIDES, a new open-source software framework designed to manage geospatial data across multiple resolutions. Its primary objective is to enable the seamless exchange of data between different resolutions, thereby eliminating the need for custom, resolution-specific software. We introduce a method to investigate the temperature, motion state distributions, and heating rates of a two-dimensional Coulomb crystal within an ion trap. By preparing a non-equilibrium mode temperature in a transverse collective excitation and preparing qubits in the $|0\rangle$ state, we excite a qubit-mode coupling that drives spin decay. This decay serves as a probe for the mode temperature, motion state distributions, and heating speeds. This approach enables the study of non-equilibrium ion lattices and their relaxation dynamics. We demonstrate this technique using a qubit-excited longitudinal phonon mode in a linear chain of $^{171}$Yb$^{+}$ ions. We present K-band observations of 10 nearby galaxies, including the Centaurus A radio galaxy, conducted using the Sardinia Radio Telescope. This study investigates the entropy changes in ammonium sulfate ($\rm NH_4HSO_4$) during its molecular caloric effect. By combining calorimetric data with first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the entropy variation induced by an electric field is primarily driven by alterations in vibrational entropy. This finding contradicts the conventional view that such entropy changes stem from modifications in configurational entropy. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that $\rm NH_4HSO_4$ exhibits a ferroelectric caloric effect, a conclusion supported by the observation of a spontaneous polarization change under an alternating electric field. These results establish a new paradigm for molecular caloric materials, suggesting that vibrational entropy plays a more significant role than previously believed. Additionally, our methodology is broadly applicable to investigating entropy changes in various materials. Finally, we propose that the configurational entropy of $\rm NH_4HSO_4$ is likely negative, a hypothesis that could be experimentally verified by examining the temperature dependence of the entropy change. These insights may also aid in the discovery of novel molecular caloric materials. Our findings are corroborated by the case of lead zirconate titanate, where the entropy change resulting from an electric field is predominantly attributable to vibrational entropy. This suggests that the entropy change in ferroelectrics is generally dominated by vibrational entropy, a perspective that could guide the design of advanced ferroelectric materials. Our work also underscores the necessity of employing first-principles calculations to explore the entropy changes in caloric materials. Finally, our results may contribute to the development of new materials for vibrational entropy engineering. This study investigates the link between specific RL model parameters and the activity of neurons in the midbrain, a region pivotal to decision-making. We developed a novel, interpretable neural encoding framework that quantifies how midbrain neurons represent various components of a decision, including expected rewards, action selection, and learning mechanisms. Applying this framework to data from a probabilistic learning task, we identified distinct neural signals corresponding to both suboptimal and characteristic RL strategies. Furthermore, we observed that the magnitude of these neural representations correlates with individual behavioral performance. These findings suggest that the midbrain encodes distinct signals for different RL mechanisms, with the strength of these signals varying according to task difficulty. Consequently, our results support the hypothesis that the midbrain plays a critical role in RL, potentially by signaling prediction errors to facilitate learning. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our approach for interpreting neural data within the context of RL. We investigate how electron outflow and nonlocality influence gap-plasmons as the interval between two identical semi-infinite jellium slabs approaches zero. The analysis reveals that these effects can be modeled by substituting the bulk plasma frequency with an effective frequency that varies with the wave vector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the wave-vector dependence of this effective plasma frequency can be accurately approximated by a simple expression derived from the electron density at the critical point of the jellium model. Finally, we show that this formulation successfully predicts the wave-vector dependence of the resonance frequency for gap-plasmons. Additionally, we examine the impact of these factors on the damping of gap-plasmons. Our findings indicate that, in the limit of vanishing intervals, both bulk and surface Landau damping become independent of the wave vector. However, the outflow of electrons from the interface into the gap results in enhanced Landau damping, which is particularly significant at short wavelengths. Ultimately, we conclude that, under these conditions, gap-plasmons behave as wave packets rather than plane waves. This conclusion is supported by an analysis of the group velocity and the spatial decay of the associated evanescent fields. Finally, we provide numerical results for gold, silver, and aluminum. Our results for gold and silver align well with existing experimental data. In contrast, for aluminum, the agreement is less satisfactory, primarily due to the presence of interband transitions, which are not accounted for in our theoretical framework. Nevertheless, the overall agreement remains reasonable. We also note that the theoretical model for gap-plasmons in aluminum has been validated for other systems, such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides. Consequently, we anticipate that this model will prove valuable for future experimental investigations. To facilitate this, we have provided a Mathematica notebook containing the relevant code. Digital health records (DHRs) are essential for healthcare, yet their unstructured nature and data silos hinder effective analysis. While recent methods have attempted to model these records using natural language processing, they often overlook the complex relationships between different record types. To address this, we introduce DSGNN, a diverse similarity graph neural network designed to learn representations of digital health records. DSGNN constructs a graph where nodes represent individual health records and edges capture diverse similarities between them. We validate this approach using a disease classification task, demonstrating that it surpasses baseline models. Our findings indicate that incorporating diverse similarity information significantly enhances the model's performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/DSGNN. This study examines the electric double layer (EDL) adjacent to a charged soft interface within an electrolyte solution. The interface's surface charge is modeled as a Gaussian chain of dipoles, while the solution is treated as a dielectric continuum. We introduce a novel approach to determine the EDL structure, accounting for the dielectric properties of both the interface and the surrounding solution. Our findings indicate that solvent polarization significantly influences the EDL, particularly when the interface is highly polarizable. Furthermore, we observe that the potential decays exponentially as one moves away from the interface into the bulk solution. These results offer valuable insights for designing soft materials with tailored interfacial characteristics. Additionally, the proposed methodology is applicable to a broader range of soft materials. Finally, our theoretical framework is validated through comparison with existing experimental data. Software specifications are essential for developing and maintaining software systems. However, in many organizations, these documents are often absent, outdated, or fail to capture the system's current state. Consequently, developers frequently waste significant time and resources searching for or creating these specifications from scratch. This paper introduces an approach that automatically generates accurate and up-to-date specifications by analyzing unorganized texts, such as commit messages. We validated this method using a dataset of 1.5 million Java projects, demonstrating that the resulting specifications are both correct and current. Furthermore, we conducted a user study to evaluate the approach's usability, which yielded positive outcomes. Our method is accessible at https://github.com/CodeAsSpecs/codeasperts. The source code and data utilized in this study can be found at https://github.com/CodeAsSpecs/codeasperts-data. Our findings indicate that unorganized texts are a valuable resource for automatically deriving specifications, and our approach effectively leverages this resource to produce precise and current documents. Additionally, the approach is extensible to other unorganized texts, such as issue descriptions. We anticipate that this method will be particularly beneficial for large software systems, where specifications are critical for development and maintenance, and where the volume of unorganized texts is substantial. Ultimately, we expect our approach to significantly reduce the time and effort required to create accurate and up-to-date specifications. This paper is an extended version of [1].
